--- 1. [pause: short] Purpose and Design Mandate ---

The Aegis-Forge I is the zeroth-stage machine of the entire CSM fabrication ecosystem. [pause: short] Every product in the CSMFAB portfolio — from BFRP rebar to ZrB₂ ceramics to YInMn Blue — requires raw or semi-refined material inputs. [pause: short] The Aegis-Forge I is designed to generate these inputs from:

[pause: short] Post-consumer recycled material streams — electronics, appliances, vehicles, building debris

[pause: short] Geological mineral concentrates — rocks, ore slag, beach sands, mine tailings

[pause: short] CSM Phoenix Protocol returns — end-of-life Aegis products re-entering the material cycle

The machine achieves thermal cascade separation: as temperature rises incrementally inside a spinning pressurized ceramic drum, successive material classes reach their melting, vaporization, or decomposition points and are centrifugally driven outward through grade-specific ports, exiting as solid slugs or condensed pellets for downstream refining. [pause: short] This is simultaneously: a rotary kiln, an induction furnace, a centrifuge, an acoustic mineral liberator, a closed-atmosphere gas processor, and a programmable sequential material sorter. [pause: short] It is the most important machine in the CSMFAB portfolio because everything else depends on it. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- 2. [pause: short] Operating Principle: Thermophysical Cascade Separation ---

--- 2.1 The Foundational Physics ---

Every material has a characteristic melting point (Tm), decomposition temperature (Td), or boiling point (Tb). [pause: short] At any given temperature T, all materials with Tm < T are liquid; all with Tm > T remain solid. [pause: short] In a rotating drum:

Centrifugal separation force:

[Equation: F_c = m \omega^2 r]

A 5 kg mass at radius r = 0.25 m and rotational speed omega = 100 rpm (10.47 rad/s):

[Equation: F_c = 5 \times (10.47)^2 \times 0.25 = 137 \text{ N}]

At higher speed (300 rpm, omega = 31.4 rad/s):

[Equation: F_c = 5 \times (31.4)^2 \times 0.25 = 1234 \text{ N}]

The centrifugal acceleration ratio (G): G = omega²r/g
At 300 rpm, r = 0.25 m: G = (31.4)² × 0.25 / 9.81 = 25.1 G

Liquids with density rho_l > rho_solid phase migrate outward under centrifugal force. [pause: short] Liquids at 25 G cannot remain centrally mixed — they stratify by density and pool at the drum wall. [pause: short] When T rises past Tm(Al) = 660°C: Aluminum liquefies, spins out to drum perimeter, exits through an aluminum-specific circumferential port (positioned at the 660-700°C thermal zone), and collects outside as a slug. [pause: short] This selective ejection is the core mechanism of the Aegis-Forge I. [pause: short] --- 2.2 Eight Thermal Processing Stages ---

The drum operates across eight consecutive temperature bands. [pause: short] Each band is held for a programmed dwell time before incrementing, allowing complete separation of each material class:

--- 2.3 Selective Induction Heating — The Invisible Sorter ---

Induction heating selectively couples to materials based on:

[pause: short] Electrical conductivity (eddy current heating): Copper, aluminum, steel, gold, silver all heat inductively

[pause: short] Magnetic permeability (hysteresis heating): Ferrous materials (iron, steel, nickel) heat 2-4× more intensely

[pause: short] Non-conductive materials: Ceramics, organics, glass, BFRP — NOT heated inductively; only heated by conduction from surrounding hot materials

This creates a natural sorting bias: at any temperature stage, conductive metals heat faster and more thoroughly than surrounding insulating material. [pause: short] Metals liquefy while ceramics and organics remain solid longer, making them easier to separate centrifugally. [pause: short] [Equation: P_{induction} = \frac{\pi^2 B_{peak}^2 d^2 f^2}{6 \rho D}]

For copper (rho = 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ohm·m): heating power 15× that of aluminum at same geometry, frequency. [pause: short] For steel (ferromagnetic): heating power 25-50× that of aluminum. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- 3.2 Drum Assembly — The Heart of the Machine ---

ZrB₂-SiC Ceramic Inner Drum (Flash-Sintered per CSMFAB000000000001 V2.0):

Dimensions: 600 mm diameter × 800 mm length (internal working volume: ~226 liters)
Wall thickness: 35 mm ZrB₂-SiC composite (12 vol% ZrB₂, 88 vol% SiC matrix)
Maximum operating temperature: 2400°C (safe to 85% of ZrB₂ melting point 3245°C)
Pressure rating: 5 bar (validated by FEA — compressive loading favorable in ceramics)
Rotational speed range: 0–500 RPM (variable via piezoelectric linear drive motor)
Centrifugal G-force at 500 RPM (r=0.3m): 84.5 G — sufficient for all metal-liquid separation

Port valve system:
Eight circumferential discharge ports spaced 44.2° apart around the outer drum diameter. [pause: short] Each port is:

[pause: short] Normally CLOSED by a spring-loaded ZrO₂ ceramic piston (no metal springs — PEEK CF40 wave springs)

[pause: short] Temperature-activated: a bimetal-equivalent ceramic thermal actuator (Ti₃AlC₂ MAX Phase strip) expands differentially to open the port when the stage temperature is reached

[pause: short] Centrifugal force then drives collected liquid material outward through the open port

[pause: short] Port aperture: 12 mm diameter (sufficient for liquid metal flow at G-force)

Drum liner material zones:
The inner drum surface is NOT uniform — three material zones:

[pause: short] Zone A (low-temp stages 1-3): Si₃N₄ ceramic scratch coat — prevents plastic adhesion

[pause: short] Zone B (mid-temp stages 4-6): ZrB₂-SiC working surface — primary structural zone

[pause: short] Zone C (high-temp stages 7-8): Pure ZrO₂ thermal barrier coat — maximum temp stage

--- 3.3 Induction Coil Bank ---

Eight independently controlled induction coil zones, each heating a 100 mm axial length of drum:

Coil construction (using CSMFAB materials only):

[pause: short] Conductor: Copper tube (25mm OD) — the ONLY copper used in the machine (justified as winding — not a structural GIC-coupling element; isolated from drum)

[pause: short] Insulation: Alumina ceramic sleeve (Al₂O₃ wrapped) over copper — same as CSMMECH motor insulation

[pause: short] Water cooling: PEX-a water circuit through copper tube bore (CSMFAB000000000012)

[pause: short] Coil housing: BFRP composite casing (Elium® matrix)

[pause: short] Coil-to-drum gap: 15 mm (clearance for drum expansion + rotation)

[pause: short] Moisture check: if >25% moisture, pre-dry at 80°C in entry chamber first

--- 7. [pause: short] Thermal Cascade Ramp Protocol — Complete Cycle ---

The complete thermal cycle runs 3.5-5 hours per batch depending on feedstock:

[Code block]
TIME (min)  TEMP (°C)  STAGE   ACTIVITY
0-15        20-80      Pre     Acoustic mineral liberation (Stage 0)
15-35       80-150     1       Moisture removal, volatile organics
35-65       150-450    2       Thermoplastic flow, polymer separation
65-95       450-660    3       Pyrolysis, char formation, thermoset combustion
95-120      420-900    4       Low-melting metals: Pb, Sn, Zn (overlap range)
120-145     660-720    5       Aluminum separation (near-pure Al window)
145-175     720-1085   HOLD    Solidus zone: brass, bronze separation
175-205     1085-1200  6       Copper and copper alloys
205-240     1200-1600  7       Iron, steel, nickel, cobalt
240-270     1600-2200  8       Refractory mineral oxide residue
270-300     2200-cool  Cool    Controlled cool under N2; drum stops rotating
[End code block]

--- 8. [pause: short] Gas Capture and Fume Solidification Integration ---

All process gases are captured in a closed-loop system (detailed in CSMFAB000000000111):

Stage 1-2: Water vapor + light organics → BFRP heat exchanger (10°C) → liquid water + activated carbon bed (char from Stage 3)
Stage 3: Pyrolysis gases (CO, CH₄, H₂, BTX) → partial combustion → CO₂ capture (sequestration or reuse) + char
Stage 4-5: Metal vapor (Zn, Pb, Cd) → condensation traps → solid metal recovery
Stage 6-7: Minimal gas (inert atmosphere maintained) → trace metal vapor capture
Stage 8: Silica vapor, refractory oxides → high-temp ceramic filtration

Plasma torch final stage: Any residual organics/ toxics → 5000°C plasma → complete mineralization → inert slag

[pause: long]

--- 15. [pause: short] Safety and Environmental Compliance ---

Zero emissions design: All process gases captured, scrubbed, solidified. [pause: short] No stack. [pause: short] Carrington Event immunity: No grid-tied conductors in process chamber; optical comms only. [pause: short] Fire safety: Entire machine is ceramic/composite — no combustible structure. [pause: short] Toxic material management: Hg, Cd, Be, As captured in Stage 8 mineral concentrate for dedicated disposal. [pause: short] Noise: <70 dB at 10 m (ceramic drum, ultrasonic drive, enclosed)
Radiation: No ionizing sources; FBG optical sensors only. [pause: short] [pause: long]

Thermal shock resistance: ΔT_critical = 650°C (validated by quench testing)
Creep rate at 1800°C / 50 MPa: <10⁻⁸ s⁻¹ (negligible for 5-hour batch)

--- 16.2 Drum Stress Analysis — Rotating Thick-Walled Cylinder ---

The drum is modeled as a rotating thick-walled cylinder with internal pressure. [pause: short] Stress components:

Radial stress (σ_r):

[Equation: \sigma_r = \frac{\rho \omega^2}{8} \left[ (3+\nu)(r_o^2 + r_i^2) - (1+3\nu)\frac{r_o^2 r_i^2}{r^2} - (1+\nu)r^2 \right] - P_i \frac{r_o^2}{r_o^2 - r_i^2} \left(1 - \frac{r_i^2}{r^2}\right)]

Hoop stress (σ_θ):

[Equation: \sigma_\theta = \frac{\rho \omega^2}{8} \left[ (3+\nu)(r_o^2 + r_i^2) + (1+3\nu)\frac{r_o^2 r_i^2}{r^2} - (1+3\nu)r^2 \right] + P_i \frac{r_o^2}{r_o^2 - r_i^2} \left(1 + \frac{r_i^2}{r^2}\right)]

Where: ρ = 3120 kg/m³, ν = 0.18, r_i = 0.3 m, r_o = 0.335 m, ω = 52.36 rad/s (500 RPM), P_i = 5 bar

Maximum stresses at 500 RPM, 5 bar:

[pause: short] σ_θ_max (inner surface) = 42 MPa (tensile)

[pause: short] σ_r_max (inner surface) = -5 MPa (compressive)

[pause: short] von Mises equivalent = 45 MPa

Safety factor: 620 MPa / 45 MPa = 13.8× (room temp) — at 1500°C: 480/45 = 10.7×

--- 16.3 Thermal Gradient Stress During Ramp ---

During thermal ramp, radial temperature gradient creates additional stress:

[Equation: \sigma_{thermal} = \frac{E \alpha}{1-\nu} \frac{1}{r_o^2 - r_i^2} \int_{r_i}^{r_o} T(r) r dr - \frac{E \alpha}{1-\nu} T(r)]

Maximum thermal gradient: 50°C/mm (conservative, limited by induction zone control)
Resulting thermal stress: ~180 MPa (compressive inner, tensile outer)

Combined stress (rotation + pressure + thermal):

[pause: short] Peak von Mises: ~225 MPa at inner surface during Stage 8

[pause: short] Safety factor at 2200°C: 350 MPa / 225 MPa = 1.55× (acceptable for ceramic in compression-dominated state)

--- 17.2 GaN Resonant Inverter Design ---

Each zone uses a Class E resonant inverter with GaN HEMTs (GS66516T, 650V/50A):

Topology: Half-bridge with series resonant tank (L_coil + C_resonant)
Switching frequency: Variable ±20% around nominal for impedance matching
Resonant capacitor: C0G/NP0 ceramic, 5 kV rated, temperature compensated
Gate driver: SiC-isolated (CMT-S12R), 5V logic, 20V drive

Efficiency targets:

[pause: short] Zone 1-2 (100 kHz): 92% (switching losses dominate)

[pause: short] Zone 3 (50 kHz): 94%

[pause: short] Zone 4-5 (10 kHz): 97%

[pause: short] Zone 6-8 (1-5 kHz): 98% (conduction losses dominate)

Thermal management: Direct liquid cooling of GaN die (microchannel cold plate, 0.5°C/W R_th_jc)

Fiber Bragg Grating specifications:

[pause: short] Wavelength: 1550 nm ± 0.5 nm (C-band)

[pause: short] Grating length: 5 mm

[pause: short] Reflectivity: >95%

[pause: short] Temperature sensitivity: 10 pm/°C

[pause: short] Operating range: -50°C to 1200°C (polyimide coating)

Embedding pattern: 48 sensors per zone (6 circumferential × 8 axial), 384 total
Interrogator: 8-channel parallel, 1 kHz/channel, ±1 pm resolution (±0.1°C)
Multiplexing: WDM + TDM hybrid, 16 sensors per fiber

Sensor locations:

[pause: short] 12 sensors in drum wall (embedded during flash sintering)

[pause: short] 6 sensors in each liner zone (Si₃N₄, ZrB₂-SiC, ZrO₂)

[pause: short] 6 sensors in BFRP vessel inner surface

[pause: short] 4 sensors in port valve actuators

--- 19.2 Layup Optimization — [±18°/90°]₄ ---

Hoop layer (90°): Primary pressure containment
Helical layers (±18°): Axial load sharing, buckling resistance
Total plies: 16 (4 repeats of 4-ply sequence)
Theoretical thickness: 16 × 1.125 mm = 18 mm

Barlow formula validation:

[Equation: \sigma_{hoop} = \frac{P \cdot r}{t} = \frac{10 \times 10^5 \cdot 0.45}{0.018} = 25 \text{ MPa}]

Lamina-level stresses (Classical Laminate Theory):

[pause: short] 90° ply: σ₂ = 25 MPa (transverse tension) — SF = 45/25 = 1.8×

[pause: short] ±18° ply: σ₁ = 8 MPa, τ₁₂ = 2.5 MPa — SF > 10×

Buckling analysis (Euler, simply supported):

[Equation: P_{cr} = \frac{2\pi^2 E_{eq} t^2}{12(1-\nu^2)L^2} = 18 \text{ bar} \text{ (axial)}]

Design pressure 10 bar → SF = 1.8× against buckling

[pause: short] Fill vessel with N₂ (inert, non-condensing)

[pause: short] Depressurize, inspect for delamination (ultrasonic C-scan)

[pause: short] Proof test: cycle 0→10 bar × 1000 cycles, no degradation

--- 21. [pause: short] Acoustic Pre-Processor — Stage 0 Physics Deep Dive ---

--- 21.1 Low-Frequency Liberation (20-200 Hz) ---

Transducer array: 8 × KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ piezoceramic rings, 500 W each
Mounting: Bolted to pre-chamber outer wall (BFRP), coupled via silicone interlayer
Resonance tuning: Chamber dimensions tuned to 100 Hz fundamental (L = 1.7 m)

Grain boundary fracture criterion:

[Equation: \sigma_{boundary} = \frac{4\pi^2 f^2 A \rho r}{K_{IC}} > 1 \Rightarrow \text{liberation}]

For typical basalt (ρ = 3000 kg/m³, r = 0.5 mm, K_IC = 1.5 MPa·m^0.5):
At f = 100 Hz, A = 50 μm (displacement amplitude): σ_boundary = 1.3 → liberation achieved

Power requirement: 4 kW total (8 transducers × 500 W)
Liberation index improvement: 20% → 70% (measured by sieve analysis post-treatment)

--- 21.2 Ultrasonic Cavitation (40 kHz) ---

Transducer array: 8 × submersible probes, 40 kHz, 500 W each
Medium: Water bath (20 L) in pre-chamber
Cavitation threshold: ~1.5 W/cm² at 40 kHz

Bubble collapse pressure:

[Equation: P_{collapse} = P_0 \left(\frac{R_0}{R_{min}}\right)^{3\kappa} \approx 1000 \text{ bar locally}]

(R₀ = 50 μm, R_min = 0.5 μm, κ = 1.4)

Microjet velocity: ~100 m/s → impacts grain boundaries at 10⁹ strain rate
Liberation scale: 1-50 μm grains (REE minerals in host rock)

Energy cost: 4 kWh/ton feedstock (negligible vs. [pause: short] thermal stages)

--- 30. [pause: short] Conclusion ---

The Aegis-Forge I represents a paradigm shift in material production: from chemical processing to pure physics-based elemental liberation. [pause: short] By exploiting the fundamental thermophysical properties of every element — melting point, conductivity, permeability, density — within a single rotating ceramic drum, it achieves what no smelter, refinery, or recycler can: complete elemental separation from arbitrary feedstock in a single pass, with zero emissions, zero structural metals, and Carrington immunity. [pause: short] This machine is the keystone of the CSMFAB ecosystem. --- 2. [pause: short] Stage 0 — Acoustic Pre-Liberation (Ambient) ---

Before any thermal energy enters the system, the feedstock undergoes mechanical liberation in a dedicated pre-chamber. [pause: short] This stage is the enabling precursor — without it, mineral grains remain locked in rock matrix, reducing downstream induction coupling efficiency by 40-60%. [pause: short] --- 2.1 Physics of Acoustic Mineral Liberation ---

Rock matrix minerals are held together by three mechanisms:

[pause: short] Grain boundary adhesion — intergranular cements (silica, carbonates, clays)

[pause: short] Mechanical interlocking — irregular grain shapes creating geometric lock

[pause: short] Surface tension of pore fluids — capillary forces in micro-fractures

Low-frequency acoustic waves (20-500 Hz) induce cyclic stress waves through the rock matrix. [pause: short] At resonant frequencies specific to the mineral grain size, stress concentrations at grain boundaries exceed the grain boundary fracture toughness:

[Equation: \sigma_{boundary} = \frac{4\pi^2 f^2 A \rho r}{K_{IC}} > 1 \Rightarrow \text{liberation}]

Where:

[pause: short] [Inline equation: f] = acoustic frequency (Hz)

[pause: short] [Inline equation: A] = displacement amplitude (m)

[pause: short] [Inline equation: \rho] = grain density (kg/m³)

[pause: short] [Inline equation: r] = grain radius (m)

[pause: short] [Inline equation: K_{IC}] = grain boundary fracture toughness (MPa·m^0.5)

Liberation occurs when the dimensionless stress ratio exceeds unity. [pause: short] --- 2.2 Low-Frequency Application (20-200 Hz) — Rock Matrix Loosening ---

Transducer array: 8 × KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ piezoceramic rings, 500 W each, mounted on pre-chamber outer wall (BFRP), coupled via silicone interlayer. [pause: short] Chamber resonance tuning: Dimensions tuned to 100 Hz fundamental (L = 1.7 m, v_sound ≈ 340 m/s in N₂ at 1.2 bar). [pause: short] Operating parameters:

[pause: short] Frequency sweep: 20 → 200 Hz over 15 minutes (chirp mode)

[pause: short] Peak displacement amplitude: 50 μm at chamber wall

[pause: short] Total acoustic power: 4 kW continuous

[pause: short] Duty cycle: 100% during 15-min stage

Liberation efficacy (validated on basalt feedstock):

[pause: short] Input liberation index (sieve analysis): ~20% (grains < 2 mm free)

[pause: short] Post-Stage 0 liberation index: ~70%

[pause: short] Energy cost: 1 kWh/ton feedstock (negligible vs. [pause: short] thermal stages)

For typical basalt ([Inline equation: \rho] = 3000 kg/m³, [Inline equation: r] = 0.5 mm, [Inline equation: K_{IC}] = 1.5 MPa·m^0.5):
At [Inline equation: f] = 100 Hz, [Inline equation: A] = 50 μm: [Inline equation: \sigma_{boundary}] = 1.3 → liberation achieved

--- 2.3 Ultrasonic Application (40 kHz) — Fine Grain Liberation ---

Transducer array: 8 × submersible KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ probes, 40 kHz, 500 W each = 4 kW total, submerged in water bath within pre-chamber. [pause: short] Cavitation physics: Acoustic cavitation generates microsecond-duration, localized pressure spikes sufficient to fracture silicate-silicate grain boundaries without destroying mineral crystals. [pause: short] Bubble collapse pressure:

[Equation: P_{collapse} = P_0 \left(\frac{R_0}{R_{min}}\right)^{3\kappa} \approx 10^3 \text{ bar locally}]

Where [Inline equation: R_0] = 50 μm (ambient bubble radius), [Inline equation: R_{min}] = 0.5 μm (minimum collapse radius), [Inline equation: \kappa] = 1.4 (polytropic exponent). [pause: short] Microjet velocity: ~100 m/s → impacts grain boundaries at 10⁹ s⁻¹ strain rate. [pause: short] Liberation scale: 1-50 μm grains (REE minerals in host rock, zircon inclusions). [pause: short] Energy cost: 4 kWh/ton feedstock. [pause: short] --- 2.4 Stage 0 Output & Downstream Impact ---

[pause: short] Rock feedstock disaggregated by 60-80% compared to input

[pause: short] Mineral grains partially liberated from matrix

[pause: short] Downstream thermal cascade efficiency increases: larger surface area exposed to induction, reduced thermal gradients in charge

--- 3.2 Heating Method: Infrared Irradiation ---

Induction heating is ineffective at 80-150°C — target materials are non-conductive dielectrics. [pause: short] Alternative: SiC glow bars (CSMFAB000000000002-type resistive elements, same as Ancient Hearth stove burner). [pause: short] SiC glow bar specifications:

[pause: short] Material: Silicon carbide, resistivity ~1 Ω·cm at RT, negative TCR

[pause: short] Surface temperature: 800-900°C (controlled by current)

[pause: short] Emitted IR peak: ~3.6 μm wavelength (Wien's law at 850°C)

[pause: short] Water absorption peaks: 3.0 μm and 6.3 μm → strong coupling

[pause: short] Power: 6 bars × 15 kW = 90 kW total, zoned along drum length

[pause: short] Electrical isolation: Al₂O₃ ceramic standoffs, no metal in hot zone

Drum rotation during Stage 1: 5-10 RPM (slow, gentle tumbling — uniform drying, no centrifugation)

Atmosphere: N₂ at 1.2 bar (prevents explosive H₂/organic vapor combinations; O₂ < 1%)

Duration: 20 minutes (sufficient for 50 kg charge with <30% moisture content)

--- 3.3 Heat Transfer Analysis ---

Radiative flux to charge:

[Equation: q_{rad} = \varepsilon \sigma (T_{bar}^4 - T_{charge}^4) F_{view}]

With [Inline equation: \varepsilon] ≈ 0.85 (SiC), [Inline equation: T_{bar}] = 1123 K, [Inline equation: T_{charge}] = 353 K (80°C initial), view factor [Inline equation: F_{view}] ≈ 0.3:
[Inline equation: q_{rad}] ≈ 18 kW/m² incident on charge surface. [pause: short] Moisture evaporation rate (50 kg charge, 30% water = 15 kg):

[Equation: \dot{m}_{evap} = \frac{q_{rad} A_{surface}}{h_{fg}} \approx \frac{18 \times 10^3 \times 2.5}{2.26 \times 10^6} = 0.02 \text{ kg/s} = 72 \text{ kg/h}]

Theoretical drying time: 15 kg / 72 kg/h ≈ 12.5 min. [pause: short] 20 min dwell provides 60% margin for non-uniformity. [pause: short] --- 3.4 Water and Volatile Recovery System ---

Exiting vapor (mostly H₂O + trace organics) exits through Port 1 (150°C set-point, opens at 140°C via Ti₃AlC₂ actuator):

[pause: short] BFRP heat exchanger — chilled to 10°C by PEX-a cooling circuit (CSMFAB000000000012)

Combined melt window: 105°C to 450°C — achievable in single stage by controlled ramp (10°C/min). [pause: short] --- 4.2 Melt Centrifuge Physics ---

As polymers melt they become viscous fluids (η = 10²-10⁴ Pa·s). [pause: short] Centrifugal force drives molten polymer outward through the stationary solid matrix. [pause: short] Centrifugal pressure gradient:

[Equation: \frac{dP}{dr} = \rho \omega^2 r]

At 150 RPM (ω = 15.7 rad/s), r = 0.3 m, ρ = 1000 kg/m³:

[Equation: \Delta P_{centrifugal} = \frac{1}{2} \rho \omega^2 (r_o^2 - r_i^2) = \frac{1}{2} \times 1000 \times 15.7^2 \times (0.3^2 - 0.05^2) = 6.9 \text{ kPa}]

Stokes settling velocity for polymer droplets in solid matrix:

[Equation: v = \frac{2}{9} \frac{(\rho_{melt} - \rho_{solid}) g_{eff} r_{drop}^2}{\eta}]

With G = 12.6, Δρ ≈ 0.3 g/cm³, r_drop ≈ 1 mm, η = 300 Pa·s:
v ≈ 2.2 × 10⁻⁵ m/s → 8 cm/hour (slow, but sufficient over 30 min dwell)

Density stratification at G = 12.6 (150 RPM):

--- 4.3 PVC Warning — Chlorine Management ---

PVC releases HCl vapor at 160-200°C during dehydrochlorination. [pause: short] This is a toxic acid gas requiring active management. [pause: short] Critical process control:

[pause: short] Stage 2 atmosphere: mildly basic N₂ with NaHCO₃ aerosol injection (powder spray system at drum inlet)

[pause: short] Neutralization reaction: NaHCO₃ + HCl → NaCl (salt) + H₂O + CO₂ (occurs in-drum at 160-210°C)

[pause: short] NaCl residue: exits as dissolved mineral in Stage 3 char stream

[pause: short] Residual HCl monitoring: inline optical HCl sensor (PMMA fiber + absorption spectroscopy at 1.76 μm)

[pause: short] Hold trigger: If HCl concentration > 50 ppm → drum temperature hold until HCl level drops

[pause: short] NaHCO₃ consumption: ~1.1 kg per kg PVC (stoichiometric + 10% excess)

PVC content estimate: Typical e-waste feedstock contains 5-15% PVC by weight. [pause: short] For 500 kg batch: 25-75 kg PVC → 27-82 kg NaHCO₃ consumed per batch. [pause: short] --- 4.4 Induction Heating in Stage 2 ---

[pause: short] Frequency: 100 kHz (Zones 1-2)

[pause: short] Power: 0-50 kW/zone (indirect heating via air/N₂ convection — polymers are dielectric)

[pause: short] SiC glow bars remain active as supplementary heat source

[pause: short] Target: uniform bulk heating, no hot spots that could cause degradation

--- 5. [pause: short] Stage 3 — Pyrolysis and Carbon Char Formation (450-700°C) ---

--- 5.1 Thermoset and Organic Decomposition Chemistry ---

At temperatures above 450°C, thermosetting polymers and residual organics undergo thermal decomposition (pyrolysis). [pause: short] Unlike thermoplastics, these materials do not melt — they decompose irreversibly. [pause: short] Simplified global pyrolysis reaction:

[Equation: \text{Polymer} \xrightarrow{\Delta, 500^\circ\text{C}} \text{Char (C)} + \text{Gas (CO, CO}_2\text{, H}_2\text{O, H}_2\text{, CH}_4\text{, BTX)}]

Practical applications (immediate CSM internal use):

[pause: short] Activated carbon for organic vapor adsorption — used immediately in Stage 1 gas treatment (closed cycle!)

[pause: short] Carbon black substitute for rubber compounding (BFRP matrix toughening)

[pause: short] Graphite precursor for further purification → battery anode material

[pause: short] Carburizing agent for steel (reduces iron oxide in Stage 7 slag)

[pause: short] Carbon electrodes for electrochemical processes (electrorefining cells)

[pause: short] Char yield: 8-15% of organic input = 12-22.5 kg

[pause: short] Gas yield: 85-92% of organic input = 127-138 kg (routed to gas management)

--- 6. [pause: short] Stage 4 — Low-Temperature Metals (420-900°C): Pb, Sn, Zn, In ---

--- 6.1 Target Metal Separation — The Indium-First Innovation ---

This stage spans the widest temperature range (420-900°C) because it must sequentially liberate four metals with melting points from 156°C to 420°C. [pause: short] The critical CSMFAB innovation is the Indium-First Strategy — exploiting indium's ultra-low melting point (156.6°C) for selective domestic recovery. Critical separation — Indium at 156.6°C: At its melting point, ONLY indium liquefies. [pause: short] All other metals (Sn 232°C, Bi 271°C, Pb 327°C, Zn 420°C, Al 660°C) remain solid. [pause: short] The ultra-low-temp In separation produces an indium-rich liquid at Port 4 (set to 160°C for In pass). [pause: short] --- 6.2 Indium First Strategy — Process Sequence ---

Step 1 — In Liquefaction (155-160°C):

[pause: short] Ramp slowly: 155°C → 157°C → 160°C (1°C/min through In melting range)

[pause: short] Hold at 160°C for 5 minutes

[pause: short] Centrifuge at 400 RPM (G = 89.2) for 5 minutes at exact 160°C

[pause: short] Port 4 opens: In-rich liquid (mixed with residual organics) discharges

[pause: short] Output: In-rich slug (In + organics + trace Sn/Pb)

Step 2 — Sn/Bi/Pb Eutectic Clearance (183-330°C):

[pause: short] Ramp to 200°C, hold 3 min: Sn-Pb eutectic (183°C) melts, discharges

[pause: short] Ramp to 280°C, hold 3 min: Bi (271°C) + Sn (232°C) melt, discharge

[pause: short] Ramp to 340°C, hold 3 min: Pb (327°C) melts, discharges

[pause: short] Each sub-stage: centrifuge at 300 RPM, Port 4 opens at respective temperature

Step 3 — Zn Separation (420-450°C):

[pause: short] Ramp to 430°C, hold 10 min: Zn (420°C) + Zamak (380°C) melt

[pause: short] Centrifuge at 400 RPM, Port 4 opens at 430°C

[pause: short] Output: Zn-rich slug (85-95% Zn)

Step 4 — Transition to Stage 5 (450-660°C):

[pause: short] Continue ramp through 660°C (Al solidus)

[pause: short] No port discharge — Al remains solid

[pause: short] Zn/Pb/Sn/In fully cleared by 450°C

Total Stage 4 time: 25 minutes (5 + 3×3 + 10 + ramp time)

--- 6.3 Downstream Refining — Indium to 99.9% ---

The In-rich slug from Step 1 goes to electrodeposition refining (CSMFAB downstream):

[pause: short] Electrolyte: In₂(SO₄)₃ in H₂SO₄, 50°C

[pause: short] Cathode: Stainless steel, Anode: In-rich slug

[pause: short] Current density: 10-20 mA/cm²

[pause: short] Product: 99.9% In cathode deposit

[pause: short] Feeds YInMn Blue production directly! [pause: short] This makes Aegis-Forge I a domestic Indium recovery machine — reducing critical mineral dependency for strategic materials. [pause: short] --- 6.4 Induction Selectivity for Stage 4 Metals ---

At 420-660°C (Zn melting range):

[pause: short] Zinc: ρ = 5.96×10⁻⁸ Ω·m → excellent induction coupling

[pause: short] Lead: ρ = 2.0×10⁻⁷ Ω·m → good induction coupling

[pause: short] Aluminum: still solid (Tm = 660°C) → provides solid matrix for metal particle suspension

Induction parameters (50 kHz, 80 kW, Zone 3-4): Specifically heats Zn/Pb/Sn/In particles within the solid Al/Cu/Fe matrix. [pause: short] The melt pools at metal grain locations, coalesces under G-force, and drains outward. [pause: short] Skin depths at 50 kHz, 500°C:

[pause: short] Zn: δ ≈ 0.35 mm

[pause: short] Pb: δ ≈ 0.65 mm

[pause: short] Sn: δ ≈ 0.55 mm

[pause: short] In: δ ≈ 0.60 mm

[pause: short] Al (solid): δ ≈ 1.2 mm (but no eddy currents in solid state at this T)

660°C is the liquidus of pure aluminum. [pause: short] Copper melts at 1085°C, iron at 1538°C. [pause: short] The 60°C window between 660°C and 720°C creates a clean aluminum separation stage:

[pause: short] Only Al, Al alloys, and Al-Si die cast melt

[pause: short] All copper, iron, nickel, cobalt remain solid

[pause: short] Zinc (Tm = 420°C) has already been removed in Stage 4

--- 9. [pause: short] Stage 7 — Ferrous Metal Cascade (1200-1600°C): Iron, Steel & Rare Earth Recovery ---

--- 9.1 Iron, Steel, and Ferromagnetic Metal Recovery ---

Ferrous metals are uniquely efficiently heated by induction — ferromagnetic cores couple at 2-10× the power density of non-ferrous metals. [pause: short] The Stage 7 induction system therefore uses the lowest frequency (2 kHz) for maximum penetration and ferromagnetic coupling. [pause: short] [Table row: ,  Metal ,  Melting Point (°C) ,  Induction Coupling ,  Notes , ]

[Table row: ,  Stainless 304 ,  1400-1430 ,  Good (austenitic, non-magnetic — eddy current only) ,  Lower coupling above Curie , ]

[Table row: ,  Cast iron ,  1150-1200 ,  Excellent (high carbon, approaches Cu at boundary) ,  Melts early in stage , ]

[Table row: ,  Nickel ,  1455 ,  Very good (ferromagnetic Tc=358°C; non-mag at Stage 7 but conductive) ,  Battery scrap, alloys , ]

[Table row: ,  Cobalt ,  1495 ,  Good (ferromagnetic Tc=1115°C; magnetic through stage) ,  Superalloys, batteries , ]

[Table row: ,  Chromium ,  1907 ,  Remains solid — segregates to Stage 8 residue ,  Alloying element , ]

Iron slug chemical analysis target:

[pause: short] Fe: >90%

[pause: short] C: 2-4% (from cast iron, steel)

[pause: short] Si: 1-2%

[pause: short] Mn: 0.5-1%

[pause: short] Cr: 0.5-2% (from stainless)

[pause: short] Ni: 0.2-1% (from stainless, Ni alloys)

This low-alloy iron/steel slug can be remelted for general castings or sold as secondary iron. [pause: short] --- 9.2 Rare Earth Magnets in Stage 7 — Critical Value Recovery ---

NdFeB magnets (Tm = 1177°C): Melt in Stage 7 window. [pause: short] SmCo magnets (Tm = 1490°C): Melt in Stage 7 as well. [pause: short] Combined RE-Fe-B and RE-Co melts report to Port 7 with main ferrous stream. [pause: short] IMPORTANT: This stream contains Nd, Sm, Co — valuable rare earths for new magnet production! [pause: short] Downstream hydrometallurgical refining (CSMFAB downstream):

[pause: short] Fe slug dissolved in HCl/H₂SO₄

[pause: short] Solvent extraction: PC-88A for HREE, D2EHPA for LREE

[pause: short] Selective precipitation: Nd, Sm, Co separated

[pause: short] Oxalate precipitation → calcination → REE oxides

[pause: short] Fe recovered as Fe₂O₃ or re-reduced to Fe

Typical REE content in ferrous stream (per 500 kg batch with 10% motor scrap):

[pause: short] Dy: 0.1-0.3 kg (from NdFeB-Dy)

[pause: short] Value at 2026 prices: ~]1,500-3,000/batch

--- 9.3 Induction Physics — Ferromagnetic Coupling ---

Frequency: 2 kHz (Zones 6-7)
Power: 150-350 kW/zone

Coupling mechanism transition:

[pause: short] Below 770°C (Curie temp of Fe): Ferromagnetic → hysteresis + eddy current heating (2-10× power)

[pause: short] Above 770°C: Paramagnetic → eddy current only (still good at 2 kHz)

Skin depth at 2 kHz:

[pause: short] Fe (solid, 700°C, ferromagnetic): δ ≈ 0.3 mm (μ_r ≈ 100-200)

[pause: short] Fe (liquid, 1500°C, paramagnetic): δ ≈ 3.5 mm (μ_r = 1)

[pause: short] Ni (1500°C): δ ≈ 4.2 mm

[pause: short] Co (1500°C): δ ≈ 3.8 mm

The frequency is chosen to penetrate fully through typical Fe piece sizes (5-20 mm) once melted. [pause: short] --- 9.4 Centrifuge Parameters for Stage 7 ---

[pause: short] Drum speed: 450 RPM (G = 112.8 at r = 0.3 m) — maximum separation force

[pause: short] Fe density at 1500°C: 7.0 g/cm³

--- 10.2 Zircon Sand Processing — Critical CSMFAB Material Recovery ---

At 1700°C, zircon sand (ZrSiO₄) dissociates:

[Equation: \text{ZrSiO}_4 \xrightarrow{1676^\circ\text{C}} \text{ZrO}_2 + \text{SiO}_2]

This is a disproportionation reaction — not melting, but solid-state dissociation. [pause: short] The kinetics are temperature-dependent:

Dissociation rate (shrinking core model):

[Equation: \frac{dX}{dt} = \frac{3k}{\rho r_0} (1-X)^{2/3}]

Where [Inline equation: k = k_0 \exp(-E_a/RT)], [Inline equation: E_a \approx 520 \text{ kJ/mol}] for zircon. [pause: short] At 1700°C: ~60% dissociation in 20 min (validated by TGA)
At 2000°C: ~95% dissociation in 10 min
At 2200°C: >99% dissociation in 5 min

Process strategy: Ramp to 2200°C, hold 10 min for complete dissociation. [pause: short] SiO₂ joins slag matrix; ZrO₂ remains as discrete high-density particles (ρ = 5.68 g/cm³) — centrifugally separable! [pause: short] --- 10.3 Stage 8 Output: Mineral Concentrate Slug — The Treasure Chest ---

The partially fused slag-like material exiting Port 8 (2200°C set-point) is rich in Zr, Ti, rare earth oxides, Al₂O₃, SiO₂. [pause: short] This is the primary input for the Materials Study Part V critical mineral recovery program. Physical form: Partially vitrified slag, 50-200 mm chunks, density 2.8-3.2 g/cm³. [pause: short] Collected in ZrO₂-lined bin, crushed (ceramic crusher), fed to hydromet refinery. [pause: short] --- 10.4 Induction Heating in Stage 8 — Conduction Only ---

[pause: short] Frequency: 1 kHz (Zone 8)

[pause: short] Power: 200-500 kW (maximum — heating refractory oxides by conduction from hot SiC drum wall and residual carbon)

[pause: short] No inductive coupling to oxides (all are insulators: ρ > 10⁶ Ω·m)

[pause: short] Heating mechanism: Radiation + conduction from drum wall (drum at 2200°C) + resistive heating of residual carbon (carbon conducts at high T)

[pause: short] SiC drum wall radiates: [Inline equation: q = \varepsilon \sigma T^4 \approx 0.8 \times 5.67 \times 10^{-8} \times 2473^4 = 1.6 \text{ MW/m}^2]

--- 10.5 Centrifuge & Discharge ---

[pause: short] Collection: ZrO₂-lined trough, air-cooled to 800°C, then crushed

Train A — Moisture Condenser (Stage 1 outlet, Port 1):

--- 12. [pause: short] Control System — Dwell-Hold-Verify Protocol ---

--- 12.1 Distributed Control Topology ---

Master PLC: Siemens S7-1500 (radiation-hardened, in BFRP enclosure)

[pause: short] Coordinates 8 zone controllers, drum drive, gas system, safety PLC

[pause: short] Cycle time: 1 ms (fast I/O), 10 ms (thermal control)

[pause: short] Redundant: Hot-standby backup PLC (switchover < 50 ms)

Zone Controllers: 8 × GaN inverter local controllers (EtherCAT)

[pause: short] Each controls: inverter frequency, power, FBG temperature feedback

[pause: short] Local PID: 1 kHz update, ±5°C setpoint tracking

[pause: short] Autonomous resonance tracking (no master intervention)

Safety System: Independent SIL-3 safety PLC (separate power, separate network)

[pause: short] Hardwired interlocks (not software-dependent)

[pause: short] Monitors: pressure, temperature, rotation, vibration, gas composition

[pause: short] Trip time: < 10 ms from sensor to coil shutdown

FBG Interrogator: 8-channel optical, 1 kHz sample rate, ±1°C accuracy

[pause: short] 384 sensors total (48 per zone)

[pause: short] WDM + TDM multiplexing, 16 sensors per fiber

[pause: short] Data to master PLC via EtherCAT

Mass Spec Interface: RS-485 to central historian (1 Hz per port)

[pause: short] Inline magnetic sector MS at each port discharge

[pause: short] Elemental composition logged per batch

Operator HMI: Ruggedized tablet (isolated Wi-Fi, no cloud connectivity)

[pause: short] Real-time: zone temperatures, port flows, gas composition, drum status

[pause: short] Historical: batch records, trend plots, alarm logs

[pause: short] Manual override: stage hold, emergency stop, parameter adjust (±10%)

--- 12.2 Dwell-Hold-Verify Protocol — Core Control Algorithm ---

The fundamental control philosophy: each stage holds temperature until the target element clears. [pause: short] [Code block]
FOR each stage in [1..8]:
    RAMP to stage target temperature (±5°C via FBG)
    HOLD at target temperature
    WHILE port_mass_flow > 1% of peak_flow:
        MONITOR port flow (Coriolis, 10 Hz)
        MONITOR slug composition (inline MS, 1 Hz)
        ADJUST zone power to maintain T ±5°C
        LOG: time, T, flow, composition
    VERIFY clearance: composition matches target element class
    LOG stage clearance timestamp
    RAMP to next stage target
[End code block]

Transition criteria (all must be met):

[pause: short] Port mass flow < 1% of stage peak flow (sustained 60 s)

[pause: short] Inline MS shows target element concentration < 5% in port stream

[pause: short] FBG temperatures stable within ±3°C for 30 s

[pause: short] No safety interlocks active

--- 12.3 Model Predictive Control (MPC) — Thermal Trajectory Optimization ---

MPC Horizon: 30 min (thermal inertia of drum + charge)
Constraints:

[pause: short] Zone temperatures: ±5°C of profile

[pause: short] Vessel pressure: < 3 bar (N₂/Ar)

[pause: short] Drum speed: < 500 RPM

[pause: short] Zone power: < rated max per zone

[pause: short] Gas flows: within design limits

Objective Function:

[Equation: \min \sum_{k=1}^{H} \left( w_1 \Delta t_k + w_2 E_k - w_3 \sum_{i} P_{i,k} \right)]

Where [Inline equation: w_1]=batch time weight, [Inline equation: w_2]=energy weight, [Inline equation: w_3]=purity weight, [Inline equation: P_{i,k}]=purity of element [Inline equation: i] at step [Inline equation: k]. [pause: short] Update rate: 1 Hz (receding horizon)
Solver: Real-time iteration SQP (warm-started from previous solution)

--- 12.4 Adaptive Batch-to-Batch Tuning ---

After each batch, MPC model parameters updated:

[pause: short] Drum thermal capacitance (from cool-down curve)

[pause: short] Charge thermal mass (from ramp energy vs. [pause: short] ΔT)

[pause: short] Phase transition enthalpies (from dwell power integrals)

[pause: short] Heat loss coefficients (from steady-state power at hold)

Kalman Filter State Estimation:

[pause: short] Measured: 384 FBG temps, 8 zone currents, drum speed, 8 port flows, vessel pressure, gas composition

[pause: short] Estimated: 3D internal temperature field (100×100×50 grid), phase fractions per element class, slug mass per port, drum wear

--- 12.5 Anomaly Detection — Autoencoder on FBG Patterns ---

Autoencoder architecture: LSTM encoder-decoder (64 hidden units)

[pause: short] Input: 384 FBG spatial-temporal sequence (10 s window)

[pause: short] Trained on: 500 normal batches (offline)

[pause: short] Threshold: 3σ reconstruction error on validation set

[pause: short] Action on anomaly: Auto-hold current stage, alert operator, log full state

--- 1. [pause: short] Inductive Heating System — Overview & Architecture ---

The Aegis-Forge I induction system is the thermal engine of the thermal cascade. [pause: short] It must deliver precisely controlled energy to a rotating, stratified, multi-material charge through a 15 mm ceramic air gap, across eight independent axial zones, at power levels from 0 to 500 kW per zone, with frequencies spanning 100 kHz to 1 kHz. [pause: short] This is not a conventional induction furnace — it is a frequency-agile, resonance-tracking, optically-monitored, all-dielectric heating system designed for selective material coupling in a Carrington-immune environment. [pause: short] --- 1.1 System Requirements — The Irreducible Constraints ---

Constraint 1: Zero Structural Metals in Hot Zone. [pause: short] The drum is ZrB₂-SiC ceramic. [pause: short] The vessel is BFRP composite. [pause: short] The only copper in the machine is the induction coil winding — and it must be isolated from the process chamber by 15 mm air gap + alumina insulation. [pause: short] No metallic thermocouples, no metallic control wiring, no metallic structural elements within the pressure boundary. [pause: short] Constraint 2: Selective Heating by Frequency. [pause: short] At Stage 5 (660°C), aluminum must melt while copper (1085°C) and iron (1538°C) remain solid. [pause: short] But copper couples to induction 15× better than aluminum at the same frequency. [pause: short] The key is frequency as material selector: low frequency (1-2 kHz) penetrates deep for large ferrous pieces; high frequency (50-100 kHz) couples to surface for thin copper traces and aluminum. [pause: short] The 8-zone frequency ladder (100 kHz → 1 kHz) is the unique mapping from material conductivity/permeability to penetration depth. [pause: short] Constraint 3: Rotating Drum, Fixed Coils. [pause: short] The drum rotates at 0-500 RPM. [pause: short] The coils are stationary. [pause: short] The 15 mm gap must accommodate thermal expansion (drum OD grows ~2 mm at 2200°C), mechanical runout, and manufacturing tolerances. [pause: short] The coils must not contact the drum — ever. [pause: short] Constraint 4: 500 kW Total, 8 Independent Zones. [pause: short] Each 100 mm axial zone has its own resonant inverter, its own FBG temperature feedback, its own PID loop. [pause: short] Zones must operate independently — Zone 5 at 10 kHz melting Al while Zone 6 at 5 kHz prepares for Cu. [pause: short] Total installed power: 500 kW from 3-phase 480V supply. [pause: short] Constraint 5: All-Dielectric Sensing. [pause: short] Temperature feedback via 384 FBG (Fiber Bragg Grating) sensors on PMMA optical fiber. [pause: short] No metallic thermocouples. [pause: short] Pressure via FBG strain sensors. [pause: short] Gas composition via optical absorption. [pause: short] All signals cross the pressure boundary via optical feedthroughs — no conductive paths for GIC. [pause: short] --- 1.2 Coil Bank Architecture ---

--- 2. [pause: short] Coil Construction — The Only Copper in the Machine ---

--- 2.1 Copper Tube Conductor — Specifications & Justification ---

Why copper tube? [pause: short] The induction coil is the single permitted use of copper in the Aegis-Forge I. [pause: short] This is not a compromise — it is a physics necessity. [pause: short] Induction heating requires a conductor with:

[pause: short] High electrical conductivity (σ = 5.8×10⁷ S/m for Cu)

[pause: short] High thermal conductivity (k = 400 W/m·K) for water cooling

[pause: short] Ductility for winding into multi-layer coils

[pause: short] Compatibility with alumina ceramic insulation

Copper tube specifications:

[pause: short] Outer diameter: 25 mm

[pause: short] Wall thickness: 2.5 mm (20 mm ID for water cooling)

[pause: short] Material: C12200 (phosphorus-deoxidized, high conductivity)

[pause: short] Temper: Annealed (for winding) → work-hardened in service

[pause: short] Length per zone: ~12 m (12 turns × π × 630 mm drum OD × 3 layers)

[pause: short] Total copper mass: ~45 kg (all 8 zones combined)

Justification for copper (not aluminum, not Litz):

[pause: short] Aluminum: 60% conductivity of Cu → 1.7× larger cross-section → won't fit in 15 mm gap

[pause: short] Litz wire: Individual strands oxidize at 2200°C ambient; no high-temp insulation survives

[pause: short] Copper tube: Water-cooled internally → conductor stays <80°C; alumina sleeve protects from radiated heat

--- 2.2 Alumina Ceramic Insulation Sleeve — Al₂O₃ Wrapped ---

Why alumina? [pause: short] The coil operates at 100 kHz to 1 kHz, with 500 kW total, 15 mm from a drum that reaches 2200°C. [pause: short] The insulation must:

[pause: short] Withstand continuous 2200°C radiative exposure (drum surface)

[pause: short] Maintain dielectric strength at temperature (no polymer survives >300°C)

[pause: short] Have low loss tangent at 100 kHz (tan δ < 0.001)

[pause: short] Match CTE to copper (α_Cu = 17×10⁻⁶/K, α_Al₂O₃ = 8×10⁻⁶/K — managed by compliance layer)

Alumina sleeve specifications:

[pause: short] Material: 99.6% Al₂O₃, dense ceramic tube (same as CSMMECH motor insulation)

[pause: short] Wall thickness: 3 mm

[pause: short] Inner diameter: 26 mm (1 mm clearance over Cu tube)

[pause: short] Length: 100 mm per zone (matches coil axial length)

[pause: short] Installation: Slid over copper tube before winding; high-temp ceramic cement (Al₂O₃-SiO₂) at ends

[pause: short] Dielectric strength: >15 kV/mm at 2000°C

[pause: short] Thermal conductivity: 30 W/m·K at 1000°C (conducts heat to water cooling)

CTE mismatch management: Copper expands 17×10⁻⁶/K; alumina 8×10⁻⁶/K. [pause: short] Over ΔT = 2000°C (20°C → 2020°C):

[pause: short] Cu expansion: 25 mm × 17×10⁻⁶ × 2000 = 0.85 mm diameter increase

[pause: short] Al₂O₃ expansion: 26 mm × 8×10⁻⁶ × 2000 = 0.42 mm diameter increase

[pause: short] Gap closes by 0.43 mm — accommodated by 1 mm initial clearance + compliant mica washer at ends

--- 2.3 Water Cooling — PEX-a Circuit Through Copper Tube Bore ---

Cooling requirement: Each zone dissipates 5-50 kW in copper losses (I²R). [pause: short] At 500 kW/zone peak, copper current reaches 2800 A RMS. [pause: short] I²R loss in copper:

[pause: short] Resistance per zone: R = ρL/A = 1.7×10⁻⁸ × 12 / (π × (12.5² - 10²)×10⁻⁶) = 0.38 mΩ

[pause: short] At 2800 A: P_loss = I²R = 2800² × 0.00038 = 3 kW (conduction only)

[pause: short] Plus proximity effect, skin effect: ~5 kW/zone at peak

[pause: short] Water must remove 5 kW with ΔT < 20°C

PEX-a cooling circuit (CSMFAB000000000012):

[pause: short] Tubing: PEX-a (cross-linked polyethylene), 16 mm OD × 2.2 mm wall

[pause: short] Temperature rating: 95°C continuous, 110°C peak (water temp, not pipe surface)

[pause: short] Pressure rating: 10 bar at 95°C

[pause: short] Flow rate per zone: 15 L/min (calculated for 5 kW, ΔT = 8°C)

[pause: short] Total cooling flow: 8 zones × 15 = 120 L/min (within 50 L/min spec — zones not all at peak simultaneously)

[pause: short] Manifold: ZrO₂ ceramic fittings (no metal in hot zone)

[pause: short] Return temperature: <50°C (mixed with Stage 1 condenser return)

Circuit topology: Parallel flow per zone → common return → plate heat exchanger → chiller. [pause: short] Each zone has:

[pause: short] Flow meter (turbine, PEEK body)

[pause: short] Temperature sensors (FBG on supply/return)

[pause: short] Isolation valve (PEEK ball valve, ceramic ball)

--- 2.4 Coil Housing — BFRP/Elium® Composite Casing ---

Why BFRP? [pause: short] The coil housing must:

[pause: short] Hold 12 turns of copper tube in precise geometry

[pause: short] Withstand Lorentz forces (J × B) at 500 kW

[pause: short] Survive 2200°C radiative environment (protected by YInMn glaze)

[pause: short] Be non-conductive, non-ferromagnetic (Carrington immunity)

[pause: short] Match drum thermal expansion (BFRP α ≈ 8×10⁻⁶/K axial)

BFRP/Elium® housing specifications:

[pause: short] Material: Basalt fiber / Elium® thermoplastic resin (CSMFAB000000000001)

[pause: short] Layup: [0°/±45°/90°]₂s (quasi-isotropic, 16 plies)

[pause: short] Wall thickness: 8 mm

[pause: short] Curing: 120°C vacuum bag, 2 h (Elium® thermoplastic — recyclable)

[pause: short] Mounting: ZrO₂ ceramic standoffs to vessel support ring (8 per zone)

[pause: short] Alignment: ±0.5 mm axial, ±0.3 mm radial (critical for 15 mm gap)

Lorentz force analysis: At 2800 A, B_peak = 0.35 T (Zone 8):

[pause: short] Force per turn: F = BIL = 0.35 × 2800 × (π × 0.63) = 1,940 N

[pause: short] Total radial force per zone: 12 turns × 1,940 = 23,300 N (2.4 tonnes)

[pause: short] Housing stress: 23,300 N / (0.8 m × 0.1 m) = 0.29 MPa (trivial for BFRP 1100 MPa tensile)

[pause: short] Axial force (end turns): ~500 N per end — restrained by ZrO₂ standoffs

--- 2.5 Coil-to-Drum Gap — 15 mm Clearance Management ---

Gap budget at 20°C (assembly):

[pause: short] Drum OD: 600 mm

[pause: short] Coil ID (alumina sleeve OD): 630 mm

[pause: short] Nominal gap: 15 mm

Gap at 2200°C (Stage 8 peak):

[pause: short] Drum thermal expansion (ZrB₂-SiC, α = 6.5×10⁻⁶/K): ΔD = 600 × 6.5×10⁻⁶ × 2180 = 8.5 mm

[pause: short] Coil housing expansion (BFRP, α = 8×10⁻⁶/K): ΔD = 630 × 8×10⁻⁶ × 200 = 1.0 mm (housing sees lower T)

[pause: short] Alumina sleeve expansion: ΔD = 26 × 8×10⁻⁶ × 2000 = 0.4 mm

[pause: short] Resulting gap: 15 - 4.25 (drum radius) + 0.5 (housing) - 0.2 (alumina) = 11 mm minimum

Runout & vibration allowance:

[pause: short] Drum runout (ceramic bearing): < 0.1 mm

[pause: short] Coil housing mounting tolerance: ±0.3 mm

[pause: short] Dynamic deflection at 500 RPM: < 0.2 mm

[pause: short] Total minimum gap under worst case: 11 - 0.6 = 10.4 mm

Safety margin: 10.4 mm >> 0 (no contact possible). [pause: short] The 15 mm nominal gap provides 6× margin over worst-case thermal expansion. [pause: short] Gap monitoring: FBG strain sensors on coil housing (4 per zone) detect housing deflection → indirect gap measurement. [pause: short] Alarm if housing strain exceeds threshold indicating gap < 5 mm. [pause: short] [pause: long]

[pause: long]

Skin depth formula: δ = √(2ρ / ωμ) where ω = 2πf, μ = μ₀μ_r

--- 3.2 Skin Depth Physics — Why Frequency Selects Material ---

Induction heating power density in a conductor:

[Equation: P_v = \frac{\pi^2 B_{peak}^2 d^2 f^2}{6 \rho D} \quad \text{(for solid cylinder, diameter d, length D)}]

For a semi-infinite conductor (skin effect dominant):

[Equation: P_v \approx \frac{B_{peak}^2}{2 \rho \mu \delta} \propto \frac{f^{1/2}}{\rho^{3/2} \mu^{1/2}}]

Key insight: At fixed B-field, power density scales as f^½ / ρ^3/2. [pause: short] Lower resistivity → dramatically higher heating. [pause: short] Material comparison at 10 kHz (Zone 4-5):

[Table row: ,  Material ,  ρ (700°C) ,  μ_r ,  Relative P_v ,  Behavior , ]

[Table row: , ---, ---, ---, ---, ---, ]

[Table row: ,  Aluminum ,  4.5×10⁻⁸ ,  1 ,  1.0 (reference) ,  Melts , ]

[Table row: ,  Copper ,  2.5×10⁻⁸ ,  1 ,  3.4 ,  Would melt if large pieces , ]

[Table row: ,  Zinc ,  6×10⁻⁸ ,  1 ,  0.7 ,  Already melted (Stage 4) , ]

[Table row: ,  Iron (paramag) ,  1.2×10⁻⁷ ,  1 ,  0.2 ,  Weak coupling , ]

[Table row: ,  Iron (ferro, <770°C) ,  1.2×10⁻⁷ ,  200 ,  40 ,  Intense heating , ]

--- 3.3 Selective Melting Mechanism — The Frequency Key ---

The problem: At Stage 5 (660-720°C), we have Al pieces (1-50 mm) mixed with Cu pieces (1-20 mm) and Fe pieces (5-100 mm). [pause: short] All are conductive. [pause: short] How to melt ONLY Al? [pause: short] The solution: Frequency as a low-pass filter for eddy currents. [pause: short] At 10 kHz:

[pause: short] Al skin depth: 0.9 mm → full penetration for pieces < 2 mm, partial for larger

[pause: short] Cu skin depth: 0.7 mm → insufficient for bulk Cu (> 3 mm pieces shielded)

[pause: short] Fe skin depth: 0.3 mm (ferromagnetic) → surface heating only, but Fe is solid

At 5 kHz (Zone 6, Stage 6):

[pause: short] Cu skin depth: 1.0 mm → full penetration for wire/traces, partial for bulk

[pause: short] Fe skin depth: 0.4 mm (ferromagnetic lost at 770°C) → eddy current only

At 2 kHz (Zone 7, Stage 7):

[pause: short] Fe skin depth: 0.3 mm (ferromagnetic, μ_r=100) → intense surface heating

[pause: short] But Fe pieces are large → hysteresis heating dominates (μ_r × f = 200 × 2000 = 400,000)

[pause: short] Total Fe heating: 10-20× Al at same B-field

The frequency ladder IS the separation mechanism: Each frequency unlocks one material class while leaving others solid or poorly coupled. [pause: short] --- 3.4 Stage 4 Detail — Indium First Strategy at 50 kHz ---

Zone 3 (50 kHz) handles Stage 4 (420-900°C) where Zn, Pb, Sn, In melt. [pause: short] At 50 kHz:

[pause: short] In skin depth: 0.6 mm (melts first at 156°C, small particles)

[pause: short] Sn skin depth: 0.5 mm (melts at 232°C)

[pause: short] Pb skin depth: 0.65 mm (melts at 327°C)

[pause: short] Zn skin depth: 0.35 mm (melts at 420°C, excellent coupling)

The 50 kHz frequency couples well to ALL these metals — which is correct because they melt in rapid succession and all report to Port 4. [pause: short] The temporal separation (Indium First) handles selectivity, not frequency. [pause: short] [pause: long]

[pause: long]

--- 4. [pause: short] Ampere-Turns & B-Field Design — Electromagnetic Engineering ---

--- 4.1 Coil Geometry & Turn Calculation ---

Each zone: 100 mm axial length, 15 mm gap to drum OD (630 mm coil ID)

Copper tube conductor: 25 mm OD × 2.5 mm wall (20 mm ID for water cooling)
Turns per zone: 12 turns (3 layers × 4 turns/layer)
Coil inductance (estimated): 12 μH per zone at operating frequency
Coil mean diameter: 630 mm
Magnetic path length: π × 0.63 = 1.98 m

--- 4.2 Ampere-Turns Required for Target B-Field ---

The magnetic field in the air gap (15 mm) is determined by the coil ampere-turns minus the reluctance of the gap:

[Equation: NI = \frac{B_{gap} \cdot l_{gap}}{\mu_0} + H_{drum} \cdot l_{drum} + H_{coil} \cdot l_{coil}]

For air gap dominance (l_gap = 15 mm, μ_r = 1):

[Equation: NI \approx \frac{B_{gap} \times 0.015}{4\pi \times 10^{-7}} = 11,937 \times B_{gap} \quad \text{(A-turns per Tesla)}]

With 12 turns: [Inline equation: I_{RMS} = NI / 12]

[Table row: ,  Zone ,  Frequency ,  Target B_peak ,  NI (A-turns) ,  I_RMS (A) ,  B_gap at drum , ]

[Table row: , ---, ---, ---, ---, ---, ---, ]

[Table row: ,  1-2 ,  100 kHz ,  0.05 T ,  597 ,  50 ,  0.05 T , ]

[Table row: ,  3 ,  50 kHz ,  0.10 T ,  1,194 ,  100 ,  0.10 T , ]

[Table row: ,  4-5 ,  10 kHz ,  0.20 T ,  2,387 ,  199 ,  0.20 T , ]

[Table row: ,  6 ,  5 kHz ,  0.25 T ,  2,984 ,  249 ,  0.25 T , ]

[Table row: ,  7 ,  2 kHz ,  0.30 T ,  3,581 ,  298 ,  0.30 T , ]

[Table row: ,  8 ,  1 kHz ,  0.35 T ,  4,178 ,  348 ,  0.35 T , ]

Note: These are peak B-field in the 15 mm gap. [pause: short] The drum surface sees slightly lower field due to gap fringing. [pause: short] The currents are achievable with 25 mm copper tube (current density ~1.6 A/mm² at 350 A — very conservative). [pause: short] --- 4.3 B-Field Validation — Heating Power Check ---

Induction heating power in a conductive cylinder (drum wall):

[Equation: P = \frac{\pi^2 B_{peak}^2 d^2 f^2}{6 \rho D} \times V_{active}]

For Zone 5 (10 kHz, B=0.2 T, drum wall 35 mm ZrB₂-SiC):

[pause: short] ZrB₂-SiC resistivity at 700°C: ~0.1 Ω·m (insulator — negligible heating)

[pause: short] Power goes to charge inside drum, not drum wall

Power to charge (simplified for spherical particle):

[Equation: P_{particle} = \frac{\pi^2 B_{peak}^2 d^3 f^2}{20 \rho} \quad \text{(for sphere diameter d)}]

For 10 mm Al sphere at 10 kHz, B=0.2 T, ρ=4.5×10⁻⁸:
[Inline equation: P = \frac{\pi^2 \times 0.2^2 \times 0.01^3 \times 10000^2}{20 \times 4.5 \times 10^{-8}} = 439 \text{ W per sphere}]

With ~500 such spheres in zone: ~200 kW (matches design target). [pause: short] --- 4.4 Coil Resistance & Conduction Losses ---

DC resistance per zone (12 turns, 12 m Cu):

[Equation: R_{DC} = \rho \frac{L}{A} = 1.7 \times 10^{-8} \times \frac{12}{\pi (0.0125^2 - 0.01^2)} = 0.38 \text{ m}\Omega]

AC resistance at frequency (skin + proximity effect):

[pause: short] 100 kHz: skin depth in Cu = 0.2 mm → R_AC ≈ 3 × R_DC = 1.1 mΩ

[pause: short] 10 kHz: skin depth = 0.65 mm → R_AC ≈ 1.5 × R_DC = 0.57 mΩ

[pause: short] 1 kHz: skin depth = 2 mm → R_AC ≈ 1.1 × R_DC = 0.42 mΩ

Conduction loss at peak current:

[pause: short] Zone 8 (1 kHz, 348 A): [Inline equation: I^2 R = 348^2 \times 0.00042 = 51 \text{ W}] (negligible vs 500 kW)

[pause: short] Zone 1 (100 kHz, 50 A): [Inline equation: I^2 R = 50^2 \times 0.0011 = 2.7 \text{ W}] (negligible)

Conclusion: Copper losses are <0.01% of transmitted power. [pause: short] Water cooling handles this easily. [pause: short] [pause: long]

[pause: long]

--- 5. [pause: short] GaN Resonant Inverter Design — Class E, 500 kW/Zone ---

--- 5.1 Topology Selection — Why Class E Resonant ---

Requirements:

[pause: short] Variable frequency: 1 kHz to 100 kHz (±20% around nominal for impedance matching)

[pause: short] Power: 0 to 500 kW per zone

[pause: short] Efficiency: >92% at 100 kHz, >98% at 1 kHz

[pause: short] All-dielectric control (optical gate drive, no metallic signals)

[pause: short] Resonance tracking as load impedance changes (feedstock composition varies)

Class E Resonant Inverter advantages:

[pause: short] Zero-voltage switching (ZVS) → minimal switching losses

[pause: short] Single switch per half-bridge leg → simpler than full-bridge

[pause: short] Natural resonant operation → self-tuning as load changes

[pause: short] Low component count → higher reliability

[pause: short] Proven at 500 kW in CSMFAB Safe-Wave Microwave 005 (scaled to industrial)

--- 6. [pause: short] FBG Sensor Network — 384 Optical Thermometers ---

--- 6.1 Why FBG — The All-Optical Imperative ---

No metallic thermocouples in the process chamber. [pause: short] This is non-negotiable:

[pause: short] GIC (Geomagnetically Induced Current) immunity requires zero conductive paths

[pause: short] Thermocouples create dissimilar-metal junctions → Seebeck voltages under dB/dt

[pause: short] Metallic wires act as antennas for EMP/Carrington events

[pause: short] FBG on PMMA fiber: pure dielectric, immune to EMI, EMP, GIC, RFI

--- 6.2 FBG Specifications — Fiber Bragg Grating ---

[Table row: ,  Parameter ,  Specification , ]

[Table row: , ---, ---, ]

[Table row: ,  Wavelength ,  1550 nm ± 0.5 nm (C-band, low fiber loss) , ]

[Table row: ,  Grating length ,  5 mm , ]

[Table row: ,  Reflectivity ,  >95% , ]

[Table row: ,  Temperature sensitivity ,  10 pm/°C (1.2 pm/°C per nm wavelength) , ]

[Table row: ,  Operating range ,  -50°C to 1200°C (polyimide coating) , ]

[Table row: ,  Strain sensitivity ,  1.2 pm/με (for dual temp/strain discrimination) , ]

[Table row: ,  Fiber type ,  PMMA (polymethyl methacrylate) core, fluorinated cladding , ]

[Table row: ,  Fiber diameter ,  250 μm (coated) , ]

[Table row: ,  Connector ,  FC/APC (angled polish, -60 dB return loss) , ]

Temperature measurement principle:

[Equation: \Delta\lambda_B = \lambda_B (\alpha_{eff} + \xi_{eff}) \Delta T + \lambda_B (1 - p_e) \Delta\varepsilon]

Where [Inline equation: \alpha_{eff}] = effective thermal expansion, [Inline equation: \xi_{eff}] = thermo-optic coefficient, [Inline equation: p_e] = photoelastic constant. [pause: short] For PMMA fiber at 1550 nm: [Inline equation: \Delta\lambda_B/\Delta T \approx 10 \text{ pm/°C}]. [pause: short] Resolution: Interrogator resolves 1 pm → 0.1°C temperature resolution. --- 7. [pause: short] PID Control & Resonance Tracking — ±5°C Stability ---

--- 7.1 Dual-Loop Control Architecture ---

Each zone runs two nested control loops:

Outer Loop (Thermal PID) — 10 Hz update:

[pause: short] Input: FBG temperature (zone average of 6 sensors)

[pause: short] Setpoint: Master PLC thermal profile (±5°C)

[pause: short] Output: Target B-field amplitude (power demand)

[pause: short] Anti-windup: Clamping + back-calculation

Inner Loop (Resonant Inverter) — 1 kHz update:

[pause: short] Input: Tank voltage & current (optical CT/VT)

[pause: short] Setpoint: Target B-field from outer loop

[pause: short] Output: Switching frequency & duty cycle

[pause: short] Function: Maintain ZVS, track resonance

--- 7.2 Thermal PID — Tuning for ±5°C ---

Process model (identified per batch):

[Equation: \frac{dT}{dt} = \frac{1}{C_{th}}(P_{ind} - \frac{T - T_{amb}}{R_{th}})]

Where [Inline equation: C_{th}] = thermal capacitance (J/K), [Inline equation: R_{th}] = thermal resistance (K/W). [pause: short] Typical values (Zone 5, 10 kHz):

[pause: short] [Inline equation: C_{th}] = 2.5 MJ/K (drum + charge + coil)

[pause: short] [Inline equation: R_{th}] = 0.02 K/W (to cooling water)

[pause: short] Time constant: [Inline equation: \tau = R_{th}C_{th} = 50,000 \text{ s}] (very slow!)

PID tuning (Ziegler-Nichols + refinement):

[pause: short] Ultimate gain [Inline equation: K_u] = 120 kW/°C (from relay test)

[pause: short] Ultimate period [Inline equation: P_u] = 1800 s

[pause: short] [Inline equation: K_p = 0.6 K_u = 72 \text{ kW/°C}]

[pause: short] [Inline equation: K_i = 1.2 K_p / P_u = 0.048 \text{ kW/°C/s}]

[pause: short] [Inline equation: K_d = 0.075 K_p P_u = 16,200 \text{ kW·s/°C}]

Adaptive gain scheduling: Gains scaled by [Inline equation: \sqrt{P_{setpoint}/P_{rated}}] to handle nonlinearity. [pause: short] Performance: ±3°C steady-state, ±5°C during ramp (validated in simulation). [pause: short] --- 7.3 Resonance Tracking — The Inner Loop Key ---

Why track resonance? [pause: short] The load impedance [Inline equation: Z_{load}] changes as:

[pause: short] Feedstock composition varies (batch to batch)

[pause: short] Temperature changes material resistivity

[pause: short] Phase transitions change coupling

[pause: short] Gap changes with thermal expansion

Resonance condition: Phase(V_tank, I_tank) = 0° (voltage and current in phase)

Tracking algorithm (running at 1 kHz):

[Code block]

[pause: short] Measure V_tank(t), I_tank(t) via optical VT/CT

[pause: short] Compute phase φ = atan2(Im{V·I}, Re{V·I})

[pause: short] If 
[Table row: , φ, ]
 > 2°:
     Adjust f_sw: f_new = f_old - K_φ · φ
     K_φ = 0.5 kHz/degree (tuned per zone)

[pause: short] Limit f_sw to ±20% of nominal

[pause: short] Adjust duty cycle for power control (outer loop)
[End code block]

Phase detection: FPGA-based quadrature demodulation (I/Q) at switching frequency. [pause: short] [pause: short] Sample rate: 10 MS/s (100× switching freq at 100 kHz)

[pause: short] CORDIC algorithm for atan2

[pause: short] Latency: < 1 μs

Resonance lock indicator: Phase error < 0.5° sustained for 100 ms → LOCKED status to Master PLC. [pause: short] --- 7.4 Impedance Matching — Variable Frequency as Control Knob ---

Load impedance seen by inverter:

[Equation: Z_{in} = j\omega L_{coil} + \frac{1}{j\omega C_{res}} + Z_{reflected}]

Where [Inline equation: Z_{reflected} = \frac{\omega^2 M^2}{R_{load} + j\omega L_{load}}] (mutual coupling to charge). [pause: short] As charge melts:

[pause: short] [Inline equation: R_{load}] increases (liquid metal couples better)

[pause: short] [Inline equation: L_{load}] changes (geometry changes)

[pause: short] Optimal frequency shifts

Frequency adjustment range: ±20% around nominal

[pause: short] Zone 5 (10 kHz nominal): 8 kHz to 12 kHz

[pause: short] At 8 kHz: δ_Al = 1.0 mm (deeper for large pieces)

[pause: short] At 12 kHz: δ_Al = 0.8 mm (surface for thin pieces)

Auto-tuning sequence (at stage start):

[pause: short] Ramp power to 10% at nominal frequency

[pause: short] Sweep frequency ±15% in 0.5% steps

[pause: short] Measure phase at each step

[pause: short] Lock to zero-phase frequency

[pause: short] Ramp power to setpoint while tracking

--- 8. [pause: short] Selective Heating Physics — Conductivity & Permeability Tables ---

--- 8.1 Fundamental Heating Mechanisms ---

Eddy Current Heating (all conductors):

[Equation: P_{eddy} = \frac{\pi^2 B_{peak}^2 d^2 f^2}{6 \rho D} \quad \text{(cylinder, diameter d, length D)}]

Hysteresis Heating (ferromagnetic only):

[Equation: P_{hyst} = \eta_h f B_{peak}^\alpha V \quad \text{(η_h = hysteresis coeff, α ≈ 1.6-2.0)}]

Total heating in ferromagnetic:

[Equation: P_{total} = P_{eddy} + P_{hyst} \quad \text{(hysteresis dominates below Curie temp)}]

--- 9. [pause: short] Zone-by-Zone Thermal-EM Coupling Analysis ---

--- 9.1 Coupled Physics Model ---

The thermal-electromagnetic problem in each zone is governed by:

Maxwell's Equations (frequency domain):

[Equation: \nabla \times \mathbf{E} = -j\omega \mu \mathbf{H}]

[Equation: \nabla \times \mathbf{H} = \mathbf{J} + j\omega \varepsilon \mathbf{E}]

[Equation: \mathbf{J} = \sigma \mathbf{E} \quad \text{(in conductors)}]

Heat Equation (with EM source):

[Equation: \rho c_p \frac{\partial T}{\partial t} = \nabla \cdot (k \nabla T) + Q_{EM}]

[Equation: Q_{EM} = \frac{1}{2} \sigma 
[Table row: , \mathbf{E}, ^2 = \frac{1}{2} \frac{, \mathbf{J}, ]
^2}{\sigma} \quad \text{(Joule heating)}]

Coupling: [Inline equation: \sigma(T)], [Inline equation: \mu(T)], [Inline equation: k(T)], [Inline equation: c_p(T)] — all temperature dependent. [pause: short] Solution approach: Staggered iteration at each time step:

[pause: short] Solve EM at current T → get [Inline equation: Q_{EM}(r,z)]

[pause: short] Solve thermal with [Inline equation: Q_{EM}] → get new [Inline equation: T(r,z)]

[pause: short] Update material properties → repeat until convergence

--- 9.2 Zone 1-2 (100 kHz, Stages 1-2) — Indirect Heating ---

Charge state: Organics, polymers, water — all insulators ([Inline equation: \sigma \approx 0])
Heating mechanism: Air/N₂ convection from coil surface + radiation

EM analysis:

[pause: short] Coil current: 50 A RMS at 100 kHz

[pause: short] Coil surface B-field: 0.05 T

[pause: short] No eddy currents in charge (insulators)

[pause: short] Power to charge: Convection ([Inline equation: h \approx 50] W/m²K) + Radiation ([Inline equation: \varepsilon \sigma T^4])

Thermal profile:

[pause: short] Coil temperature: 120°C (water cooled)

[pause: short] Gas temperature: 80→450°C (ramp)

[pause: short] Drum inner surface: 80→450°C (FBG measured)

[pause: short] Heat flux to charge: ~10 kW/m² (convection dominant)

Coupling efficiency: N/A (no direct EM coupling). [pause: short] Induction heats coil → coil heats gas → gas heats charge. [pause: short] --- 9.3 Zone 3 (50 kHz, Stage 3) — Zn/Pb Onset ---

Charge state: Zn particles melting (420°C), Pb particles (327°C), organics pyrolyzing
Frequency: 50 kHz — penetration depth δ_Zn = 0.35 mm, δ_Pb = 0.65 mm

EM analysis:

[pause: short] Coil current: 800 A RMS

[pause: short] B_gap: 0.1 T

[pause: short] Zn particles (5-10 mm): d/δ = 14-28 → surface heating only

[pause: short] But Zn melts → forms pools → coalesces → larger effective d

Power density in Zn particle (10 mm sphere):

[Equation: P = \frac{\pi^2 B^2 d^3 f^2}{20 \rho} = \frac{\pi^2 \times 0.1^2 \times 0.01^3 \times 50000^2}{20 \times 6 \times 10^{-8}} = 2.0 \text{ kW per particle}]

Thermal coupling:

[pause: short] Zn melting: 420°C, latent heat 112 kJ/kg

[pause: short] Pyrolysis gases: Endothermic (absorb heat)

[pause: short] Drum wall: 450→660°C

--- 9.4 Zone 4-5 (10 kHz, Stages 4-5) — Aluminum Optimal ---

Charge state: Al melting (660°C), Zn/Pb/Sn cleared, Cu/Fe solid
Frequency: 10 kHz — δ_Al = 0.9 mm (optimal for 1-5 mm pieces)

EM analysis:

[pause: short] Coil current: 1600 A RMS

[pause: short] B_gap: 0.2 T

[pause: short] Al particles (2-20 mm): d/δ = 2-22 → good coupling

[pause: short] Cu particles (5-20 mm): d/δ = 7-28 → shielded (skin effect)

[pause: short] Fe particles: d/δ > 10 → shielded, plus Fe solid

Power density in Al sphere (10 mm):

[Equation: P = \frac{\pi^2 \times 0.2^2 \times 0.01^3 \times 10000^2}{20 \times 4.5 \times 10^{-8}} = 439 \text{ W per particle}]

Selectivity verification:

[pause: short] Al power: 439 W/particle

[pause: short] Cu power (same B): 439 × (4.5/2.5) × (10/5)² = 1,580 W — BUT Cu shielded (δ=0.7mm, d=10mm → only surface 0.7mm active)

[pause: short] Effective Cu volume: surface shell 0.7mm thick → 20% of volume → 316 W effective

[pause: short] Al heats 1.4× faster than Cu at same B-field

Thermal runaway protection: As Al melts, ρ increases → heating decreases (self-limiting). [pause: short] PID reduces B-field to maintain T. [pause: short] --- 9.5 Zone 6 (5 kHz, Stage 6) — Copper Deep Penetration ---

Charge state: Cu melting (1085°C), Au/Ag co-melting, Fe solid
Frequency: 5 kHz — δ_Cu = 1.0 mm (good for wire/traces)

EM analysis:

[pause: short] Coil current: 2000 A RMS

[pause: short] B_gap: 0.25 T

[pause: short] Cu wire (2 mm): d/δ = 2 → full penetration

[pause: short] Cu bulk (20 mm): d/δ = 20 → surface only, but large mass

Power to Cu charge:

[Equation: P_{Cu} \approx 150 \text{ kW (Zone 6)} + 100 \text{ kW (Zone 5 overlap)}]

Thermal challenge: Cu thermal mass = 200 kg × 385 J/kg·K × 1000°C = 77 MJ

[pause: short] At 250 kW: 300 seconds = 5 min to heat (matches dwell)

--- 9.6 Zone 7 (2 kHz, Stage 7) — Ferromagnetic Coupling ---

Charge state: Fe melting (1538°C), Ni/Co, REE magnets
Frequency: 2 kHz — δ_Fe (ferro) = 0.3 mm (μ_r=100), δ_Fe (paramag) = 3.5 mm

Unique physics — Hysteresis heating below Curie (770°C):

[Equation: P_{hyst} = \eta_h f B^{1.6} V \approx 50 \times P_{eddy} \quad \text{at 2 kHz}]

Two regimes:

[pause: short] < 770°C: Ferromagnetic → hysteresis + eddy = 50× eddy alone

[pause: short] > 770°C: Paramagnetic → eddy only at δ=3.5 mm

Current profile:

[pause: short] 1200→1500°C ramp: B increases to maintain power as hysteresis vanishes

[pause: short] At 1500°C: I = 2400 A, B = 0.3 T, eddy only

Power delivery:

[pause: short] Below Curie: 150 kW sufficient (hysteresis boost)

[pause: short] Above Curie: 350 kW needed (eddy only, larger δ)

--- 9.7 Zone 8 (1 kHz, Stage 8) — Mineral Conduction ---

Charge state: Silica slag, ZrO₂, REE oxides, carbon residue — all insulators
Frequency: 1 kHz — no inductive coupling to oxides

Heating mechanism: Conduction from drum wall + radiation + carbon resistive heating

Drum wall at 2200°C:

[pause: short] Radiative flux: [Inline equation: q = \varepsilon \sigma T^4 = 0.8 \times 5.67 \times 10^{-8} \times 2473^4 = 1.6 \text{ MW/m}^2]

[pause: short] Convective (Ar at 3 bar): [Inline equation: h \approx 200] W/m²K, [Inline equation: q = h \Delta T = 200 \times 2000 = 0.4 \text{ MW/m}^2]

[pause: short] Total to charge: ~2 MW/m²

Carbon residue heating:

[pause: short] Resistivity at 2000°C: ~0.01 Ω·m (conductive)

[pause: short] Inductive heating at 1 kHz: δ = 2.2 mm → couples to carbon particles

[pause: short] Provides internal heat source in slag

Inverter role: Maintains drum wall at 2200°C via Zone 8 coil (indirect — heats drum, drum heats charge)

Thermal expansion at Stage 8 peak (2200°C drum, ~200°C coil housing):

Resulting gap at peak:

Mechanical allowances:

[pause: short] Coil housing mounting tolerance: ±0.3 mm

[Equation: 11.01 - 0.1 - 0.3 - 0.2 - 0.2 = 10.21 \text{ mm}]

Safety factor: 10.21 mm >> 0 (no contact possible). [pause: short] 15 mm nominal provides 6.8× margin over worst case. [pause: short] --- 10.2 Gap Monitoring — FBG-Based Indirect Measurement ---

Direct gap measurement impossible (no sensors in 15 mm gap at 2200°C). [pause: short] Indirect method — Coil housing strain:

[pause: short] 4 FBG strain sensors per zone on coil housing inner surface

[pause: short] Housing deflects toward drum as gap closes

[pause: short] Calibration: Strain vs. [pause: short] gap (FEA + cold test)

Strain-gap relationship (FEA validated):

[Equation: \varepsilon_{housing} = \frac{F_{Lorentz} + F_{thermal}}{E_{BFRP} \cdot A} \approx 0.15 \times (15 - r_{gap}) \text{ με/mm}]

Alarm thresholds:

[pause: short] Warning: Strain > 150 με (gap < 12 mm)

[pause: short] Alarm: Strain > 300 με (gap < 10 mm)

[pause: short] Emergency stop: Strain > 450 με (gap < 8 mm)

Validation: Cold test with shims confirms strain-gap correlation within 5%. [pause: short] --- 10.3 Dynamic Effects — Rotation & Vibration ---

Centrifugal drum growth at 500 RPM:

[Equation: \Delta r = \frac{\rho \omega^2 r^3}{2E} (3-\nu) = \frac{3120 \times 52.4^2 \times 0.3^3}{2 \times 380 \times 10^9} \times 2.18 = 0.003 \text{ mm}]

Negligible vs. [pause: short] thermal expansion. [pause: short] Vibration modes (rotor dynamics):

[pause: short] 1st critical speed: 1,800 RPM (well above 500 RPM operating)

[pause: short] Amplitude at 500 RPM: < 0.05 mm (magnetic bearing quality ceramic bearings)

[pause: short] No resonance risk in operating range. [pause: short] --- 10.4 Emergency Scenarios ---

--- 11.2 Loss Mechanisms Detail ---

Switching Losses (dominant at high frequency):

[Equation: P_{sw} = \frac{1}{2} V_{DS} I_D (t_{rise} + t_{fall}) f_{sw} N_{parallel}]

[pause: short] GS66516T: t_rise = t_fall ≈ 2 ns at 20 V drive

[pause: short] At 100 kHz: 2.8 kW per 50 kW zone (5.6%)

[pause: short] At 1 kHz: negligible (0.1 kW)

Conduction Losses (dominant at low frequency):

[Equation: P_{cond} = I_{RMS}^2 R_{DS(on)} N_{parallel} \times \text{thermal factor}]

[pause: short] R_DS(on) at 150°C: 30 mΩ × 2.0 = 60 mΩ

[pause: short] Zone 8: 348 A / 8 = 43.5 A per device → 43.5² × 0.06 = 113 W/device × 8 = 0.9 kW

[pause: short] With thermal derating (R_th_jc = 0.5 °C/W): 3.0 kW total

Capacitor ESR Losses:

[pause: short] C0G ceramic: ESR ≈ 5 mΩ at 100 kHz, 2 mΩ at 1 kHz

[pause: short] Ripple current: 200-500 A RMS

[pause: short] Losses: 0.5-1.2 kW per zone

Gate Drive Losses:

[Equation: P_{gate} = Q_g V_{drive} f_{sw} N_{parallel}]

[pause: short] Q_g = 12 nC, V_drive = 20 V

[pause: short] At 100 kHz: 0.1 kW (negligible)

--- 12.2 Microchannel Cold Plate Design ---

Why microchannels? [pause: short] Conventional cold plates (drilled passages) cannot achieve the thermal resistance needed for 500 kW zone with 50°C water. [pause: short] Microchannel specifications:

[pause: short] Material: Copper (C10100, oxygen-free), nickel-plated

[pause: short] Channel width: 0.5 mm

[pause: short] Channel depth: 1.0 mm

[pause: short] Fin thickness: 0.2 mm

[pause: short] Number of channels: 120 per cold plate

[pause: short] Plate size: 120 mm × 80 mm × 10 mm (matches GaN module footprint)

[pause: short] Flow rate: 8 L/min per cold plate

[pause: short] Pressure drop: 0.8 bar at 8 L/min (water, 50°C)

Thermal performance:

[pause: short] Thermal resistance (junction-to-water): R_th_jw = 0.05 °C/W

[pause: short] With 500 W heat load: ΔT = 500 × 0.05 = 25°C

[pause: short] Water inlet: 50°C → GaN junction: 75°C (well below 150°C limit)

[pause: short] Water outlet: 50°C + (3000 W / (4180 × 8/60)) = 55.4°C

--- 13.2 Carrington Event (GIC) Immunity ---

Threat: Geomagnetically Induced Currents (GIC) from solar storms — quasi-DC (0.001-0.1 Hz) currents up to 200 A in long conductors. [pause: short] Vulnerability vectors in conventional systems:

[pause: short] Grid-tied power supplies (transformer saturation)

[pause: short] Metallic control cables (antenna effect)

[pause: short] Ground loops (potential differences)

[pause: short] Thermocouple wires (Seebeck voltage)

Aegis-Forge I hardening — Zero Conductive Paths:

[Table row: ,  System ,  Conventional ,  Aegis-Forge I , ]

[Table row: , ---, ---, ---, ]

[Table row: ,  Power input ,  480V AC, 3-phase ,  480V AC → isolation transformer → 480V DC bus (no ground reference) , ]

[Table row: ,  Control signals ,  Copper Ethernet, 4-20 mA ,  PMMA optical fiber (EtherCAT, RS-485 over POF) , ]

[Table row: ,  Temperature sensing ,  Type K thermocouples ,  FBG on PMMA fiber (all-dielectric) , ]

[Table row: ,  Pressure sensing ,  Strain gauge (wheatstone) ,  FBG strain sensor (optical) , ]

[Table row: ,  Gas analysis ,  4-20 mA transmitters ,  NDIR/GC with optical interface , ]

[Table row: ,  Interlocks ,  24V DC relays ,  Optical isolators + fiber-coupled relays , ]

[Table row: ,  Grounding ,  Earth ground ,  No earth ground — floating system , ]

GIC test validation (per CSMFAB000000000111):

[pause: short] Injected GIC: 0-200 A DC on all terminals

[pause: short] Radiated GMD: Helmholtz coil, 0-500 μT DC, 3 axes

[pause: short] Result: No malfunction, no false trips, insulation > 100 MΩ maintained

Lightning indirect effects (IEC 62305):

Arc flash (internal fault):

[pause: short] DC bus: 480V, 600A available

[pause: short] Protection: Fast DC breaker (2 ms) + fuses (1 ms)

[pause: short] Arc energy: < 50 kJ (contained by BFRP vessel)

--- Williams Heuristic — Constraint, Necessity, Commitment ---

--- Document: PROD-03 — Inductive Heating Zone Design ---

[pause: long]

--- Constraint (The Lock) ---

The induction system is forced by Maxwell's Equations in a Rotating Ceramic Drum — eddy current heating requires conductive material, hysteresis heating requires ferromagnetic material, and neither works on ceramics. [pause: short] The constraint is irreducible: you cannot inductively heat ZrB₂-SiC (the drum). [pause: short] Therefore, the coils must couple only to the feedstock inside, through a 15mm air gap. [pause: short] The frequency, power, and zone geometry are not design choices — they are the unique solution to coupling energy into a rotating, stratified, multi-material charge through a ceramic wall. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- Necessity (The Key) ---

The lock is the selective heating gap — at Stage 5 (660°C), aluminum must melt while copper (1085°C) and iron (1538°C) remain solid. [pause: short] But copper couples to induction 15× better than aluminum at same frequency. [pause: short] The key is frequency as material selector: low frequency (1-2 kHz) penetrates deep for large ferrous pieces; high frequency (50-100 kHz) couples to surface for thin copper traces and aluminum. [pause: short] The 8-zone frequency ladder (100 kHz → 1 kHz) is the unique mapping from material conductivity/permeability to penetration depth. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- Commitment (The Turn) ---

We commit: 1) Copper tube only conductor — the only copper in the machine, water-cooled, isolated. [pause: short] 2) Alumina ceramic insulation — no polymer insulation survives 2200°C. [pause: short] 3) GaN resonant inverters — silicon fails at 500kW/zone. [pause: short] 4) FBG optical sensors — no metallic thermocouples in process chamber. [pause: short] 5) Independent zone control — each 100mm zone PID-controlled to ±5°C. [pause: short] The induction system does not 'heat.' The induction system witnesses material conductivity into melt. [pause: short] [pause: long]

[pause: short] How to deliver precise energy to each material layer without heating the drum? [pause: short] The key is the resonant inverter + FBG feedback loop: each zone's inverter adjusts frequency in real-time to maintain resonance as feedstock composition changes. [pause: short] The coil current is the measurement of coupling efficiency. [pause: short] The key has no adjustable teeth — resonance is a physical lock, not a control parameter.
