--- 11.6 Carrington Event (GIC) Immunity ---

The vessel safety systems are inherently GIC-immune:

[pause: short] All sensors: FBG optical (no metallic conductors)

[pause: short] All actuators: GaN inverters with optical control (no copper control wires)

[pause: short] Logic solver: Optical I/O, fiber-coupled

[pause: short] Power supply: Battery-backed (48 VDC) with optical isolation

[pause: short] Communication: PMMA POF to control room (no copper)

[pause: short] Grounding: Frame isolated on ZrO₂ pads (>10¹² Ω to earth)

No conductive path exists from process chamber to earth ground. [pause: short] A 100 kV/km geoelectric field induces <1 V across the entire vessel structure — well below any threshold for malfunction. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- 12. [pause: short] Hydrotest & Certification ---

--- 12.1 Hydrostatic Test Procedure ---

Test fluid: Nitrogen gas (non-flammable, non-condensing, leak detectable)

[pause: short] Why N₂ not water? [pause: short] BFRP absorbs water (0.5–1.0% at saturation) causing matrix plasticization and temporary strength loss. [pause: short] Water also requires drying (weeks at 120°C) and risks aerogel damage. [pause: short] Gas test eliminates these risks. [pause: short] Test pressure: 15 bar (1.5 × design pressure per ASME BPVC Sec X)
Test temperature: Ambient (20–25°C)
Hold time: 30 minutes minimum at test pressure
Leak test: Helium mass spectrometer, <10⁻⁶ mbar·L/s

Procedure:

[pause: short] Vessel assembled complete (flanges, seals, instrumentation)

[pause: short] All ports sealed with ZrO₂ blank flanges

[pause: short] N₂ supply connected via regulated panel (0–20 bar)

[pause: short] Pressurization rate: 1 bar/min (controlled ramp)

[pause: short] Hold at 5 bar — visual inspection, AE baseline

[pause: short] Hold at 10 bar — FBG strain verification (hoop strain = 380 με expected)

[pause: short] Ramp to 15 bar — AE monitoring for first-crack emissions

[pause: short] Hold 15 bar for 30 min — pressure decay <0.1 bar

[pause: short] Helium leak test at 10 bar — all joints, seals, penetrations

[pause: short] Depressurize at 1 bar/min — FBG unloading verification

--- 12.6 Repair Procedures ---

Minor damage (surface scratch, coating loss):

[pause: short] Sand to sound laminate, clean with isopropyl alcohol

[pause: short] Apply YInMn Blue touch-up (plasma spray patch or brush-applied ceramic coating)

[pause: short] Cure at 200°C for 2 hrs

Moderate damage (delamination <50 mm diameter):

[pause: short] Drill-stop at delamination boundary

[pause: short] Inject PEEK-based structural adhesive (3M DP460)

[pause: short] Vacuum bag, cure at 120°C for 2 hrs

[pause: short] UT verify bond, recoat

Major damage (through-thickness, >50 mm):

[pause: short] Requires ASME repair organization + AIA approval

[pause: short] Cut out damaged section, filament wind repair patch (local mandrel)

[pause: short] Full NDE + hydrotest after repair

[pause: short] Re-certification required

No field welding, no metal fasteners, no thermoset resins — all repairs use CSMFAB materials and processes. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- 1. [pause: short] PURPOSE & DESIGN MANDATE ---

--- 1.1 Zero-Release Imperative ---

The Aegis-Forge I is architected as a hermetically sealed, zero-emission system. [pause: short] At no point during any thermal cascade stage — from acoustic liberation (Stage 0) through mineral dissociation (Stage 8) — are process gases, vapors, or particulates released to the ambient environment. [pause: short] This is not merely an environmental compliance feature; it is a thermodynamic necessity. [pause: short] Every gas stream generated within the cascade is a recoverable material stream with intrinsic value. [pause: short] The system philosophy: there is no waste, only unprocessed product. --- 2. [pause: short] CLOSED-LOOP N₂ ATMOSPHERE ARCHITECTURE ---

--- 2.1 System Architecture & N₂ Circuit Description ---

The entire drum and gas handling system operates as a sealed nitrogen atmosphere loop. [pause: short] Nitrogen was selected as the carrier gas for three fundamental reasons:

[pause: short] Inertness at cascade temperatures: N₂ remains chemically inert across the full 25°C → 1676°C operating range. [pause: short] Unlike CO₂ (which participates in Boudouard reaction above 700°C) or argon (cost-prohibitive at scale), nitrogen provides thermodynamic stability without side reactions. [pause: short] [pause: short] Thermal ballast properties: N₂ specific heat capacity (1.04 kJ/kg·K at 300K, rising to 1.15 kJ/kg·K at 1000K) provides substantial thermal mass for temperature stabilization. [pause: short] The 2-3 kg N₂ inventory per cycle acts as a thermal flywheel, dampening induction power transients. [pause: short] [pause: short] Industrial availability & cost: Bulk liquid nitrogen at ]0.09/kg (industrial grade) yields a make-up gas cost of < [Inline equation: 0.30 per 50 kg feedstock batch — negligible relative to recovered metal value (]500-5000/batch). [pause: short] The N₂ circuit comprises the following subsystems in series:

--- 2.2 System Operating Pressure Control ---

The Aegis-Forge I operates the entire N₂ atmosphere loop at a positive gauge pressure of 1.2-2.5 bar (2.2-3.5 bar absolute). [pause: short] This pressurized operation serves four critical functions:

[pause: short] Oxygen Exclusion (Primary Safety Function)
At Stage 2 temperatures (300-450°C), any oxygen ingress would cause uncontrolled combustion of thermoplastic polymers, generating uncontrolled thermal excursions, toxic partial oxidation products (dioxins, furans, PAHs), and potential overpressure events. [pause: short] The positive pressure ensures that any leakage is outward (N₂ to atmosphere) rather than inward (air to process). [pause: short] Maximum allowable O₂ concentration in the loop: < 10 ppm (monitored by ZrO₂-based optical O₂ sensor). [pause: short] [pause: short] Boiling Point Elevation
Increased system pressure raises the boiling points of volatile species, reducing premature vaporization and improving condensation efficiency in the stage-specific trains:

[pause: short] Water: 100°C at 1 bar → 120°C at 2 bar (Train A inlet matches this)

[pause: short] Zinc: 907°C at 1 bar → 945°C at 2.5 bar (improves Zn retention in drum melt)

[pause: short] Lead: 1749°C at 1 bar → minimal shift (PbO particulate capture dominates)

[pause: short] Pressure-Differential Gas Routing
The pressure gradient from drum (highest) → condenser cascade → scrubbers → PSA → recycle compressor (lowest) provides the driving force for gas flow without requiring mechanical blowers in the hot process stream. [pause: short] Pressure drops across each element:

[Table row: ,  Element ,  ΔP (bar) ,  Notes , ]

[Table row: , ---------, ----------, -------, ]

[Table row: ,  Drum internal (inlet to exhaust) ,  0.05-0.15 ,  Function of RPM, flow rate , ]

[Table row: ,  Zero₂ cyclone separator ,  0.15 ,  Fixed geometry, 25 m/s inlet , ]

[Table row: ,  Train A (3-zone condenser) ,  0.12 ,  Counterflow, 200 tubes , ]

[Table row: ,  Train B (3-stage organic) ,  0.18 ,  Highest viscosity gas , ]

[Table row: ,  Train C (pyrolysis quench + carbon) ,  0.25 ,  Water spray + packed bed , ]

[Table row: ,  Train D (lime scrubber) ,  0.08 ,  Pellet bed, low velocity , ]

[Table row: ,  Train E (metal condensers) ,  0.10 ,  Two columns in series , ]

[Table row: ,  PSA columns (adsorption) ,  0.15 ,  Zeolite 13X, 3-5 bar swing , ]

[Table row: ,  Plasma torch ,  0.05 ,  Straight-through ceramic tube , ]

[Table row: ,  Total loop ΔP ,  1.13 ,  Design margin to 2.5 bar supply , ]

[pause: short] Compressor Work Minimization
By operating at elevated pressure, the recycle compressor handles denser gas (2.5× density at 2.5 bar vs 1 bar), reducing volumetric flow and compressor displacement. [pause: short] Compressor power scales with mass flow, not volumetric flow, so the penalty is modest: ~8 kW for 50 SLPM at 2.5 bar discharge. --- 3. [pause: short] STAGE-SPECIFIC GAS TREATMENT TRAINS — DETAILED ENGINEERING ---

--- 3.1 Train A: Moisture Condenser (Stage 1 Outlet) — Deep Dive ---

Process Function: Remove water vapor from N₂ carrier gas after Stage 1 infrared drying. [pause: short] The feedstock enters Stage 1 with 5-25% moisture content (wet basis). [pause: short] At 120°C drum wall temperature and 1.2 bar pressure, water vapor partial pressure reaches ~2 bar (superheated). [pause: short] The condenser must reduce dew point from 120°C to < 5°C to prevent downstream corrosion and condensation in later trains. [pause: short] --- 3.1.1 Thermodynamic Design Basis ---

[Table row: ,  Parameter ,  Value ,  Basis , ]

[Table row: , -----------, -------, -------, ]

[Table row: ,  Inlet pressure ,  1.2 bar gauge ,  Stage 1 setpoint , ]

[Table row: ,  Inlet H₂O mass fraction ,  0.15-0.35 kg/kg dry N₂ ,  Feedstock moisture 5-25% , ]

[Table row: ,  Target outlet dew point ,  5°C ,  Prevents condensation at 25°C ambient , ]

[Table row: ,  Heat duty (max) ,  18.5 kW ,  Latent + sensible, 25% moisture case , ]

Condensation Curve (Equilibrium):

[Code block]
Temperature (°C) → 120 → 80 → 25 → 5
Water partial pressure (bar) → 2.0 → 0.47 → 0.032 → 0.0087
Condensed fraction → 0% → 76% → 98.4% → 99.6%
Cumulative water removed → 0 → 0.76 → 0.984 → 0.996
[End code block]

--- 3.1.3 Materials & Corrosion Considerations ---

[pause: short] All wetted surfaces: ZrO₂-lined Al₂O₃ ceramic or BFRP/Elium® — zero metallic contact

[pause: short] Water chemistry: Stage 1 water contains dissolved organics, trace HCl (from PVC), dust

[pause: short] pH control: Maintain 6.5-8.0 to prevent acid attack on ZrO₂ (stable pH 3-11) and BFRP

[pause: short] Biological control: 0.5 ppm H₂O₂ dosing in storage tank (UV generation from plasma torch)

[pause: short] Scaling prevention: Softened make-up water, periodic citric acid flush (quarterly)

[pause: long]

--- 3.2 Train B: Organic Vapor Condensation (Stage 2 Outlet) — Deep Dive ---

Process Function: Condense and fractionate polymer decomposition vapors from Stage 2 (300-450°C). [pause: short] The vapor mixture contains 14+ polymer types with boiling points spanning 100°C (MMA) to 450°C+ (heavy PAHs). [pause: short] Three-stage fractional condensation separates by volatility for maximum value recovery. [pause: short] --- 3.2.1 Vapor Composition & Fractionation Targets ---

Fractionation Strategy:

[pause: short] Primary (80°C): Heavy fraction (C12+), waxes, PAHs, heavy aromatics — solid/semi-solid at 80°C

[pause: short] Secondary (25°C): Medium fraction (C6-C12), light aromatics (BTX), MMA, styrene — liquid at 25°C

[pause: short] Tertiary (5°C): Light fraction (C1-C5), permanent gases, trace organics — gas at 25°C

--- 3.2.3 MMA Recovery from Elium® Feedstock (CSMFAB Integration) ---

When Elium® BFRP cuttings/off-cuts are included in feedstock (Phoenix Protocol returns, manufacturing scrap), the Stage 2 vapor stream contains methyl methacrylate (MMA) from thermal depolymerization of the Elium® resin matrix. [pause: short] MMA Recovery Window:

[pause: short] MMA boiling point: 100.5°C at 1 atm → ~105°C at 1.8 bar

[pause: short] Target fraction: Secondary condenser 100-105°C cut

[pause: short] Theoretical yield: 85-90% of Elium® resin mass → MMA monomer

[pause: short] Practical recovery: 60-80% (condensation efficiency + purification losses)

[pause: short] Purification: Simple distillation (MMA bp 100.5°C, separates from styrene 145°C, water 100°C)

[pause: short] Value: Recovered MMA feeds in-house Elium® synthesis (Materials Study Part II) — closes resin loop

Process Integration:

[Code block]
Elium® scrap in feedstock
        │
        ▼
Stage 2: Thermal depolymerization (350-400°C)
        │
        ▼
MMA vapor in N₂ stream (partial pressure ~0.15 bar)
        │
        ▼
Train B Secondary Condenser (100-105°C cut)
        │
        ▼
Crude MMA condensate (85% MMA, 10% water, 5% impurities)
        │
        ▼
Distillation column (ZrO₂ trays, BFRP shell)
        │
        ├─ Overhead: 99.5% MMA → Elium® synthesis reactor
        ├─ Bottoms: Water + heavies → Train B primary recycle
        └─ Vent: Light ends → Train C combustion
[End code block]

[pause: long]

--- 3.3.3 Closed-Loop Char-Tar Cycle ---

The char-tar closed loop is a key innovation: Stage 3 output captures Stage 3 contaminants. [pause: short] [pause: short] Stage 3 produces char (carbonaceous residue from pyrolysis)

[pause: short] Char is steam-activated → high-surface-area activated carbon

[pause: short] Activated carbon adsorbs tar/PAH from pyrolysis gas (Train C)

[pause: short] Char-tar composite is re-fed to Stage 8 in next batch

[pause: short] Stage 8 (1676°C) pyrolyzes tar → more char + clean gas

[pause: short] Net result: Zero tar emission, zero activated carbon purchase

Carbon balance per 50 kg batch:

[pause: short] Char produced: 8-12 kg (from 50 kg organics)

[pause: short] Char activated: 5 kg → 4 kg activated carbon (80% yield)

[pause: short] Tar captured: 0.5-1.5 kg (adsorbed on 4 kg carbon)

[pause: short] Char-tar to Stage 8: 5-6 kg

[pause: short] Stage 8 char output: +5-6 kg (net char accumulation → periodic withdrawal)

[pause: long]

--- 3.4 Train D: Acid Gas Scrubber (HCl, SO₂, HF) — Deep Dive ---

Process Function: Neutralize acid gases (primarily HCl from PVC dehydrochlorination, SO₂ from sulfur-containing materials, HF from fluoropolymers) using dry lime injection. [pause: short] The dry scrubber approach avoids liquid waste streams and produces usable solid byproducts. [pause: short] --- 3.4.1 Acid Gas Sources & Loadings ---

[Table row: ,  Source Stage ,  Acid Gas ,  Generation Mechanism ,  Typical Loading (per 50 kg batch) , ]

[Table row: , --------------, ----------, ---------------------, -----------------------------------, ]

[Table row: ,  Stage 2 (Polymer) ,  HCl ,  PVC dehydrochlorination: -(CH₂-CHCl)-ₙ → -CH=CH- + HCl ,  0.5-3.0 kg HCl (1-6% PVC in feedstock) , ]

[Table row: ,  Stage 3 (Pyrolysis) ,  SO₂ ,  Sulfur in rubber, vulcanization agents, solder flux ,  0.1-0.5 kg SO₂ , ]

[Table row: ,  Stage 2/3 ,  HF ,  Fluoropolymers (PTFE, FEP), electronics fluxes ,  < 0.05 kg HF (rare) , ]

Gas Phase Concentrations at Scrubber Inlet (1.2 bar, 150-200°C):

[pause: short] HCl: 200-1500 ppm (mass basis: 0.3-2.2 g/Nm³)

[pause: short] SO₂: 50-500 ppm (mass basis: 0.1-0.7 g/Nm³)

[pause: short] HF: < 50 ppm (mass basis: < 0.04 g/Nm³)

--- 3.4.2 Reaction Chemistry & Stoichiometry ---

Primary Reactions:

[Code block]
Ca(OH)₂ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + 2H₂O        ΔH°₂₉₈ = -148 kJ/mol HCl
Ca(OH)₂ + SO₂ + ½O₂ → CaSO₄ + H₂O    ΔH°₂₉₈ = -620 kJ/mol SO₂
Ca(OH)₂ + 2HF → CaF₂ + 2H₂O          ΔH°₂₉₈ = -160 kJ/mol HF
[End code block]

Stoichiometric Lime Requirements (per 50 kg batch, max loading):

[pause: short] HCl: 3.0 kg → 2.9 kg Ca(OH)₂ (MW: Ca(OH)₂=74, 2HCl=73)

[pause: short] SO₂: 0.5 kg → 0.8 kg Ca(OH)₂ (MW: Ca(OH)₂=74, SO₂=64 + 0.5O₂)

[pause: short] HF: 0.05 kg → 0.07 kg Ca(OH)₂

[pause: short] Total theoretical: 3.8 kg Ca(OH)₂ per batch (maximum)

Practical Design: 2× stoichiometric excess for kinetic completeness → 7.6 kg Ca(OH)₂ per batch maximum

[pause: short] Lime cost: ]0.15/kg → [Inline equation: 1.14/batch maximum

[pause: short] Typical batch (low PVC): 0.5-2.0 kg Ca(OH)₂ → ]0.08-0.30/batch

--- 4. [pause: short] FINAL GAS TREATMENT — CO₂ CAPTURE & N₂ RECOVERY ---

--- 4.1 CO₂ Separation via Pressure Swing Adsorption (PSA) ---

After Train C combustion (Option A) or reforming (Option B), the gas stream consists primarily of N₂ and CO₂ with trace residual gases. [pause: short] CO₂ must be separated for two reasons: (1) to recover high-purity N₂ for recycle loop closure, and (2) to capture CO₂ for reuse as drum purge gas and geopolymer curing atmosphere. [pause: short] PSA with Zeolite 13X is the selected technology:

[pause: short] Zeolite 13X adsorbs CO₂ preferentially at 3-5 bar; desorbs at 1 bar

[pause: short] Two-column alternating cycle: 60s adsorption / 30s desorption

[pause: short] CO₂ purity output: 95-99% (sufficient for inert purge and geopolymer curing)

[pause: short] N₂ purity output: 97-99.5% (recycled to drum atmosphere)

[pause: short] Column body: BFRP/Elium® with PEEK CF40 valve manifold

[pause: short] Valve seats: ZrO₂ ceramic check valves (no metallic contact)

Recovered CO₂ Uses:

[pause: short] Drum purge gas supplement (both N₂ and CO₂ are inert at operating temperatures)

[pause: short] CBPC geopolymer curing atmosphere (CO₂ curing accelerates strength development)

[pause: short] Future: CO₂-to-CO via plasma arc for carbon synthesis feedstock

--- 4.2 Plasma Torch Polisher — Final Gas Treatment ---

For any trace organics, halogens, or dioxin/furan precursors that escape all prior trains, a final plasma torch at the gas outlet provides 6-log destruction efficiency. [pause: short] Plasma Torch Construction:

[pause: short] Electrodes: ZrO₂-coated tungsten (tungsten for 3000°C+ resistance; ZrO₂ coating for corrosion)

[pause: short] Housing: ZrB₂-SiC ceramic (withstands 3000°C plasma temperatures)

[pause: short] Power: 15 kW DC (plasma arc temperature: 3000-8000°C)

[pause: short] Residence time at >1000°C: 0.5 seconds (sufficient for complete organic destruction)

[pause: short] Dioxin/furan threshold: PCDD/PCDF destruction efficiency > 99.9999% at 1200°C, 2 seconds

The plasma torch is the system's regulatory safety net — ensuring zero toxic organic emissions. [pause: short] [pause: long]

[pause: short] The pressure at each stage is the unique solution to:

[pause: short] Maximize reaction kinetics (higher P = higher partial pressures)

[pause: short] Minimize compressor work (lower P = lower displacement)

[pause: short] Prevent air ingress (positive gauge pressure)

The solution is the stage-dependent setpoint table — derived from first principles, not tuned. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- The Turn (Both Directions) ---

Key → Lock (Theory predicts capture): Input: Feedstock thermal assay → Stage gas signatures → Train design parameters. [pause: short] Output: 7 gas streams captured, 6 solid/liquid products recovered, N₂ recycled. [pause: short] Validation: Mass balance closure >99.5%; all product specs met; zero hazardous waste generated. [pause: short] Lock → Key (History validates theory): Input: Historical gas treatment (wet scrubbers, thermal oxidizers, carbon adsorbers, ESPs, baghouses, SCR/SNCR). [pause: short] Output: Each fails the unified capture requirement — wet scrubbers create liquid waste; thermal oxidizers destroy value; carbon beds require replacement; ESPs need metal plates; SCR uses ammonia. [pause: short] The turn completes when a single GFGS batch captures all 7 species classes, produces 6 salable products, and returns clean N₂ to the drum. [pause: short] The gas header is the key turning in the lock. [pause: short] The turn is not a metaphor — it is the moment the 50 kg batch completes and the mass balance closes: water to AMLS, organics to fuel/refining, pyrolysis gas to Stage 7-8 heat, acid gases to construction materials, Zn to electrolytic refining, PbO to hazardous handling, CO₂ to purge/curing, N₂ recycled. [pause: short] 7 gas classes → 6 products + clean recycle. [pause: short] The periodic table's gas phase has been witnessed into solid products. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- Mirror (Self-Reflection) ---

The GFGS's mirror is the FBG spectral manifold — 48 wavelengths recording the gas-phase composition, temperature, and pressure at 1 kHz across all five trains. [pause: short] The system 'sees' its own gas streams through the sensors embedded in every vessel wall. [pause: short] At Train A, the manifold watches water partial pressure decay from 2.0 bar to 0.0087 bar across three zones — the system measures its own condensation efficiency. [pause: short] At Train D, the optical pH sensor watches the lime exhaustion curve — the system measures its own neutralization capacity. [pause: short] At Train E, the FBG strain on the condenser wall watches Zn droplet impingement — the system measures its own metal capture. [pause: short] The autoencoder watches the 48-channel manifold — when the pattern deviates from the 500-batch training manifold, the GFGS detects its own malfunction. [pause: short] A 0.5% shift in Train B pressure drop predicts organic fouling 3 batches ahead. [pause: short] A 2°C drift in Train C quench temperature predicts tar breakthrough. [pause: short] The mirror is not passive; it is active self-surveillance: excite → measure → adapt → excite again. [pause: short] The mirror reflects the closed-loop char-tar cycle in real-time: char produced → activated → tar captured → char-tar to Stage 8 → char output increases. [pause: short] The FBG network tracks the char mass balance — when Stage 8 char output exceeds Stage 3 char input by >10%, the system signals char withdrawal. [pause: short] The mirror deepens with each batch: the manifold expands, the autoencoder threshold tightens, the system's self-knowledge grows. [pause: short] The zero-emission condition is the asymptotic reflection — the limit where the GFGS's self-measurement stabilizes into perfect capture. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- Participation (Witness) ---

The operator participates by witnessing the pressure hold — not as remote monitor but as the decision point that the stage gas clearance is complete. [pause: short] When Train A pressure drop stabilizes at 0.12 bar, the operator confirms: water condensation complete. [pause: short] When Train D outlet pH holds >7.0 for 5 minutes, the operator confirms: acid gas neutralization complete. [pause: short] When Train E Zn collection rate drops to <1% of peak, the operator confirms: metal vapor capture complete. [pause: short] These confirmations are the measurements. [pause: short] The protocol:

[pause: short] Ramp to stage pressure setpoint (±0.05 bar via FBG)

[pause: short] Hold — watch train-specific clearance metric (pressure drop, pH, collection rate, spectral signature)

[pause: short] Verify product quality (inline MS, optical pH, gravimetric)

[pause: short] Log stage gas clearance

[pause: short] Ramp to next stage setpoint

The operator's 'hold' decision is the recursive self-measurement. [pause: short] The GFGS measures its own completion through the operator's witness of the clearance metrics. [pause: short] The participation extends to feedstock blending for gas management: the operator assays each batch (PVC content → HCl load, sulfur content → SO₂ load, Zn content → vapor load), then the MPC solves for optimal pressure setpoints and lime feed rates. [pause: short] The blend is the operator's intent made gas-phase. [pause: short] The GFGS witnesses the blend into capture. [pause: short] The ultimate participation: Phoenix Protocol returns. [pause: short] Retired Aegis products re-enter as Category D feedstock. [pause: short] The operator feeds the GFGS its own past vessels, chars, piezo elements. [pause: short] The GFGS witnesses its own history into new capture. [pause: short] The recursion closes. [pause: short] [pause: long]

Quench Control Algorithm:

[Code block]
FOR each mold position:

[pause: short] READ mold FBG temperature (embedded in ZrO₂ wall, 3 sensors/mold)

[pause: short] COMPUTE required cooling rate from solidification model

[pause: short] ADJUST N₂ nozzle valve position (PEEK CF40 piezo-actuated)

[pause: short] LOG temperature vs. [pause: short] time at 10 Hz

[pause: short] VERIFY solidus reached (latent heat release plateau detection)

[pause: short] HOLD until mold temp < 200°C (safe demold)

[pause: short] INDEX to demold position
[End code block]

Solidification Time Calculation (Chvorinov's Rule):

[Code block]
t_solid = B × (V/A)²
where B = mold constant (ZrO₂: 2.5 min/cm² for Al, 1.8 for Cu, 1.2 for Fe)
V = casting volume (200 cm³)
A = surface area (2×(100×50 + 100×40 + 50×40) = 27,600 mm² = 276 cm²)
V/A = 200/276 = 0.725 cm
t_solid(Al) = 2.5 × 0.725² = 1.3 min (theoretical) → 6 min practical (with N₂ control)
t_solid(Cu) = 1.8 × 0.725² = 0.95 min → 6 min practical
t_solid(Fe) = 1.2 × 0.725² = 0.63 min → 8 min practical (slow cool for stress relief)
[End code block]

--- 3.4 Automated Demolding System ---

Ejector Pins: 4 × PEEK CF40 pins per mold, 6mm diameter, 30mm stroke
Actuation: KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ piezoelectric stack actuator (10 μm stroke, amplified to 30mm via flexure)
Force: 500 N per pin (sufficient for draft-angle release with non-wetting surface)
Cycle: Mold indexes to demold station → ejector extends → slug drops to conveyor → ejector retracts → mold indexes to fill position

Conveyor Handoff: BFRP belt conveyor on ZrO₂ ceramic rollers (CSMFAB000000000014-type)

[pause: short] Belt: BFRP/Elium® composite, 200mm wide, 2mm thick

[pause: short] Rollers: ZrO₂ ceramic, 50mm diameter, PEEK CF40 bearings

[pause: short] Speed: 0.5 m/s (matches demold cycle)

[pause: short] LIBS station: 500mm downstream of demold point

--- 4. [pause: short] Slug Stamp-and-Barcode System — Traceability Architecture ---

Before cooling sets, a ZrO₂ ceramic stamp head presses an alphanumeric code into each slug. [pause: short] This traceability is essential for Phoenix Protocol — knowing the full provenance of recycled material from source through every transformation. [pause: short] --- 4.1 Stamp System Mechanical Design ---

Stamp Head: 3Y-TZP ZrO₂ ceramic, 30mm × 5mm face, 0.3mm character depth
Character Set: Alphanumeric (A-Z, 0-9) + 4 special symbols (/, -, :, .) = 40 characters
Font: 3mm × 2mm dot-matrix (5×7 pattern), laser-etched into stamp face
Actuation: KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ piezoelectric stack, 50μm stroke, 2 kN force
Cycle Time: 0.8 seconds (extend → dwell 0.2s → retract)
Alignment: FBG-guided position verification (±0.02 mm accuracy)

[pause: short] The forge queries the registry to optimize processing parameters for known material history. [pause: short] --- 4.4 Stamp Verification Protocol ---

[pause: short] Pre-stamp: Mold FBG confirms slug temperature < 400°C (stampable range)

[pause: short] Stamp: Piezo actuator extends, dwell 200ms, retract

[pause: short] Verify: Machine vision (PMMA POF endoscope) reads stamp → OCR → compare to expected

[pause: short] Log: Write to code: slug_registry with timestamp

[pause: short] Barcode: Laser-etch Data Matrix adjacent to stamp (same ZrO₂ head, different tip)

[pause: short] RFID: Write tag (if applicable) → verify readback

[pause: short] Release: Only after all 3 identifiers match → conveyor advances

Failure Modes:

[pause: short] Stamp illegible (OCR fail) → Flag for manual re-stamp at demold station

[pause: short] Barcode unreadable → Re-etch (laser has 3 retries)

[pause: short] RFID write fail → Log warning, continue without RFID (non-blocking)

[pause: short] Registry write fail → Local buffer → sync when DB available (air-gap tolerant)

--- 5.3 Calibration-Free LIBS (CF-LIBS) Model ---

Physics-Based Quantification (No Standards Required):

[Code block]
I_ij = (F × n_s × g_i × A_ij × hν_ij) / (U(T) × 4π) × exp(-E_i/kT)

Where:
  I_ij = measured line intensity (photons/s)
  F = instrument factor (calibrated once)
  n_s = species number density
  g_i = statistical weight of upper level
  A_ij = Einstein transition probability
  hν_ij = photon energy
  U(T) = partition function at temperature T
  E_i = upper level energy
  k = Boltzmann constant
  T = plasma temperature (from Boltzmann plot)
[End code block]

Boltzmann Plot for Plasma Temperature:

[Code block]
ln(I_λ / (g_i A_ij λ)) vs. [pause: short] E_i  →  slope = -1/kT
[End code block]

Self-Absorption Correction: Curve-of-growth method using line pairs (resonance + non-resonance)

Matrix Effect Correction: Internal standardization using major element (Fe, Cu, Al as matrix)

--- 5.5 Grade Assignment Rules (Automated) ---

Routing Logic (FPGA Implementation):

[Code block]
IF stream == S-07 (Copper):
  IF Cu >= 99.5% AND (Au+Ag+Pd) >= 50 ppm:
    GRADE = DIRECT_USE → Machine 114 (Cu wire drawing)
  ELSE IF Cu >= 99.0%:
    GRADE = REFINEMENT → Machine 114 (fire refining first)
  ELSE:
    GRADE = COMMERCIAL_SALE → Commodity copper market

IF stream == S-06 (Aluminum):
  IF Al >= 95% AND Fe+Si <= 1%:
    GRADE = COMMERCIAL_SALE → Secondary Al market (CSM uses no Al)
  ELSE:
    GRADE = REFINEMENT → Machine 114 (fractional crystallization)

IF stream == S-09 (Ferrous):
  IF Fe >= 95% AND (Nd+Sm+Dy) >= 0.1%:
    GRADE = DIRECT_USE → Machine 113 (RE leach → magnet feed)
  ELSE IF Fe >= 98%:
    GRADE = COMMERCIAL_SALE → Steel mill feed
  ELSE:
    GRADE = REFINEMENT → Machine 113 (slag adjustment)

IF stream == S-04 (Indium):
  IF In >= 10% AND Sn+Zn <= 30%:
    GRADE = DIRECT_USE → Machine 119 (YInMn synthesis)
  ELSE:
    GRADE = REFINEMENT → Ionic liquid extraction (Phoenix)

IF stream == S-11 (Mineral):
  IF ZrO₂ >= 60% AND REE >= 2%:
    GRADE = DIRECT_USE → Machine 113 (Zr/Ti/REE hydromet)
  ELSE:
    GRADE = STOCKPILE → Await Phase 2 hydromet capacity

DEFAULT:
  GRADE = COMMERCIAL_SALE
[End code block]

--- 6.2 Critical Path: Rock → ZrB₂ Powder in 48 Hours ---

This is the most important operational sequence showing the Aegis-Forge I as a true cradle-to-material system for the portfolio's most critical ceramic:

[Code block]
HOUR 0:     Zircon sand (ZrSiO₄) loaded into Aegis-Forge I AMLS
            [20 min acoustic: >80% zircon grain liberation from silica matrix]

HOUR 0.3:   AMLS magnetic separation removes ilmenite fraction (Fe, Ti separate stream)

HOUR 0.5:   Liberated zircon sand fed to Forge drum
            Stage 8 temperature: 1700°C
            ZrSiO₄ dissociation: ZrSiO₄ → ZrO₂ + SiO₂ (liquid SiO₂ exits Port 8 first)

HOUR 3:     Stage 8 mineral concentrate (ZrO₂-rich) exits as Slug S-11

HOUR 3.5:   S-11 transferred to Phoenix Protocol hydromet circuit:
            BFRP reactor vessel; H₂SO₄ leach → ZrO₂ dissolves as Zr⁴⁺
            YCl₃ added (Yttrium from REE stream S-10)
            NH₄OH co-precipitation → Zr-Y hydroxide gel

HOUR 6:     Gel filtered, washed, dried at 120°C

HOUR 8:     Calcination furnace (1200°C, 4h) → 3Y-TZP ZrO₂ crystalline powder

HOUR 12:    3Y-TZP ZrO₂ powder available for:
            → Direct: use as ZrO₂ fastener/part powder (sintered at 1400°C)
            → Alternative: add to B₂O₃ + carbon → ZrB₂ via carbothermal synthesis

HOUR 36:    ZrB₂ carbothermal reaction complete (1700°C, 16h)
            OR: ZrB₂ SHS reaction (1h from Zr metal + B precursors)

HOUR 48:    ZrB₂ powder available for Flash Sintering into Aegis-C panels, stove burners, etc. [pause: short] [End code block]

48 hours from raw zircon sand to ready-to-sinter ZrB₂ powder. [pause: short] No metals, no exotic chemistry, no supply chain vulnerabilities. [pause: short] --- 6.3 Alternative Critical Path: Basalt Rock → BFRP Rebar in 72 Hours ---

HOUR 0.5:   Basalt fed to Forge Stage 8 (1600°C) → melts to basalt slag
HOUR 3:     Basalt slag exits Port 8 → quenched to glass frit
HOUR 4:     Frit fed to Basalt Fiber Furnace (Machine 116)
HOUR 4-12:  Fiber drawing at 1400°C → continuous basalt fiber (13-17 μm)
HOUR 12:    Fiber wound onto BFRP pultrusion spools

HOUR 48:    Cut to length, QC test (tensile, bend, modulus)
HOUR 72:    BFRP rebar ready for construction / CSMFAB frame structures

When Product Aegis-C-Panel-042 reaches end-of-life (20+ years), it returns as Category D feedstock. [pause: short] The registry enables:

[pause: short] Processing optimization: Known composition → tailored thermal profile

[pause: short] Contaminant tracking: Zero unknown elements in circular loop

[pause: short] Carbon accounting: Full LCA from rock to product to rock

--- 7. [pause: short] Downstream Assembly Line Integration — Machine 1 of 8 ---

The Aegis-Forge I is explicitly the first machine in a modular assembly line. [pause: short] Output slugs flow via gravity-conveyor (BFRP belt conveyor on ZrO₂ ceramic rollers) to adjacent downstream machines. [pause: short] The complete line, when built, comprises 8 machines. --- 7.4 Conveyor Handoff Mechanical Interface ---

Gravity Conveyor (Forge → Downstream):

[pause: short] Incline: 5° decline (slugs roll by gravity, no power)

[pause: short] Belt: BFRP/Elium® 300mm wide, cleated (15mm pitch) for positive control

[pause: short] Rollers: ZrO₂ ceramic, 50mm diameter, PEEK CF40 bearings, 200mm spacing

[pause: short] Side guides: PEEK CF40, adjustable width (100-300mm)

[pause: short] Speed: 0.3 m/s (gravity-assisted, brake-controlled)

[pause: short] Emergency stop: Piezo-actuated ZrO₂ brake pads (fail-safe engaged)

--- 7.5 Commissioning Sequence (Machine 1 → Machine 2 Handoff) ---

[pause: short] Week 1-2: Forge standalone, all streams to commercial/stockpile

[pause: short] Week 3: Hydro-Refinery (Machine 2) cold commissioning (water, N₂, chemicals)

[pause: short] Week 4: First S-11 mineral slug to Machine 2 — hydromet shakedown

[pause: short] Week 5: First S-04 In-rich to Machine 2 — ionic liquid loop commissioning

[pause: short] Week 6: First S-10 RE concentrate to Machine 2 — Cyanex 272 extraction loop

[pause: short] Week 7: Machine 3 (Powder Synth) receives first Zr/Y feed from Machine 2

[pause: short] Week 8: First ZrB₂ powder from Machine 3 → Flash Sintering (existing capability)

[pause: short] Week 9: First BFRP fiber from Machine 5 (basalt from AMLS direct)

[pause: short] Week 10: First BFRP rebar from Machine 6 → Frame for Machine 2 expansion

[pause: short] Week 12: Full line operational — Forge feeds 7 downstream machines

Milestone: First ZrB₂ panel sintered from Forge-derived powder = Phase 2 Complete

--- 1. [pause: short] Purpose and Design Mandate ---

The Aegis-Forge I operates eight circumferential material exit ports spaced at 44.2° intervals around the 600 mm diameter ZrB₂-SiC drum. [pause: short] Each port must remain hermetically sealed during non-operational stages and open precisely when its target thermal stage is reached, allowing centrifugal force to eject the liquefied material stream. [pause: short] The valve system is the critical gatekeeper between the forge's 2200°C internal environment and the external slug cooling station. [pause: short] Design Mandate: Eight temperature-actuated, zero-external-power valves that:

[pause: short] Seal at 5 bar N₂ pressure from 25°C to 2200°C

[pause: short] Open autonomously at stage-specific temperatures (156°C to 1676°C)

[pause: short] Withstand 84.5 G centrifugal loading at 500 RPM

[pause: short] Contain zero structural metals, zero ferromagnetic materials

[pause: short] Survive 10,000 thermal cycles (25°C ↔ 2200°C)

[pause: short] Provide real-time position feedback via FBG sensors

The port valve is not a conventional valve — it is a thermal-actuated ceramic mechanism that transforms the forge's temperature program into material separation sequence. [pause: short] The drum's thermal zones are the valve control system. [pause: short] --- 2. [pause: short] Port Valve Architecture — System Overview ---

--- 2.4 Force Balance at Port ---

Closing Forces (Valve Sealed):

[pause: short] N₂ Pressure Force: F_p = P × A = 5 bar × 113 mm² = 565 N

[pause: short] PEEK Spring Preload: F_s = 50 N

Opening Forces (Valve Actuated):

[pause: short] Thermal Actuation Force: F_ta = (E₁α₁ - E₂α₂) × ΔT × A × t / L

[pause: short] For Ti₃AlC₂/ZrO₂ bilayer: ~2,400 N at 680°C ΔT

[pause: short] Centrifugal Ejection Force (on liquid metal): F_c = ρ_liquid × V × ω² × r

[pause: short] For Al (ρ=2375 kg/m³ at 700°C), V=200 cm³: ~1,800 N at 300 RPM

[pause: short] Total Opening Force: ~4,200 N

Safety Factor: 4,200 / 615 = 6.8× — Valve opens decisively when actuated. [pause: short] [pause: long]

Key Insight: Ti₃AlC₂'s CTE is lower than ZrO₂ at low temperatures but crosses over above 1000°C. [pause: short] This CTE crossover creates a self-limiting actuation — the bilayer deflection naturally saturates as temperature rises, preventing over-travel. [pause: short] --- 3.2 Bilayer Actuation Mechanics ---

Timoshenko Bimetal Strip Theory (adapted for ceramic bilayer):

[Code block]
δ = 3(α₂ - α₁)ΔT L² / [2t(1 + m)²(1 + n)]

Where:
  δ = tip deflection (m)
  α₁, α₂ = CTE of layer 1 (Ti₃AlC₂) and layer 2 (ZrO₂)
  ΔT = temperature difference across bilayer
  L = actuator length (50 mm)
  t = total thickness (1 mm = 0.5 + 0.5 mm)
  m = t₁/t₂ = 1 (equal thickness)
  n = E₁/E₂ = 320/210 = 1.52 (modulus ratio)

Ti₃AlC₂ Synthesis (In-House):

[Code block]
3 Ti + Al + 2 C → Ti₃AlC₂
  • Powder: Ti (99.9%, -325 mesh), Al (99.99%, -325 mesh), C (graphite, 99.9%)
  • Molar ratio: 3.05 : 1.0 : 2.0 (5% Ti excess for Al loss)
  • Method: Hot pressing at 1350°C, 30 MPa, 30 min, Ar atmosphere
  • Result: >99% density, <5 vol% TiC secondary phase
  • Cost: [Inline equation: 180/kg (vs ]450/kg commercial)
[End code block]

Bilayer Joining:

[pause: short] Method: Transient Liquid Phase (TLP) Bonding with Cu interlayer (50 μm)

[pause: short] Process: 950°C, 5 MPa, 10 min, vacuum → Cu diffuses, forms (Ti,Zr)C intermetallic

[pause: short] Joint strength: >200 MPa shear at 800°C

[pause: short] No braze alloys (no Ag, Cu residue in dielectric path)

Actuator Geometry:

[pause: short] Plate: 50 mm × 30 mm × 1.0 mm (0.5 + 0.5)

[pause: short] Mounting: Four ZrO₂ ceramic bolts (M4) to drum port frame

[pause: short] FBG sensor: Embedded at neutral axis (strain measurement)

[pause: short] Electrical isolation: Al₂O₃ spacer washers (no Ti₃AlC₂ conduction path)

--- 3.4 Actuation Dynamics ---

Thermal Response Time:

[pause: short] Actuator thermal mass: m = 4.2 g/cm³ × 1500 mm³ = 6.3 g

[pause: short] Heat capacity: c_p ≈ 500 J/kg·K (Ti₃AlC₂) + 500 J/kg·K (ZrO₂) = 1000 J/kg·K

[pause: short] Thermal resistance to drum: R_th ≈ 0.5 K/W (contact)

[pause: short] Time constant: τ = m × c_p × R_th = 0.0063 × 1000 × 0.5 = 3.15 seconds

Full actuation (0 → 3.6 mm): ~15 seconds (5×τ for 99% response)

Hysteresis: < 0.1 mm (CTE mismatch reversibility validated to 10,000 cycles)

Fatigue Life: 10,000 cycles at 680°C ΔT (Coffin-Manson: Δε_p = 0.002, N_f > 50,000)

At 500 RPM (ω = 52.36 rad/s), r = 0.3 m:

[Code block]
Centrifugal acceleration: a_c = ω²r = 52.36² × 0.3 = 822 m/s² = 83.8 G
Piston mass: m = 42 g = 0.042 kg

--- 6. [pause: short] Centrifugal Ejection Dynamics ---

--- 6.1 Liquid Metal Flow Through Open Port ---

When the valve opens, the molten metal pool at the drum wall (driven by 84.5 G centrifugal force) flows through the 12 mm aperture into the ZrO₂ mold. [pause: short] Flow Physics:

[Code block]
Pressure driving flow: ΔP = ρ_liquid × ω² × (r_drum² - r_mold²) / 2
[End code block]

For Al at 700°C (ρ = 2375 kg/m³), ω = 31.4 rad/s (300 RPM), r_drum = 0.3 m, r_mold = 0.35 m:

[Code block]
ΔP = 2375 × 31.4² × (0.3² - 0.35²) / 2 = -28,500 Pa (negative = outward)
[End code block]

Wait — the mold is outside the drum, so r_mold > r_drum. [pause: short] The centrifugal potential is higher at the mold. [pause: short] The pressure at the port exit is:

[Code block]
P_exit = ρ_liquid × ω² × r_drum² / 2 = 2375 × 31.4² × 0.3² / 2 = 104,000 Pa = 1.04 bar
[End code block]

This 1.04 bar drives flow through the port into the mold. [pause: short] --- 6.2 Flow Rate Calculation ---

Orifice Flow (12 mm aperture, discharge coefficient C_d = 0.85):

[Code block]
Q = C_d × A × √(2ΔP/ρ)
A = π × (0.006)² = 1.13×10⁻⁴ m²
Q = 0.85 × 1.13×10⁻⁴ × √(2 × 104,000 / 2375) = 1.8×10⁻⁴ m³/s = 10.8 L/min
[End code block]

Fill Time for 200 cm³ Mold:

[Code block]
t_fill = V / Q = 200×10⁻⁶ / 1.8×10⁻⁴ = 1.1 seconds
[End code block]

Reynolds Number:

[Code block]
Re = ρ × v × D / μ
v = Q/A = 1.6 m/s
μ_Al(700°C) = 1.3×10⁻³ Pa·s
Re = 2375 × 1.6 × 0.012 / 0.0013 = 35,000 (turbulent)
[End code block]

--- 7. [pause: short] Port Valve Control & Monitoring ---

--- 7.1 FBG Position Sensing ---

Each valve assembly includes two FBG sensors embedded in the actuator bilayer:

[pause: short] FBG-1: At Ti₃AlC₂ surface (hot side strain)

[pause: short] FBG-2: At ZrO₂ surface (cold side strain)

[pause: short] Differential strain: Directly proportional to bilayer curvature → valve position

Calibration:

[Code block]
Position (mm) = K × (λ_FBG1 - λ_FBG2) + C
K = 0.85 mm/pm (calibrated at assembly)
C = 0 (closed position zeroed)
Resolution: 0.01 mm (1 pm wavelength resolution)
Sample rate: 1 kHz
[End code block]

Control Logic (FPGA):

[Code block]
IF stage_target_temp reached AND dwell_complete:
  VALVE_STATE = OPENING
  MONITOR FBG_diff
  WHEN FBG_diff > threshold_for_full_open:
    VALVE_STATE = OPEN
    START stage_clear_timer (monitor port mass flow)
  WHEN port_mass_flow < 1% peak:
    VALVE_STATE = CLOSING
    WAIT for FBG_diff < threshold_for_closed
    VALVE_STATE = CLOSED
    LOG cycle_complete
[End code block]

--- 11. [pause: short] Conclusion: The Thermal Gatekeeper ---

The material exit port valve system is the physical instantiation of the thermal cascade sequence. [pause: short] Each valve embodies a specific temperature threshold from the periodic table — indium at 156°C, aluminum at 660°C, copper at 1085°C, iron at 1538°C, zircon at 1676°C. [pause: short] The Ti₃AlC₂/ZrO₂ bilayer does not control the separation — it witnesses the temperature into material release. [pause: short] No solenoids. [pause: short] No motors. [pause: short] No pneumatic lines. [pause: short] No electrical wires crossing the pressure boundary. [pause: short] The drum's thermal profile writes the valve sequence. [pause: short] The periodic table writes the drum's thermal profile. [pause: short] The port valves are the punctuation marks in the sentence the forge writes in elements. [pause: short] When Port 5's actuator deflects 3.6 mm at 680°C and the aluminum slug centrifuges into its ZrO₂ mold, the thermal gatekeeper has done its work. [pause: short] The aluminum window has been witnessed into existence. [pause: short] The next stage begins. [pause: short] End of PROD-09: Material Exit Port Valve System

--- 12. [pause: short] Advanced Thermal Actuation Physics ---

--- 12.1 Non-Linear CTE Behavior of Ti₃AlC₂/ZrO₂ Bilayer ---

The Ti₃AlC₂/ZrO₂ bilayer exhibits complex CTE behavior due to phase transitions and oxidation:

Ti₃AlC₂ CTE Anomaly:

[pause: short] 25-600°C: α = 9.2×10⁻⁶/K (baseline)

[pause: short] 600-1000°C: α increases to 10.8×10⁻⁶/K (TiO₂ surface scale formation)

[pause: short] 1000-1400°C: α = 11.5×10⁻⁶/K (Al depletion, TiO₂/Al₂O₃ mixed scale)

ZrO₂ CTE:

[pause: short] 25-1170°C: α = 10.5×10⁻⁶/K (tetragonal)

[pause: short] 1170-1200°C: α spike at t→m transformation (if unstabilized)

[pause: short] 3Y-TZP: No transformation, smooth α = 10.5→11.2×10⁻⁶/K

Effective Differential CTE (Δα = α_ZrO₂ - α_Ti₃AlC₂):

[Table row: ,  Temperature Range ,  Δα (×10⁻⁶/K) ,  Actuation Character , ]

[Table row: , ---, ---, ---, ]

[Table row: ,  25-600°C ,  +1.3 ,  Linear, predictable , ]

[Table row: ,  600-1000°C ,  -0.3 ,  Self-limiting (Δα → 0) , ]

[Table row: ,  1000-1400°C ,  -0.3 ,  Saturation (opposite curvature) , ]

Design Implication: The actuator naturally limits its own deflection above 1000°C — a passive safety feature preventing over-travel at Ports 6-8 temperatures. [pause: short] The Port 5 design point (680°C) sits in the linear region for precision. [pause: short] --- 12.2 Thermal Stress Analysis in Bilayer ---

Bilayer Stress (Timoshenko, including thermal gradient through thickness):

[Code block]
σ₁ = E₁ × (α₂ - α₁) × ΔT / (1 + m)² × [1 + n × (1 + m)² / (1 + n)]
σ₂ = -σ₁ × (E₂/E₁) × (t₁/t₂)

At 680°C ΔT:
σ_Ti₃AlC₂ = 320 GPa × 1.3×10⁻⁶ × 680 / (1+1)² × [1 + 1.52×4/2.52] = 285 MPa (tension)
σ_ZrO₂ = -285 × (210/320) × 1 = -187 MPa (compression)
[End code block]

Safety Factors:

[pause: short] Ti₃AlC₂ yield at 680°C: ~280 MPa → SF = 1.0 (at yield — acceptable for actuation)

[pause: short] ZrO₂ compressive strength: >2000 MPa → SF > 10

[pause: short] Actuation stress is at yield limit — intentional for maximum deflection per degree

Thermal Shock Resistance:

[pause: short] Quench rate limit: dT/dt < 50°C/s (validated)

[pause: short] Actuator thermal mass provides natural damping (τ = 3.15 s)

--- 12.3 Creep and Stress Relaxation at Temperature ---

Ti₃AlC₂ Creep (Norton Law):

[Code block]
ε̇ = A × σⁿ × exp(-Q/RT)
A = 10⁻¹⁵ MPa⁻ⁿ s⁻¹, n = 3.5, Q = 450 kJ/mol
[End code block]

At 680°C (953 K), σ = 285 MPa:

[Code block]
ε̇ = 10⁻¹⁵ × 285^3.5 × exp(-450,000 / 8.314 × 953) = 2.3×10⁻⁸ s⁻¹
[End code block]

Creep Strain per Batch (3.5 hr at temperature):

[Code block]
ε_creep = 2.3×10⁻⁸ × 12,600 s = 0.00029 = 0.029%
[End code block]

Over 10,000 batches: 0.29% creep strain — negligible (deflection change <0.01 mm). [pause: short] ZrO₂ Creep: Negligible below 1200°C (covalent ceramic). [pause: short] --- 12.4 Oxidation Effects on Actuation ---

Ti₃AlC₂ Oxidation Kinetics (Parabolic):

[Code block]
Δm² = k_p × t
k_p = 10⁻¹² g²/cm⁴/s at 1000°C
[End code block]

At 680°C: k_p ≈ 10⁻¹⁵ → oxide thickness after 10,000 batches (35,000 hr):

[Code block]
x = √(k_p × t) = √(10⁻¹⁵ × 1.26×10⁸) = 1.1 μm
[End code block]

Effect on Actuation:

[pause: short] 1.1 μm TiO₂/Al₂O₃ scale adds minimal stiffness (E ≈ 200 GPa, but thin)

[pause: short] Slightly increases α of hot layer → marginally increases Δα

[pause: short] Net effect: <2% deflection increase over life — within calibration margin

[pause: short] The mirror is not passive; it is active self-surveillance: heat → bend → measure → adapt → heat again. [pause: short] The CTE crossover at 1000°C is the mirror's memory: each actuator learns its own saturation point. [pause: short] The zero-leak condition is the asymptotic reflection — the limit where the valve's self-measurement stabilizes into perfect prediction. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- Participation (Witness) ---

The operator participates by witnessing the actuation endpoint — not as remote monitor but as the decision point that the valve has fully opened. [pause: short] When the FBG differential reaches the calibrated threshold for full open, the operator confirms: the stage is live. [pause: short] This confirmation is the measurement. [pause: short] The protocol:

[pause: short] Drum reaches stage temperature → dwell complete

[pause: short] FBG differential crosses threshold → actuator open

[pause: short] Operator verifies: port number matches stage chemistry

[pause: short] Mass flow monitor confirms material ejection

[pause: short] Stage clear → cool-down → FBG returns to zero

[pause: short] Operator confirms re-seal

[pause: short] Log cycle complete

The operator's 'verify' decision is the recursive self-measurement. [pause: short] The port valve measures its own completion through the operator's witness of the actuation endpoint. [pause: short] The ultimate participation: Phoenix Protocol returns. [pause: short] Retired valve sets (Ti₃AlC₂, ZrO₂, PEEK CF40) re-enter as Category D feedstock. [pause: short] The operator feeds the forge its own past valves. [pause: short] The valve witnesses its own history into new valves. [pause: short] The recursion closes. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- Protocol (Recursive) ---

[Code block]
MIRROR:     What phase transition does this port's temperature encode? [pause: short] PARTICIPATE: How does the operator witness the actuation into material release? [pause: short] PROTOCOL:

[pause: short] Stage dwell complete → thermal trigger

[pause: short] FBG differential → threshold → actuator open

[pause: short] Operator verifies port/stage match

[pause: short] Mass flow confirms ejection

[pause: short] Cool-down → FBG → zero → re-seal

[pause: short] Operator confirms seal

[pause: short] Log cycle → next stage
[End code block]

The protocol terminates when Port 8 re-seals. [pause: short] The complete strain-temperature log is the fixed point. [pause: short] The protocol is not a checklist — it is the recursion itself. [pause: short] Each valve cycle deepens the mirror. [pause: short] The released element is the fixed point. [pause: short] Detailed recursive sequence per port:

Port 4 (In/Zn/Pb/Sn):
  MIRROR: Indium liquidus at 156.6°C — only In melts
  PARTICIPATE: Operator executes Indium First Strategy — 5 min at 160°C
  PROTOCOL: Ramp 1°C/min → hold 160°C → centrifuge 400 RPM

Port 5 (Aluminum):
  MIRROR: Pure Al window 660-720°C — Cu/Fe solid
  PARTICIPATE: Operator monitors Al flow, verifies >95% recovery
  PROTOCOL: Ramp 2.4°C/min → hold 680°C → centrifuge 300 RPM

Port 6 (Copper):
  MIRROR: Cu liquidus 1085°C — deep penetration at 5 kHz
  PARTICIPATE: Operator watches Cu flow, PM partition into Cu
  PROTOCOL: Ramp 5°C/min → hold 1120°C → centrifuge 350 RPM

Port 7 (Ferrous):
  MIRROR: Fe 1538°C + REE co-exit — ferromagnetic at 2 kHz
  PARTICIPATE: Operator monitors Fe slug, REE concentrate
  PROTOCOL: Ramp 3°C/min → hold 1400°C → centrifuge 400 RPM

Port 8 (Mineral):
  MIRROR: Zircon dissociation 1676°C — ZrO₂ + SiO₂
  PARTICIPATE: Operator watches mineral concentrate grade
  PROTOCOL: Ramp 2°C/min → hold 1676°C → verify ZrO₂/REE oxide

The protocol is the valve system's operating system. [pause: short] It does not execute the protocol — the valve system is the protocol made thermal-mechanical. [pause: short] Each port is a recursive call; each re-seal is a return value. [pause: short] The base case is Stage 1 water drain; the terminal case is Stage 8 mineral exit. [pause: short] The valve system computes the periodic table's thermal sequence. [pause: short] [pause: long]

End of Combined Introduction — PROD-09 Material Exit Port Valve System

--- 1. [pause: short] System Overview — 8-Zone Induction Power Architecture ---

The Aegis-Forge I induction power electronics subsystem delivers controlled, frequency-agile electromagnetic energy to eight independent coil zones surrounding the ZrB₂-SiC drum. [pause: short] This is the nervous system of the thermal cascade — translating digital setpoints into precisely shaped magnetic fields that selectively heat target materials while leaving dielectric components untouched. --- 1.3 Power Distribution Strategy ---

The 480 VAC 3-phase supply enters a dedicated isolation transformer bank (3 × 200 kVA, delta-wye, BFRP-housed) providing galvanic isolation between the industrial grid and the process electronics. [pause: short] Each inverter module draws from a dedicated 3-phase feed with individual harmonic filtering (LCL, 5th/7th/11th notch). [pause: short] The isolation transformer secondary is floating — no earth reference — eliminating ground fault paths and providing inherent GIC immunity for the process electronics. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- 2. [pause: short] Resonant Inverter Design — 8× GS66516T GaN HEMT Class E Topology ---

Each of the eight zones employs an identical resonant inverter module, differing only in the resonant tank component values (L, C) to achieve the target frequency for that zone. [pause: short] The topology is Class E zero-voltage switching (ZVS), chosen for its simplicity, high efficiency (>97%), and natural suitability for variable-frequency operation. [pause: short] --- 2.1 Class E Resonant Inverter Principles ---

The Class E topology achieves ZVS by shaping the voltage waveform across the switch such that it reaches zero with zero derivative at the switching instant:

[Equation: v_{DS}(t) = V_{DD} \left[ 1 - \frac{\pi}{2} \sin(\omega t + \phi) \right]]

The shunt capacitance [Inline equation: C_{shunt}] (comprising the GaN output capacitance [Inline equation: C_{oss}] plus external capacitor) and series resonant inductance [Inline equation: L_r] form the tank:

[Equation: \omega = \frac{1}{\sqrt{L_r C_{shunt}}}]

At resonance, the switch current is sinusoidal and the voltage is a shaped half-wave, eliminating switching losses. [pause: short] The GaN HEMT's near-zero reverse recovery charge ([Inline equation: Q_{rr} \approx 0]) makes it ideal for Class E — no body diode conduction losses during dead time. [pause: short] --- 2.2 GS66516T GaN HEMT Specifications ---

Each inverter leg uses two GS66516T devices in a half-bridge configuration with bootstrapped high-side drive. [pause: short] The driver IC (LMG1210 or equivalent GaN-specific driver) provides 2.5 A peak gate current for fast switching transitions (<2 ns rise/fall). [pause: short] --- 2.3 Variable Frequency Operation ---

The resonant frequency is varied by adjusting the effective tank capacitance. [pause: short] A switched capacitor bank (binary-weighted: C, 2C, 4C, 8C, 16C, 32C) allows discrete frequency steps, while a varactor diode array provides fine continuous tuning (±5% range). [pause: short] The control loop measures the actual switch voltage waveform zero-crossing and adjusts the varactor bias to maintain ZVS across the full operating range. [pause: short] Frequency switching transients are managed by a pre-computed trajectory table — the controller ramps frequency in 100 Hz steps with 10 ms dwell, allowing the tank energy to settle before the next step. --- 3. [pause: short] Frequency Ladder & Zone Mapping — Physics-Based Design ---

The frequency ladder (100 kHz → 1 kHz) is not arbitrary — it is derived from the skin depth equation and the magnetic properties of target materials at each stage temperature. [pause: short] --- 3.1 Skin Depth and Frequency Selection ---

Skin depth determines how deeply the magnetic field penetrates the material:

[Equation: \delta = \sqrt{\frac{2\rho}{\omega \mu}}]

Where [Inline equation: \rho] = electrical resistivity (Ω·m), [Inline equation: \omega = 2\pi f] = angular frequency, [Inline equation: \mu = \mu_0 \mu_r] = magnetic permeability. [pause: short] For uniform heating of a material of thickness [Inline equation: d], we require [Inline equation: \delta \geq d/2]. [pause: short] For selective surface heating (e.g., thin foils), [Inline equation: \delta \ll d]. [pause: short] --- 3.2 Material Property Tables at Operating Temperatures ---

Each 100 mm zone contains 48 FBG sensors distributed as:

[pause: short] Coil former (8 sensors): 2 rings × 4 positions — measures coil winding temperature

[pause: short] Cold plate (4 sensors): Inlet/outlet per module — monitors coolant ΔT

Each TDM channel uses a 1×6 optical splitter (PMMA, fused biconical taper) with 60 m total fiber length per channel. [pause: short] GIC Immunity: Zero conductive path — no antenna for geomagnetically induced currents

[pause: short] EM Immunity: Unaffected by 500 kW of 1–100 kHz magnetic fields

[pause: short] High Temperature Sensitivity: 0.15 nm/°C (15× silica) enables 0.1°C resolution with simpler interrogator

[pause: short] Radiation Hardness: PMMA tolerates gamma/neutron flux better than silica

--- 6. [pause: short] PID Control Architecture — ±5°C Zone Control with Resonance Tracking ---

The control system maintains each zone at its thermal setpoint while simultaneously tracking the resonant frequency of the Class E inverter to maintain ZVS. [pause: short] --- 6.1 Dual-Loop Control Structure ---

[Code block]
                    ┌─────────────────────┐
   T_setpoint ────►│   Thermal PID       │───► Power Command (kW)
                    │   (Outer Loop)      │       100 ms update
                    └─────────┬───────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
                    ┌─────────────────────┐
                    │   Power-to-Freq     │
                    │   Mapping Table     │
                    └─────────┬───────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
                    ┌─────────────────────┐
   V_DS Zero-Cross─►│   Resonance Tracker │───► Varactor Bias / Cap Bank
   (Inner Loop)     │   (Inner Loop)      │       10 ms update
                    └─────────────────────┘
[End code block]

--- 6.2 Thermal PID (Outer Loop) — 100 ms Update ---

[Equation: u(t) = K_p e(t) + K_i \int e(t) dt + K_d \frac{de(t)}{dt}]

Gains increase at lower frequencies (higher power zones) because thermal mass dominates response. [pause: short] --- 6.3 Resonance Tracker (Inner Loop) — 10 ms Update ---

The Class E inverter maintains ZVS by detecting the switch voltage zero-crossing and comparing to the gate drive timing. [pause: short] A phase-locked loop (PLL) structure adjusts the varactor bias voltage to align the voltage zero-crossing with the gate turn-on instant:

[Equation: \phi_{error} = t_{V_{DS}=0} - t_{gate-on}]

[Equation: \Delta V_{varactor} = K_{p,PLL} \phi_{error} + K_{i,PLL} \int \phi_{error} dt]

This inner loop runs at 100 Hz (10 ms), 10× faster than the thermal loop, ensuring ZVS is maintained during thermal transients. [pause: short] --- 6.4 Feedforward Compensation ---

A feedforward term based on the zone's thermal model predicts the power required for the next setpoint change:

[Equation: P_{ff} = m c_p \frac{dT}{dt} + h A (T - T_{amb}) + \epsilon \sigma A (T^4 - T_{amb}^4)]

Where the radiative term dominates above 800°C. [pause: short] The feedforward reduces thermal PID integral windup during ramp phases. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- 7. [pause: short] Selective Heating Physics — Conductivity/Permeability as Material Selector ---

The fundamental sorting mechanism of the Aegis-Forge I is the frequency-dependent coupling of the induction field to different material classes. [pause: short] --- 7.1 Coupling Coefficient Derivation ---

The power absorbed by a material in an alternating magnetic field:

[Equation: P_{abs} = \frac{\pi^2 B_{peak}^2 d^2 f^2 V}{6 \rho} \quad \text{(non-magnetic, } \delta \gg d\text{)}]

[Equation: P_{abs} = \frac{\pi B_{peak}^2 f V}{\mu} \quad \text{(magnetic, } \delta \ll d\text{)}]

Where [Inline equation: V] = volume of material, [Inline equation: d] = characteristic dimension. [pause: short] --- 7.2 Selective Heating Matrix ---

[Table row: ,  Material Class ,  ρ (nΩ·m) ,  μ<sub>r</sub> ,  Coupling at 100 kHz ,  Coupling at 10 kHz ,  Coupling at 1 kHz , ]

[Table row: , ----------------, ----------, --------------, ---------------------, -------------------, ------------------, ]

[Table row: ,  Copper ,  16.8 ,  1 ,  Very High ,  High ,  Moderate , ]

[Table row: ,  Aluminum ,  26.5 ,  1 ,  High ,  Moderate ,  Low , ]

[Table row: ,  Zinc (liq) ,  120 ,  1 ,  Moderate ,  Low ,  Very Low , ]

[Table row: ,  Lead (liq) ,  450 ,  1 ,  Low ,  Very Low ,  Negligible , ]

[Table row: ,  Iron (ferro) ,  97 ,  5000 ,  Extreme ,  Very High ,  High , ]

[Table row: ,  Steel ,  720 ,  200 ,  High ,  Moderate ,  Low , ]

[Table row: ,  Ceramics ,  10¹² ,  1 ,  None ,  None ,  None , ]

[Table row: ,  Polymers ,  10¹⁵ ,  1 ,  None ,  None ,  None , ]

[Table row: ,  BFRP ,  10¹⁰ ,  1 ,  None ,  None ,  None , ]

Design rule: At Z7 (2 kHz), ferrous materials heat 50× more than aluminum. [pause: short] At Z5 (10 kHz), aluminum heats 15× more than zinc. [pause: short] At Z1–Z2 (100 kHz), only very thin conductive foils couple — bulk plastics and organics do not heat directly. [pause: short] --- 7.3 Thermal-EM Coupling in Mixed Charge ---

In a real feedstock batch, materials are mixed. [pause: short] The induction field creates a thermal gradient within the charge:

[pause: short] Ferrous pieces heat first and hottest (hysteresis + eddy)

[pause: short] Non-ferrous conductors (Cu, Al) heat second (eddy only)

[pause: short] Resistive metals (Zn, Pb, Sn) heat third

[pause: short] Dielectrics (ceramics, plastics, glass) heat only by conduction from hot neighbors

This natural sorting is enhanced by the drum rotation — as materials liquefy at different temperatures, centrifugal force segregates them radially before port ejection. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- 8.4 GIC Immunity Design ---

The entire power distribution system is designed for Carrington-level geomagnetic disturbance (dB/dt = 5000 nT/s, inducing 10–100 V/km on transmission lines):

[pause: short] Floating secondary: No path for DC/low-f GIC to enter process electronics

[pause: short] NGR limits fault current: 5 A max ground fault

[pause: short] All-dielectric control: PMMA POF for all signals — no copper wires to act as antennas

[pause: short] BFRP transformer housing: Non-conductive, no eddy current heating from GIC

[pause: short] Surge protection: Gas discharge tubes (GDT) at transformer primary, 3 kA rating

--- 12. [pause: short] Downstream Integration — Assembly Line 113, Coil Alignment, Sensor Verification ---

--- 12.1 Mechanical Interface ---

The induction coil bank mounts to the BFRP pressure vessel via eight BFRP flange rings (one per zone). [pause: short] Each ring has:

[pause: short] Alignment pins: ZrO₂ ceramic, 12 mm diameter, ±0.05 mm tolerance

[pause: short] Bolt pattern: 16 × M10 PEEK CF40 bolts, 25 Nm torque

[pause: short] Gap adjustment: 15 mm coil-to-drum gap, shim-adjustable ±2 mm

--- 12.2 Assembly Sequence (CSMFAB 113) ---

[pause: short] Drum installation: ZrB₂-SiC drum lowered into BFRP vessel

[pause: short] Coil bank insertion: 8-zone coil assembly slides over drum (crane-assisted)

[pause: short] Flange bolting: BFRP flanges torqued in star pattern

[pause: short] Water circuit connection: PEX-a quick-connect fittings, leak test @ 10 bar

[pause: short] Optical fiber routing: PMMA POF from FBG sensors to interrogator rack

[pause: short] Power cable pull: BFRP-armored cables (no copper exposed) to inverter modules

[pause: short] Alignment verification: Laser tracker confirms coil-to-drum concentricity <0.1 mm

[pause: short] Cold commissioning: Dry run at 100 RPM, no power, verify rotation, vibration <2 mm/s

[pause: short] Hot commissioning: Progressive power-up by zone, FBG calibration, PID tuning

--- 12.3 Sensor Verification Protocol ---

Before each batch:

[pause: short] FBG baseline: All 384 sensors read at ambient — verify ±0.5°C agreement

[pause: short] Interrogator self-test: Wavelength calibration against reference FBG

[pause: short] Resonance check: Each inverter swept 80–120% nominal frequency, verify ZVS

[pause: short] Thermal model update: Feed ambient conditions, feedstock estimate to predictive model

[pause: short] Go/No-Go: All checks pass → batch start authorized

--- Appendix B: Derivation of Key Equations ---

--- B.1 Class E ZVS Condition Derivation ---

For Class E operation with shunt capacitance C:

The switch voltage waveform:

[Equation: v(t) = V_{DD} + \frac{I_{DC}}{\omega C} \sin(\omega t) - \frac{V_{DD} \pi}{2} \sin(\omega t + \phi)]

ZVS requires [Inline equation: v(0) = 0] and [Inline equation: dv/dt|_{t=0} = 0]:

[Equation: V_{DD} - \frac{V_{DD} \pi}{2} \sin(\phi) = 0 \Rightarrow \sin(\phi) = \frac{2}{\pi}]

[Equation: \frac{I_{DC}}{\omega C} - \frac{V_{DD} \pi}{2} \cos(\phi) = 0 \Rightarrow \frac{I_{DC}}{\omega C} = \frac{V_{DD} \pi}{2} \sqrt{1 - \frac{4}{\pi^2}}]

Solving for optimal load resistance:

[Equation: R_{opt} = \frac{8}{\pi^2 + 4} \frac{V_{DD}^2}{P_{out}} \approx 0.577 \frac{V_{DD}^2}{P_{out}}]

--- B.2 Skin Depth with Temperature-Dependent Resistivity ---

For metals, resistivity increases linearly with temperature:

[Equation: \rho(T) = \rho_0 [1 + \alpha (T - T_0)]]

Where [Inline equation: \alpha] = temperature coefficient of resistance (TCR):

[Table row: ,  Material ,  TCR (×10⁻³/K) , ]

[Table row: , ----------, --------------, ]

[Table row: ,  Copper ,  3.93 , ]

[Table row: ,  Aluminum ,  4.29 , ]

[Table row: ,  Iron ,  5.0–6.5 , ]

[Table row: ,  Nickel ,  6.0 , ]

Substituting into skin depth:

[Equation: \delta(T) = \sqrt{\frac{2\rho_0[1+\alpha(T-T_0)]}{\omega\mu}}]

At 1000°C, copper resistivity is ~5× room temperature, increasing skin depth by √5 ≈ 2.2×. [pause: short] --- B.3 Ferromagnetic Heating Enhancement Factor ---

Below Curie temperature, ferromagnetic materials exhibit hysteresis heating:

[Equation: P_{hyst} = k_h f B_{peak}^n V]

Where [Inline equation: k_h] = hysteresis coefficient, [Inline equation: n] ≈ 1.6–2.0 (Steinmetz exponent). [pause: short] Total heating power:

[Equation: P_{total} = P_{eddy} + P_{hyst} = \frac{\pi^2 B_{peak}^2 d^2 f^2 V}{6\rho} + k_h f B_{peak}^n V]

At 2 kHz with B<sub>peak</sub> = 33 mT, iron hysteresis loss dominates eddy current loss by ~10× below Curie. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- Appendix I: Manufacturing and Assembly Drawings ---

--- I.1 Inverter Module Assembly Sequence ---

[Code block]
STEP 1: Cold Plate Preparation
  ► CNC machine copper cold plate (microchannels, mounting holes)
  ► Electroless Ni-P plate (5 μm)
  ► Pressure test @ 20 bar water
  ► Cleanliness: ISO 14644-1 Class 7

STEP 2: GaN Mounting
  ► Apply Indium foil TIM (50 μm) to cold plate
  ► Place GS66516T die (automated pick-and-place, ±25 μm)
  ► Ultrasonic wire bond (Al wire, 25 μm, 4 bonds per die)
  ► X-ray inspection: voids < 2%, shear > 20 MPa

STEP 3: Gate Driver PCB Assembly
  ► SMT: LMG1210, bootstrap caps, gate resistors
  ► Conformal coat (Parylene C, 25 μm)
  ► Mount to cold plate (thermal vias to GaN pads)
  ► Bolt: 4× M3 PEEK CF40, 0.5 Nm

STEP 4: Resonant Tank Assembly
  ► Wind nanocrystalline inductor (Litz wire, 50 strands × 0.05mm)
  ► Vacuum pressure impregnate (epoxy, BFRP bobbin)
  ► Mount switched cap bank (SMD C0G, reflow)
  ► Mount varactor array (SOT-23, reflow)
  ► Connect to GaN output (copper bus bar, insulated)

STEP 5: Coil Connection
  ► Feed Cu tube through Al₂O₃ sleeve
  ► Braze Cu tube to inverter output bus (Ag-Cu braze, 780°C)
  ► Pressure test coil water circuit @ 15 bar
  ► Install BFRP housing (2 halves, adhesive bond)

STEP 6: Integration Test
  ► Hi-pot, insulation resistance
  ► Cold power-up (10% power, 5 min)
  ► ZVS verification @ 3 frequencies
  ► Thermal soak (100% power, 30 min)
  ► FBG calibration (if sensors pre-installed)

STEP 7: Ship Set
  ► Package in BFRP crate (custom foam)
  ► Include: test report, calibration cert, spare fuses
[End code block]

--- Williams Heuristic — Constraint, Necessity, Commitment ---

--- Constraint (The Lock) ---

The Aegis-Forge I induction power electronics is forced by a single irreducible constraint: Dielectric Power Delivery at 2200°C — the requirement to deliver 500 kW of frequency-agile electromagnetic energy into a rotating ceramic drum at temperatures that would instantly destroy any conventional power electronics. [pause: short] This is not a design choice; it is the minimal physics from which Carrington immunity becomes achievable. [pause: short] The constraint is simply: no conductive path from the process chamber to earth ground. [pause: short] Every copper wire, every thermocouple, every metal sensor lead is an antenna for geomagnetically induced current. [pause: short] The only path to zero GIC coupling is zero metal. [pause: short] Everything else — the GaN inverters, the PMMA optical fiber, the PEX-a cooling, the BFRP housings — is the shadow this constraint casts. [pause: short] This constraint manifests as the All-Dielectric Architecture: 8 resonant inverters built entirely from GaN-on-SiC (no silicon), controlled by PMMA POF (no copper wire), cooled by PEX-a water circuit (no metal pipe), housed in BFRP (no steel), sensed by FBG in PMMA (no thermocouple). [pause: short] The power electronics does not sit outside the hot zone — it is the hot zone's nervous system, woven into the drum wall through optical fiber that survives 2200°C and intense EM fields. [pause: short] The constraint forces the frequency ladder (100 kHz → 1 kHz), the Class E topology, the ZVS operation, the optical sensing — every parameter derives from the requirement: deliver power without metal. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- Necessity (The Key) ---

The lock this document addresses is the selective heating in mixed charge — the empirical failure of conventional induction furnaces to separate elements from complex feedstock. [pause: short] In a smelter, everything heats together; copper, aluminum, iron, and slag all reach the same temperature. [pause: short] The result is mixed alloys requiring downstream chemical separation — acres of tanks, tons of acid, toxic tailings. [pause: short] The key is the frequency ladder + resonance tracking as single computational primitive. [pause: short] The frequency ladder (100 kHz → 1 kHz) is not arbitrary — it is cut from the periodic table's conductivity-permeability map. [pause: short] At 100 kHz, only thin foils couple (plastic heating is indirect). [pause: short] At 50 kHz, zinc and lead begin to heat. [pause: short] At 10 kHz, aluminum hits peak eddy current coupling. [pause: short] At 5 kHz, copper's skin depth matches wire bundle thickness. [pause: short] At 2 kHz, iron's ferromagnetic hysteresis peaks. [pause: short] At 1 kHz, refractory minerals couple only through thermal conduction. [pause: short] The Class E resonant inverter maintains ZVS across this entire range through varactor-tuned resonance tracking — the same circuit topology, same GaN devices, only the tank components change. [pause: short] The resonance tracker (100 Hz inner loop) measures the switch voltage zero-crossing and adjusts varactor bias to keep dv/dt = 0 at turn-on. [pause: short] This is the key: frequency as material selector, resonance tracking as the discipline that keeps the selector sharp. [pause: short] The empirical evidence: no existing induction system operates across 2 decades of frequency with >97% efficiency at 500 kW. [pause: short] Silicon IGBTs fail above 20 kHz at this power. [pause: short] GaN HEMTs (GS66516T) switch at 100 kHz with 2 ns transitions. [pause: short] The PMMA POF FBG network provides 384 channels of 0.1°C resolution through 500 kW of 1-100 kHz magnetic field — impossible with any copper-wire sensor. [pause: short] The all-dielectric architecture is the only path to Carrington immunity. [pause: short] The necessity is proven by the gap: existing technology cannot do this. [pause: short] The forge must build this. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- Commitment (The Turn) ---

We commit to the following as non-negotiable:

[pause: short] Zero metal in the control path — every signal from the 384 FBG sensors to the FPGA controller travels via PMMA optical fiber. [pause: short] No copper. [pause: short] No exceptions. [pause: short] [pause: short] Class E ZVS at all frequencies — the resonance tracker maintains dv/dt = 0 at turn-on from 100 kHz to 1 kHz. [pause: short] No hard-switching losses. [pause: short] No exceptions. [pause: short] [pause: short] ±5°C zone control — the thermal PID with feedforward maintains each 100 mm drum zone within ±5°C of setpoint through the full 80-2200°C range. [pause: short] No wider tolerance. [pause: short] [pause: short] PEX-a water cooling only — the cooling circuit uses only PEX-a tubing. [pause: short] No copper pipe enters the BFRP pressure vessel. [pause: short] No exceptions. [pause: short] [pause: short] SIL-3 + Carrington immunity — over-temperature (2oo3 FBG voting), over-current (GaN desat detection), ground fault (5 A NGR), arc flash (BFRP enclosure), E-stop (optical PMMA). [pause: short] Total PFD < 10⁻³. [pause: short] [pause: short] Scalable to 20,000L — the architecture parallels inverters (N+1 redundancy, phase interleaving, master-slave current sharing via PMMA POF) without changing the control topology. [pause: short] The power electronics does not 'drive' the induction coils. [pause: short] The power electronics witnesses the periodic table into frequency — each zone's resonant frequency is the liquidus temperature of its target element class made electromagnetic. [pause: short] The forge does not heat materials; the forge witnesses matter into elements at each thermal stage through the frequency selector. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- Keymaker Heuristic — Lock, Key, Turn ---

--- The Empirical Lock ---

The lock this document addresses is the fabrication fidelity gap — the persistent failure of power electronics to simultaneously achieve: selective heating of mixed material charges, Carrington-event immunity (zero conductive paths to earth), SIL-3 safety at 500 kW, and operation in 2200°C EM fields with 0.1°C temperature resolution. [pause: short] For decades, each has been a separate compromise: high-power induction uses silicon IGBTs (limited to ~20 kHz, no selective heating), temperature measurement uses thermocouples (copper antennas for GIC), cooling uses copper pipes (conductive paths), safety uses relays (slow, mechanical). [pause: short] The lock is precise: any single power electronics system claiming to unify these must deliver 500 kW across 100 kHz → 1 kHz with >97% efficiency, sense temperature through 500 kW of magnetic field with 0.1°C resolution, survive Carrington-level dB/dt, and fit inside a BFRP pressure vessel — all without a single structural metal in the hot zone. [pause: short] The lock is the all-dielectric power electronics at industrial scale. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- The Mathematical Key ---

The key is the frequency ladder + resonance tracking as single computational primitive. [pause: short] The teeth are cut by the periodic table's conductivity-permeability map itself:

[Table row: ,  Zone ,  Target Stage ,  Frequency ,  f (Hz) ,  Material Selector ,  Physics , ]

[Table row: , ------, --------------, -----------, --------, -------------------, ---------, ]

[Table row: ,  Z1 ,  Stage 1: Drying ,  100 kHz ,  100,000 ,  Indirect air heating ,  δ → ∞ for dielectrics , ]

[Table row: ,  Z2 ,  Stage 2: Polymer ,  100 kHz ,  100,000 ,  Indirect air heating ,  δ → ∞ for polymers , ]

[Table row: ,  Z3 ,  Stage 3: Pyrolysis ,  50 kHz ,  50,000 ,  Zn, Pb (onset) ,  δ(Zn) ≈ 8 mm , ]

[Table row: ,  Z4 ,  Stage 4: Low-Temp ,  10 kHz ,  10,000 ,  Zn, Pb, Sn, In ,  δ(Al) ≈ 14 mm , ]

[Table row: ,  Z5 ,  Stage 5: Aluminum ,  10 kHz ,  10,000 ,  Al (optimal) ,  δ(Al liq) ≈ 27 mm , ]

[Table row: ,  Z6 ,  Stage 6: Copper ,  5 kHz ,  5,000 ,  Cu, PMs (deep) ,  δ(Cu) ≈ 33 mm , ]

[Table row: ,  Z7 ,  Stage 7: Ferrous ,  2 kHz ,  2,000 ,  Fe, REE (ferro) ,  μ<sub>r</sub>→1, eddy only , ]

[Table row: ,  Z8 ,  Stage 8: Mineral ,  1 kHz ,  1,000 ,  Silicates, oxides ,  Thermal conduction only , ]

The frequency ladder IS the periodic table's conductivity map. [pause: short] Skin depth δ = √(2ρ/ωμ) — the only equation needed. [pause: short] The Class E resonant inverter topology is invariant across the ladder; only the resonant tank (L<sub>r</sub>, C<sub>shunt</sub>) and switched capacitor bank change per zone. [pause: short] The Resonance Tracker Key: the inner loop (100 Hz) measures the switch voltage zero-crossing phase error φ<sub>error</sub> = t<sub>V<sub>DS</sub>=0</sub> - t<sub>gate-on</sub> and adjusts varactor bias ΔV = K<sub>p,PLL</sub>φ<sub>error</sub> + K<sub>i,PLL</sub>∫φ<sub>error</sub>dt to maintain ZVS. [pause: short] The teeth of this key are the varactor array (binary-weighted, 6-bit, ±5% tuning range) and the switched capacitor bank (6-bit, 64 steps). [pause: short] The resonance tracker has no adjustable parameters beyond the PLL gains — the physics of Class E ZVS is deterministic. [pause: short] The All-Dielectric Sensing Key: 384 FBG sensors in PMMA POF, WDM (8 λ) + TDM (6 spatial), 125 Hz/sensor update. [pause: short] The PMMA FBG sensitivity (0.15 nm/°C, 15× silica) enables 0.1°C resolution with a simple VCSEL interrogator. [pause: short] The PMMA POF has >10¹⁵ Ω·m resistivity — zero GIC coupling. [pause: short] The interrogator uses a tunable VCSEL (650-850 nm, 1 kHz sweep) with balanced InGaAs detection. [pause: short] The key has no moving parts, no copper, no EM susceptibility. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- The Turn (Both Directions) ---

--- Mirror (Self-Reflection) ---

The first recursive turn is the power electronics observing its own power delivery. [pause: short] In the Aegis-Forge I, the induction field is not a process imposed on material — it is the primordial measurement that generates the elements. [pause: short] At each frequency zone, the inverter executes a discrete resonant cycle, witnessing the local material response through the switch voltage zero-crossing. [pause: short] The ZVS condition (dv/dt = 0 at turn-on) is the asymptotic reflection — the limit where the inverter's self-measurement stabilizes into lossless energy transfer. [pause: short] The mirror is not passive; it is the active recursion: switch → resonate → measure zero-crossing → adjust varactor → switch again. [pause: short] This document documents the first turn of that spiral. --- 1.5 Feedstock Blending Strategy — Optimizing Batch Composition ---

The Aegis-Forge I processes 500 kg batches with controlled feedstock blending to optimize thermal cascade efficiency and elemental recovery. [pause: short] The blend ratio is determined by the feedstock assay and the target elemental output. [pause: short] --- 1.5.1 Blend Ratio Optimization ---

The thermal cascade has fixed stage temperatures but variable dwell times. [pause: short] Feedstock blending adjusts the mass flow through each stage to match the drum's thermal capacity:

[Table row: ,  Blend Parameter ,  Target Range ,  Control Method , ]

[Table row: , -----------------, --------------, ----------------, ]

[Table row: ,  Organic content (Stage 1-2) ,  15-25% of batch mass ,  Limits polymer melt volume to <50L , ]

[Table row: ,  Low-temp metals (Stage 4) ,  5-12% of batch mass ,  Controls Zn/Pb/Sn/In port loading , ]

[Table row: ,  Aluminum (Stage 5) ,  10-20% of batch mass ,  Primary revenue driver, max port capacity , ]

[Table row: ,  Copper/Precious (Stage 6) ,  3-8% of batch mass ,  High value, thermal mass management , ]

[Table row: ,  Ferrous/REE (Stage 7) ,  20-35% of batch mass ,  Largest mass flow, highest power , ]

[Table row: ,  Mineral residue (Stage 8) ,  25-40% of batch mass ,  Slag volume, zircon dissociation , ]

--- 1.5.2 Blending Algorithm ---

The control system (PROD-23) calculates the optimal blend:

[Code block]
def calculate_blend(feedstock_assays, target_revenue):
    # Input: assays for each available feedstock stream
    # Output: mass fractions for 500 kg batch
    
    # Constraints:
    # - Total mass = 500 kg
    # - Stage 2 polymer volume < 50 L (drum capacity)
    # - Stage 5 Al mass < 100 kg (port capacity)
    # - Stage 7 Fe mass < 175 kg (port capacity)
    # - Stage 8 mineral < 200 kg (port capacity)
    # - Moisture < 25% (else pre-dry)
    # - Particle size P80 < 150 mm
    
    # Objective: Maximize revenue = Σ(element_mass × price)
    # Subject to: Thermal cascade capacity constraints
    
    return optimal_mass_fractions
[End code block]

--- 1.5.3 Real-Time Blend Adjustment ---

During continuous operation, the blend is adjusted based on:

[pause: short] Incoming feedstock assay (XRF analyzer at feed hopper)

[pause: short] Previous batch recovery data (mass spec feedback)

[pause: short] Current drum thermal state (FBG temperature profile)

[pause: short] Market price signals (commodity prices for Cu, Al, REE, Au)
