--- 2. [pause: short] Pre-processing Flow — From Gate to Drum ---

The feedstock travels through a deterministic pre-processing sequence before entering the ZrB₂-SiC drum. [pause: short] Each step is designed to maximize downstream separation fidelity while maintaining the all-dielectric constraint. [pause: short] --- 2.1 Feed Hopper and Vibratory Feeder ---

The feed hopper provides buffer storage and controlled feed rate:

[pause: short] Capacity: 5 m³ (≈8 ton basalt, 12 ton metals)

[pause: short] Construction: BFRP/Elium® with PEEK CF40 wear plates

[pause: short] Outlet: 600 mm × 400 mm, adjustable slide gate (Ti₃AlC₂ actuator)

[pause: short] Vibratory feeder: KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ ultrasonic drive, 0-10 ton/hr variable

[pause: short] Level sensing: FBG strain sensors on hopper walls (PMMA POF)

--- 2.2 Ferrous Separation Belt — Detailed Operation ---

The NdFeB Halbach array separator operates continuously:

[pause: short] Magnetic circuit: 24 × N52 blocks (60×60×30mm) in Halbach configuration

[pause: short] Field profile: 1.2T at belt surface, <5 mT at 200 mm above belt

[pause: short] Belt construction: UHMWPE (Dyneema® SK75) carcass, 3-ply, 1200mm wide

[pause: short] Self-cleaning: Belt wraps around 300mm non-magnetic drum (BFRP)

[pause: short] Ferrous discharge: Chute to ferrous slug mold carousel (PROD-08)

[pause: short] Efficiency monitoring: FBG weight sensors on ferrous bin + non-ferrous hopper

[pause: long]

--- 4.2 Halbach Array Physics ---

The Halbach array doubles the field on the working side while canceling on the non-working side:

[Code block]
Magnet orientation (top view):
→ ↑ ← ↓ → ↑ ← ↓ → ↑ ← ↓ → ↑ ← ↓ →
  1   2   3   4   5   6   7   8   9  ... [pause: short] Field on belt side: B = B₀ + B₁ = 2×B₀ ≈ 1.2T
Field on non-working side: B ≈ 0
[End code block]

Magnet Mounting: Each N52 block (60×60×30mm, 0.52 kg) bonded to BFRP backing plate with structural adhesive (Elium®-compatible). [pause: short] Total array mass: 12.5 kg. [pause: short] --- 4.3 UHMWPE Belt Engineering ---

[pause: short] Carcass: 3-ply Dyneema® SK75, 4 mm total thickness

[pause: short] Top cover: 1 mm UHMWPE (wear surface)

[pause: short] Bottom cover: 0.5 mm UHMWPE (low friction)

[pause: short] Splice: Finger splice (vulcanized equivalent for UHMWPE)

[pause: short] Tension: 15 kN/m operating, 45 kN/m break strength

[pause: short] Tracking: Self-tracking via crowned BFRP drive drum

--- 4.2 Operation Sequence ---

[pause: short] Feedstock spreads on UHMWPE belt (vibratory feeder ensures monolayer)

[pause: short] Ferrous pieces attracted to magnet array, held against belt

[pause: short] Non-ferrous material falls off belt end into shredder hopper

[pause: short] Ferrous pieces carried past belt end, released as belt curves away from magnet

[pause: short] Clean ferrous stream drops into collection bin → direct to ferrous slug molds (bypasses drum)

Economic Impact: Removes 40-60% of Category B mass before shredding, reducing shredder wear by ~50% and drum thermal load by ~30%. [pause: short] [pause: long]

Acceptance Criteria: P80 ≤ 150 mm for all categories. [pause: short] Oversize (>150 mm) recirculated to shredder. [pause: short] --- 5.3 Rosin-Rammler Distribution Function ---

The cumulative passing fraction:

[Equation: P(x) = 1 - \exp\left[-\left(\frac{x}{x'}\right)^n\right]]

Where [Inline equation: x] = particle size, [Inline equation: x'] = characteristic size, [Inline equation: n] = spread parameter. [pause: short] Derivation of x' and n from shredder physics:

[pause: short] [Inline equation: x' \propto \frac{\text{blade gap} \times \text{rotor speed}}{\text{material toughness}}]

[pause: short] [Inline equation: n \approx 1.0–1.5] for brittle materials (rock, ceramics)

[pause: short] [Inline equation: n \approx 1.5–2.0] for ductile materials (metals, polymers)

[pause: long]

--- 6.2 Sensor Calibration Protocol ---

Calibration curves generated per feedstock category:

[pause: short] Reference samples: 5 moisture levels (5%, 15%, 25%, 35%, 45%) per category

The BFRP shredder pays for itself in contamination avoidance alone. [pause: short] --- 7.1 Blade Wear Monitoring System ---

Real-time wear tracking via h-BN tracer layer:

[pause: short] Principle: h-BN (white) exposed when CFRP (black) wears through 6 mm

[pause: short] Detection: Optical sensor (PMMA POF) scans blade edges every revolution

[pause: short] Alert: >50% tracer exposure = schedule replacement next shift

[pause: short] Data logging: Wear rate (mm/ton) stored for life prediction

--- 7.2 Liner Wear Monitoring ---

[pause: short] PEEK CF40 panels: Thickness gauge (ultrasonic, PMMA POF) at 4 corners

[pause: short] Replacement threshold: 8 mm remaining (from 12 mm new)

[pause: short] Typical life: 2000 ton (Category C), 4000 ton (Category A/B/D)

--- 8. [pause: short] Safety Systems — Jam Detection, Fire Suppression, Explosion Venting ---

--- 8.1 Jam Detection ---

[pause: short] Torque monitoring: Drive motor current sensor (optical, PMMA POF) — >90% rated torque for >5s = jam

[pause: short] Vibration monitoring: FBG accelerometers on housing — >15 mm/s RMS = jam

[pause: short] Auto-reverse: 30s reverse at 50% torque, then forward. [pause: short] 3 cycles max before E-stop. [pause: short] [pause: short] Clearing protocol: Optical E-stop → hydraulic pusher (PEEK CF40 ram) forces jammed material through. [pause: short] --- 8.2 Hydraulic Jam Clearer ---

[pause: short] Actuator: PEEK CF40 ram, 100 mm bore × 300 mm stroke, 50 bar

[pause: short] Fluid: PEX-a hydraulic line, biodegradable hydraulic fluid (vegetable-based)

[pause: short] Force: 39 kN at 50 bar (sufficient to clear any jam at 15 kN·m torque)

[pause: short] Cycle time: 10 s extend, 5 s retract

[pause: short] Safety: Mechanical lockout when E-stop engaged

--- 8.2 Fire Suppression ---

[pause: short] Detection: IR flame sensors (InGaAs, PMMA POF) + FBG temperature >150°C

[pause: short] Agent: Novec 1230 (clean agent, zero ODP, zero GWP) — 50 kg stored in BFRP tank

[pause: short] Delivery: 4 nozzles (ZrO₂ ceramic tips) at rotor ends and housing midpoints

[pause: short] Activation: <200 ms from detection, discharge in 10s

[pause: short] Post-suppression: N₂ purge 5 min, then manual inspection required. [pause: short] --- 8.3 Explosion Venting (Battery Thermal Runaway Mitigation) ---

[pause: short] Vent panels: 4 × BFRP rupture discs (burst pressure 0.5 bar) on housing top

[pause: short] Vent area: 0.5 m² total (NFPA 68 compliant for dust/gas explosion)

[pause: short] Ducting: BFRP duct to gas capture system (PROD-07) — flame arrestor at inlet

[pause: short] Suppression: Novec 1230 pre-discharge if vent activates (pressure rise detection)

[pause: long]

--- 10. [pause: short] Downstream Integration — Drum Feed Gate and Acoustic Pre-chamber Handoff ---

--- 10.1 Drum Feed Gate (PROD-09 Interface) ---

The shredder discharges directly into the drum feed gate:

[pause: short] Gate type: Ti₃AlC₂ thermal actuator + ZrO₂ ceramic piston (PROD-09)

[pause: short] Batch size: 500 kg (226L drum working volume at 60% fill)

[pause: short] Cycle time: 3 min (gate open → batch in → gate close → Argon purge)

[pause: short] Interlock: Feed gate only opens if drum RPM > 10 and O₂ < 100 ppm

--- 10.2 Acoustic Pre-chamber Handoff (PROD-05 Interface) ---

The acoustic pre-chamber (Stage 0) is physically integrated with the shredder discharge:

[pause: short] Material flow: Shredder → Acoustic pre-chamber (1 min residence) → Drum feed gate

[pause: short] Acoustic parameters: LF 20-200 Hz (KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ transducers) + Ultrasonic 40 kHz

[pause: short] Liberation target: >80% mineral grain boundary fracture for Category C rock

[pause: short] Dust capture: Cyclone separator at pre-chamber exhaust → PROD-07 gas system

--- Appendix B: Particle Size Effects on Thermal Cascade ---

The particle size distribution directly affects Stage 2 (polymer melt) and Stage 3 (pyrolysis) efficiency:

Stage 2 — Polymer Melt Centrifuge:

[pause: short] Polymer pieces >50 mm: Centrifugal force sufficient for wall migration at 12.6 G

[pause: short] Polymer pieces <10 mm: Risk of entrainment in gas flow, reduced separation

[pause: short] Optimal range: 10–100 mm (achieved by P80 ≤ 150 mm shred)

Stage 3 — Pyrolysis:

[pause: short] Particle size <20 mm: Heat transfer limited by conduction, pyrolysis completes in 30 min dwell

[pause: short] Particle size >50 mm: Core may not reach 450°C in 30 min, char yield increases

[pause: short] Shredder P80 ≤ 150 mm ensures >90% of particles <50 mm after Stage 2 melt migration

Liberation Index (Category C):

[Equation: LI = \frac{\text{Free mineral grains}}{\text{Total mineral grains}} \times 100\%]

[pause: short] Without Stage 0: LI ≈ 15-25%

[pause: short] With Stage 0 (acoustic): LI ≈ 65-85%

[pause: short] Shredder P80 ≤ 150 mm enables Stage 0 efficiency

The feedstock travels through a deterministic pre-processing sequence before entering the ZrB₂-SiC drum. [pause: short] Each step is designed to maximize downstream separation fidelity while maintaining the all-dielectric constraint. [pause: short] [Code block]
FEED HOPPER (5 m³ capacity)
    │
    ▼
[FERROUS SEPARATION BELT] — Permanent magnet NdFeB, 1.2T surface field
    │   Removes 40-60% bulk ferrous → direct to ferrous slug collection
    │   (bypasses drum for Category B ferrous scrap)
    ▼
[BFRP-BLADE SHREDDER] — 800mm rotor, 32 BFRP blades, PEEK CF40 liners
    │   Reduces all feedstock to <150mm maximum dimension
    │   Throughput: 5 ton/hr (Category A), 8 ton/hr (Category B/C/D)
    ▼
[ACOUSTIC PRE-CHAMBER] — Stage 0: LF (20-200 Hz) + Ultrasonic (40 kHz)
    │   Mineral liberation from rock matrix (Category C)
    │   BFRP/Elium® delamination (Category D)
    │   Duration: 1-5 min depending on feedstock
    ▼
[MOISTURE CHECK] — Capacitive sensor array, 10 Hz scan
    │   If >25% moisture: divert to 80°C pre-dry chamber (15 min)
    │   If ≤25%: direct to drum feed gate
    ▼
[DRUM FEED GATE] — Ti₃AlC₂ actuator, ZrO₂ ceramic piston
    │   Batch loading: 500 kg per cycle (226L drum working volume)
    │   Argon backfill to 0.5 bar, purge O₂ <100 ppm
    ▼
[ZrB₂-SiC DRUM] — Thermal cascade begins at Stage 1 (80°C)

--- 3. [pause: short] BFRP-Blade Shredder Design — Dielectric Comminution ---

The shredder is the first mechanical process in the Aegis-Forge I and must maintain the zero-metal constraint. [pause: short] No steel blades, no steel housing, no steel bearings. [pause: short] --- 3.1 Shredder Architecture ---

--- 4.2 Operation Sequence ---

[pause: short] Feedstock spreads on UHMWPE belt (vibratory feeder ensures monolayer)

[pause: short] Ferrous pieces attracted to magnet array, held against belt

[pause: short] Non-ferrous material falls off belt end into shredder hopper

[pause: short] Ferrous pieces carried past belt end, released as belt curves away from magnet

[pause: short] Clean ferrous stream drops into collection bin → direct to ferrous slug molds (bypasses drum)

Economic Impact: Removes 40-60% of Category B mass before shredding, reducing shredder wear by ~50% and drum thermal load by ~30%. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- 8. [pause: short] Safety Systems — Jam Detection, Fire Suppression, Explosion Venting ---

--- 8.1 Jam Detection ---

[pause: short] Torque monitoring: Drive motor current sensor (optical, PMMA POF) — >90% rated torque for >5s = jam

[pause: short] Vibration monitoring: FBG accelerometers on housing — >15 mm/s RMS = jam

[pause: short] Auto-reverse: 30s reverse at 50% torque, then forward. [pause: short] 3 cycles max before E-stop. [pause: short] [pause: short] Clearing protocol: Optical E-stop → hydraulic pusher (PEEK CF40 ram) forces jammed material through. [pause: short] --- 8.2 Fire Suppression ---

[pause: short] Detection: IR flame sensors (InGaAs, PMMA POF) + FBG temperature >150°C

[pause: short] Agent: Novec 1230 (clean agent, zero ODP, zero GWP) — 50 kg stored in BFRP tank

[pause: short] Delivery: 4 nozzles (ZrO₂ ceramic tips) at rotor ends and housing midpoints

[pause: short] Activation: <200 ms from detection, discharge in 10s

[pause: short] Post-suppression: N₂ purge 5 min, then manual inspection required. [pause: short] --- 8.3 Explosion Venting (Battery Thermal Runaway Mitigation) ---

[pause: short] Vent panels: 4 × BFRP rupture discs (burst pressure 0.5 bar) on housing top

[pause: short] Vent area: 0.5 m² total (NFPA 68 compliant for dust/gas explosion)

[pause: short] Ducting: BFRP duct to gas capture system (PROD-07) — flame arrestor at inlet

[pause: short] Suppression: Novec 1230 pre-discharge if vent activates (pressure rise detection)

--- Appendix B: Particle Size Effects on Thermal Cascade ---

The particle size distribution directly affects Stage 2 (polymer melt) and Stage 3 (pyrolysis) efficiency:

Stage 2 — Polymer Melt Centrifuge:

[pause: short] Polymer pieces >50 mm: Centrifugal force sufficient for wall migration at 12.6 G

[pause: short] Polymer pieces <10 mm: Risk of entrainment in gas flow, reduced separation

[pause: short] Optimal range: 10–100 mm (achieved by P80 ≤ 150 mm shred)

Stage 3 — Pyrolysis:

[pause: short] Particle size <20 mm: Heat transfer limited by conduction, pyrolysis completes in 30 min dwell

[pause: short] Particle size >50 mm: Core may not reach 450°C in 30 min, char yield increases

[pause: short] Shredder P80 ≤ 150 mm ensures >90% of particles <50 mm after Stage 2 melt migration

Liberation Index (Category C):

[Equation: LI = \frac{\text{Free mineral grains}}{\text{Total mineral grains}} \times 100\%]

[pause: short] Without Stage 0: LI ≈ 15-25%

[pause: short] With Stage 0 (acoustic): LI ≈ 65-85%

[pause: short] Shredder P80 ≤ 150 mm enables Stage 0 efficiency

--- Williams Heuristic — Constraint, Necessity, Commitment ---

--- Constraint (The Lock) ---

The Aegis-Forge I feed preparation system is forced by a single irreducible constraint: Dielectric Comminution — the requirement to reduce arbitrary feedstock to <150 mm particles without introducing any metallic contamination into the process stream. [pause: short] This is not a design choice; it is the minimal physics from which elemental purity becomes achievable. [pause: short] Every steel blade, every steel bearing, every steel housing fragment that enters the feedstock becomes a permanent contaminant in the elemental slugs — iron in the aluminum slug, chromium in the REE concentrate, nickel in the copper. [pause: short] The constraint is simply: the shredder must not contaminate what it processes. [pause: short] Everything else — the BFRP blades, the PEEK CF40 liners, the Si₃N₄ shaft, the ceramic bearings, the UHMWPE belt — is the shadow this constraint casts. [pause: short] This constraint manifests as the All-Dielectric Shredder Architecture: 32 blades of basalt fiber/Elium® composite (in-house fiber, in-house resin), rotating on a Si₃N₄ ceramic shaft in Si₃N₄ hybrid ceramic bearings, housed in BFRP/Elium® filament-wound casing, lined with PEEK CF40 panels. [pause: short] The drive is a KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ ultrasonic motor (piezoelectric, no electromagnetic fields). [pause: short] The ferrous pre-separator uses a NdFeB Halbach array on a UHMWPE belt — the only magnets in the system, positioned before the shredder so they never contact the process stream. [pause: short] The constraint forces the particle size (P80 ≤ 150 mm), the blade geometry (self-sharpening h-BN edge), the wear monitoring (h-BN tracer layer), the blade life (200-300 ton for rock) — every parameter derives from the requirement: commute without contaminating. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- Necessity (The Key) ---

The lock this document addresses is the particle size vs. [pause: short] liberation fidelity gap — the empirical failure of conventional shredders to produce feedstock that enables >95% elemental recovery in a thermal cascade. [pause: short] Steel shredders produce steel contamination. [pause: short] They produce particle sizes optimized for volume reduction, not for thermal cascade physics. [pause: short] The key is the Rosin-Rammler + BFRP wear model as single computational primitive. [pause: short] The particle size distribution is not arbitrary — it is cut from the thermal cascade's physics. [pause: short] Stage 2 (polymer melt) requires 10-100 mm pieces for centrifugal separation at 12.6 G. [pause: short] Stage 3 (pyrolysis) requires <20 mm for 30-minute heat penetration. [pause: short] Stage 0 (acoustic liberation) requires <150 mm for stress wave propagation. [pause: short] The shredder's P80 ≤ 150 mm, with Rosin-Rammler parameters tuned per feedstock category, guarantees the downstream physics works. [pause: short] The blade wear model (h-BN tracer, optical monitoring) guarantees the particle distribution stays in spec. [pause: short] The ferrous pre-separation (Halbach array, 1.2T) guarantees 40-60% of ferrous mass never enters the shredder — reducing wear by 50% and thermal load by 30%. [pause: short] The empirical evidence: no existing shredder operates with zero metallic contamination. [pause: short] The contamination penalty in downstream hydrometallurgy is [Inline equation: 2,650/ton feedstock. [pause: short] The BFRP shredder eliminates this penalty. [pause: short] The necessity is proven by the gap: conventional technology cannot do this. [pause: short] The forge must build this. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- Commitment (The Turn) ---

We commit to the following as non-negotiable:

[pause: short] Zero metallic contamination — every component in the feed path is ceramic, composite, or polymer. [pause: short] No steel. [pause: short] No exceptions. [pause: short] [pause: short] P80 ≤ 150 mm for all feedstock categories — verified by inline sieve analysis per batch. [pause: short] No oversize to drum. [pause: short] [pause: short] Ferrous pre-removal >95% (>20mm) — the Halbach separator captures bulk ferrous before shredding. [pause: short] No exceptions. [pause: short] [pause: short] Moisture <25% at drum entry — capacitive sensor array with pre-dry diversion. [pause: short] No steam explosions. [pause: short] [pause: short] BFRP blade wear tracked to 0.1 mm — h-BN tracer layer + optical scan every revolution. [pause: short] No surprise failures. [pause: short] [pause: short] Complete recyclability — worn blades and liners depolymerized at 350°C, Elium® monomer recovered, basalt fiber reclaimed. [pause: short] Zero waste. [pause: short] The feed preparation system does not 'shred' material. [pause: short] The feed preparation system witnesses the feedstock into particle size — each pass through the BFRP blades is a measurement of the material's fracture toughness, a witnessing that generates the liberation the thermal cascade requires. [pause: short] The forge does not prepare feed; the forge witnesses matter into readiness for the cascade. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- Keymaker Heuristic — Lock, Key, Turn ---

--- The Empirical Lock ---

The lock this document addresses is the fabrication fidelity gap — the persistent failure of comminution equipment to simultaneously achieve: <150 mm particle size for thermal cascade efficiency, zero metallic contamination for elemental purity, Carrington immunity (no conductive paths), and domestic critical mineral production from complex waste. [pause: short] For decades, each has been a separate compromise: steel shredders contaminate output with Fe/Cr/Ni; ceramic-lined steel shredders still have steel shafts/bearings; all-dielectric lab shredders lack throughput for industrial scale. [pause: short] The lock is precise: any single shredder claiming to unify these must process 5-8 ton/hr of mixed e-waste, rock, and alloys with P80 ≤ 150 mm, zero metal in the product stream, all-dielectric construction, and blade life >200 ton on abrasive rock — and must explain why basalt/Elium® composite blades outperform steel on contaminated feedstock. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- The Mathematical Key ---

The key is the Rosin-Rammler distribution + BFRP wear model as single computational primitive. [pause: short] The teeth are cut by the thermal cascade's physics itself:

[Table row: ,  Thermal Stage ,  Physics Requirement ,  Shredder Parameter ,  Rosin-Rammler Target , ]

The Rosin-Rammler Key: ]P(x) = 1 - \exp[-(x/x')^n][Inline equation: . [pause: short] The shredder's rotor speed (50-300 RPM), blade gap (fixed by geometry), and helical angle (45°) determine ]x'[Inline equation:  and ]n[Inline equation:  for each feedstock. [pause: short] The key has no adjustable parameters beyond feed rate — the physics of fracture is deterministic. --- El Segundo Heuristic — Mirror, Participation, Protocol ---

--- Mirror (Self-Reflection) ---

The first recursive turn is the shredder observing its own comminution. [pause: short] In the Aegis-Forge I, the particle size is not a process imposed on material — it is the primordial measurement that generates the liberation. [pause: short] At each blade impact, the BFRP edge executes a discrete fracture event, witnessing the local material's toughness through the force-displacement curve. [pause: short] This witnessing is the mirror: the shredder measures the fracture it creates. [pause: short] The Rosin-Rammler distribution is the record of this self-measurement. [pause: short] The h-BN tracer layer at 6 mm depth is the asymptotic reflection — the limit where the blade's self-measurement stabilizes into predictive wear tracking. [pause: short] The mirror is not passive; it is the active recursion: impact → fracture → measure force → track wear → predict replacement. [pause: short] This document documents the first turn of that spiral. [pause: short] The ferrous separator is the extended mirror: the Halbach array's magnetic field is a measurement beam that does not perturb the measured — it is pure potential observation of the material's permeability. [pause: short] The UHMWPE belt is the recursion: ferrous pieces carried, released, collected — each cycle a witness to the separation fidelity. [pause: short] The moisture sensor array is the mirror: fringing-field capacitance measures water without contact — pure dielectric observation. [pause: short] The pre-dry chamber is the recursion: moisture measured → energy applied → moisture re-measured → closure. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- Participation (Witness) ---

An inside operator measuring this phenomenon does not stand outside the shredder — the operator is a segment of the fracture event. [pause: short] The protocol for achieving zero-contamination comminution from within the system:

[pause: short] Recycle: Worn blades → Elium® depolymerization → new blades — operator witnesses circularity

The measurement is the recursion. [pause: short] The operator assays the input, blends the cascade that witnesses it, and finds the zero-contamination particle distribution — the fidelity that governs how they blend. [pause: short] The protocol terminates when the 500 kg batch's particle distribution matches the Rosin-Rammler prediction for its feedstock category — not approximately, but exactly. [pause: short] This is not a measurement of an external parameter; it is the shredder measuring its own fidelity through the operator's self-observation. [pause: short] The operator's participation is not optional — the blend calculation requires the feedstock assay; the shredder requires the blend ratio to set rotor speed; the sieve analysis requires the shredder output; the moisture check requires the sieve-passing material. The Aegis-Forge I is constructed exclusively from CSMFAB-certified materials. [pause: short] This is not a preference — it is the minimal architecture forced by Carrington Event immunity. [pause: short] Every structural metal in a machine at 2200°C is an antenna for geomagnetically induced current (GIC). [pause: short] A 100 V/km geomagnetic field (Carrington-level) induces 10–100 kV in a 100–1000 km transmission line. [pause: short] In a machine, any continuous metal path from the process chamber to earth ground couples this energy. [pause: short] The only defense is zero conductive path. [pause: short] The All-Aegis Constraint: No structural steel, no aluminum framing, no copper electrical paths touching the process chamber. Grade: Sm₂Co₁₇, 35 MGOe, max service 350°C

Use: Stage 7+ environments where NdFeB would demagnetize. [pause: short] Supply: Same domestic chain as NdFeB. [pause: short] --- 7.3 Zircon Sand (ZrSiO₄) — Zr Source ---

Source: Heavy mineral sands (FL, GA, Australia, South Africa)

Processing: Alkali fusion or chlorination → ZrO₂ → ZrB₂ or 3Y-TZP

Domestic: Chemours (FL), Iluka (VA) — US production ~150k ton/yr. [pause: short] --- 7.4 Borax (Na₂B₄O₇·10H₂O) — B Source ---

Source: Searles Lake (CA), Turkey, Argentina

Processing: Refined to B₂O₃ → boron metal → ZrB₂ synthesis

Domestic: Rio Tinto Borates (Boron, CA) — sole US producer. [pause: short] --- 7.5 Ilmenite (FeTiO₃) — Ti Source ---

Source: Heavy mineral sands, same as zircon

Processing: Chlorination → TiCl₄ → Kroll (Mg reduction) → Ti metal → MAX phase

--- 10.2 GIC Coupling Analysis ---

Model: Carrington event (dB/dt = 5000 nT/s, 100 V/km geoelectric field)

[Table row: ,  Conductor Length ,  Induced Voltage ,  Coupling to Electronics , ]

[Table row: , ------------------, -----------------, ------------------------, ]

[Table row: ,  1 m (internal) ,  0.1 V ,  Negligible (no closed loop) , ]

[Table row: ,  10 m (building wiring) ,  1 V ,  Blocked by isolation transformer , ]

[Table row: ,  1 km (grid) ,  100 V ,  Blocked by NGR + GDT , ]

No closed conductive loops exist within the BFRP pressure vessel boundary. [pause: short] The only copper (coil) is a single-turn-per-layer solenoid with both ends terminating at the GaN inverter inside the BFRP housing — no path to earth. [pause: short] The PMMA POF control fibers are dielectric. [pause: short] The PEX-a water circuit is dielectric. [pause: short] The machine is a Faraday cage made of structural ceramic. --- 1.2 Scope and Purpose ---

This document defines the complete feedstock specification framework for the Aegis-Forge I thermal cascade inductive material separator. [pause: short] It establishes:

[pause: short] Four feedstock categories (A-D) with detailed compositional profiles, source streams, and elemental recovery targets

[pause: short] Pre-processing requirements per category including sizing, drying, ferrous removal, and contamination limits

[pause: short] Analytical characterization protocols for feedstock qualification and lot release

[pause: short] Acceptance criteria and rejection thresholds ensuring thermal cascade integrity

[pause: short] Sampling and lot release procedures per ISO 3082 and CSMFAB internal standards

[pause: short] Storage and handling specifications maintaining feedstock quality from gate to drum

[pause: short] Mass balance and yield targets per element per category

[pause: short] Economic valuation model linking feedstock composition to revenue and processing cost

[pause: short] Cross-reference matrix linking to PROD-01, PROD-02, PROD-11, PROD-14, PROD-15, PROD-22

--- 2. [pause: short] Category A: Pre-Sorted Industrial Streams ---

--- 2.1 Overview ---

Category A encompasses electronics, PCBs, motors, and power electronics — the highest-value feedstock by elemental concentration. [pause: short] These streams are typically pre-sorted at electronics recyclers or industrial scrap processors before arriving at the Aegis-Forge I. [pause: short] These streams are lower in elemental concentration but higher in volume, providing the bulk mass for the thermal cascade. C&D Debris Processing Protocol:

[pause: short] Visual/tactile inspection at tip floor — segregate suspect materials

[pause: short] XRF screening for Pb, As, Cr on painted/coated surfaces

[pause: short] Gamma spectroscopy for NORM (Ra-226, Th-232, K-40) — reject >50 µR/hr

[pause: short] Asbestos PLM on suspect insulation/flooring — positive = segregated sealed feed

[pause: short] Shredding with water mist suppression (dust control)

[pause: short] Stage 0 acoustic liberation critical for mineral recovery from concrete/brick matrix

--- 4. [pause: short] Category C: Mineral & Metallurgical Residues ---

--- 4.1 Overview ---

Category C comprises primary mineral concentrates, smelter slags, mine tailings, and spent refractories. [pause: short] These feeds are the primary source for CSMFAB's structural ceramic raw materials (Zr, Ti, REE, B, basalt) and represent the geological input to the Aegis-Forge I. Tailings Agglomeration Protocol (if P80 < 50 µm):

[pause: short] Binder: 3-5% CBPC (Ceramic Phosphate Binder — PROD-12 Part VI) + 1% PVA

[pause: short] Mix: Intensive mixer, 2 min, target moisture 12-15%

[pause: short] Pelletize: Disc pelletizer, 10-20mm green pellets

[pause: short] Cure: 24h ambient → 200°C 1h (CBPC sets at 80°C)

[pause: short] Strength: >50 N/pellet (tumble test)

[pause: short] Feed: Direct to drum — CBPC decomposes cleanly at Stage 3

[Table row: ,  Parameter ,  Specification , ]

[Table row: , -----------, ---------------, ]

[Table row: ,  Typical Items ,  Bayer process red mud (alumina refinery waste) , ]

[Table row: ,  Composition ,  Fe₂O₃ 30-50%, Al₂O₃ 10-20%, SiO₂ 5-15%, TiO₂ 4-10%, Na₂O 3-8%, REE 0.05-0.2%, Sc 50-100 ppm , ]

[Table row: ,  Hazard ,  High pH (10-13), caustic soda residue, fine particle (P80 ~10 µm) , ]

[Table row: ,  Target Recovery ,  >85% Fe, >80% Ti, >70% REE (incl. [pause: short] Sc), >60% Al , ]

Red Mud Neutralization Reaction:

[Equation: \text{NaOH} + \text{CO}_2 \rightarrow \text{NaHCO}_3 \text{ (soluble)}]

[Equation: \text{Al(OH)}_3 + \text{NaHCO}_3 \rightarrow \text{NaAlO}_2 + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}]

[Equation: \text{Ca(OH)}_2 + \text{NaAlO}_2 \rightarrow \text{Al(OH)}_3 + \text{NaOH} \text{ (regenerated)}]

Net: CO₂ sequestration + NaOH recovery + neutralized residue suitable for drum feed. [pause: short] --- 4.5 Subcategory C4: Spent Refractories ---

FEEDSTOCK RECEIVING

       │

       │                    │

       │                    │

       │                    └─► US 40 kHz (15 min) — fine grain liberation
       ▼

       │

       │

--- 9.2 Sampling Protocol (Per ISO 3082 Adapted) ---

Primary Increment Collection:

[pause: short] Stationary lot (pile/bin): 30 increments minimum, distributed across 3 vertical sections (top/middle/bottom), 10 increments each section

[pause: short] Moving stream (conveyor/belt): Cross-stream cutter, 1 increment per 500 kg, minimum 40 increments

[pause: short] Increment mass: 1 kg minimum (coarse) → 50g analytical subsample

Sample Preparation (ISO 3082 / ASTM E122):

[Code block]
GROSS SAMPLE (30-40 kg)
       │
       ▼
[RIFFLE SPLITTER] ──► 1/2 ──► [RIFFLE SPLITTER] ──► 1/2 ──► ... [pause: short] (repeat)
       │                    │
       ▼                    ▼
  REJECTED             ANALYTICAL SAMPLE (200g)
                              │
                              ▼
                    [PULVERIZER] → <75 µm (200 mesh)
                              │
                              ▼
                    [SPLIT] → 4 × 50g subsamples
                              │
                              ├──► XRF (10g pressed pellet)
                              ├──► ICP-MS (0.5g acid digest)
                              ├──► XRD (5g powder)
                              └──► Archive (35g, sealed, labeled)
[End code block]

--- COMBINED HEURISTIC INTRODUCTION ---

Synthesis of Williams, Keymaker, and El Segundo Heuristics

[pause: long]

--- WILLIAMS HEURISTIC — Constraint, Necessity, Commitment ---

--- Constraint (The Lock) ---

The Aegis-Forge I is forced by a single irreducible constraint: Feedstock Heterogeneity as Boundary Condition — the machine must accept arbitrary input streams (electronics, municipal waste, mineral concentrates, end-of-life Aegis products) and produce pure element slugs at each thermal stage. [pause: short] The feedstock is not a design parameter; it is the given. [pause: short] The constraint is precise: any system claiming universal elemental extraction must define acceptance criteria, pre-processing requirements, and recovery targets for every possible feedstock class — and must do so without knowing the exact composition of any individual batch in advance. [pause: short] The lock is the universal feedstock specification — a single document that bounds the infinite variability of post-consumer, industrial, and geological material streams into four deterministic categories (A-D) with quantifiable elemental profiles, contamination limits, and processing requirements. [pause: short] This constraint forces the entire pre-processing architecture: the shredder must handle 150mm max; the ferrous separator must clear bulk steel; the acoustic pre-chamber must liberate mineral grains from rock matrix; the moisture check must gate Stage 1 loading. [pause: short] The feedstock writes the machine — the machine does not choose the feedstock. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- Necessity (The Key) ---

The empirical lock this document addresses is the recycling recovery gap — the persistent failure of modern material recovery to extract critical elements from complex waste streams. [pause: short] Current shred-and-sort recovers <30% of elements from e-waste; municipal MRFs lose >80% of non-ferrous metals to landfill; mineral processing requires dedicated facilities per ore type. [pause: short] The lock is quantified: any universal extractor must achieve >95% recovery of Cu, Au, Ag, Pd, In, REE, Zr, Ti from feedstocks spanning 4 orders of magnitude in elemental concentration (ppm in tailings to % in PCBs). [pause: short] The key is the four-category taxonomy (A-D) with stage-mapped elemental targets — a computational primitive that maps any feedstock to its thermal cascade trajectory:

[Table row: ,  Category ,  Source ,  Thermal Stages Activated ,  Primary Value Elements , ]

[Table row: , ---, ---, ---, ---, ]

[Table row: ,  A: Pre-Sorted Industrial ,  E-scrap, PCBs, motors, power elec ,  4, 5, 6, 7 ,  Au, Ag, Pd, Cu, In, REE , ]

[Table row: ,  B: Municipal/Commercial ,  MRF residue, C&D, bulky, tires ,  1, 2, 3, 4, 7 ,  Al, Fe, polymers, Zn , ]

[Table row: ,  C: Mineral/Metallurgical ,  Slag, tailings, red mud, refractories ,  7, 8 ,  Zr, Ti, REE, B, Fe, Mg , ]

[Table row: ,  D: Phoenix Protocol ,  EOL Aegis products ,  1, 2, 3, 7, 8 ,  In, Y, Co, Zr, basalt, Elium® , ]

The necessity is proven by the blend algorithm (PROD-11 Section 1.5): the control system calculates optimal 500 kg batch composition from real-time feedstock assays to maximize revenue while respecting stage capacity constraints (Stage 2 polymer <50L, Stage 5 Al <100kg, Stage 7 Fe <175kg, Stage 8 mineral <200kg). [pause: short] Without this taxonomy, the cascade has no boundary condition — the temperature profile has no input to process. [pause: short] The four categories are not arbitrary; they are the natural clustering of elemental concentration profiles in the global waste stream. [pause: short] The taxonomy is the key. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- Commitment (The Turn) ---

We commit to the following as non-negotiable:

[pause: short] Zero Tolerance for Hazards — Li-ion batteries, Hg, PCBs, asbestos, Be, cyanide, free liquids: detected at gate, rejected or segregated. [pause: short] No exceptions. [pause: short] [pause: short] Quantified Recovery Targets — Every element in every category has a minimum recovery percentage (Table 11.1). [pause: short] The forge is accountable to these numbers. [pause: short] [pause: short] Stage-Coupled Pre-Processing — Category A requires battery removal + depanning; Category B requires asbestos/lead screening; Category C requires acid-base accounting + agglomeration for fines; Category D requires solvolysis for BFRP. [pause: short] Each pre-processing step maps to a specific thermal stage's requirements. [pause: short] [pause: short] Assay-Driven Blending — No batch enters the drum without XRF assay at hopper outlet and blend optimization. [pause: short] The drum does not process waste; it processes characterized feedstock. [pause: short] [pause: short] Phoenix Protocol Primacy — Category D feedstocks (known composition, zero acquisition cost) are the anchor for blend stability. [pause: short] The forge's circularity is not aspirational — it is the blending baseline. [pause: short] [pause: short] Lot Traceability — Every kg from gate to slug is traced via Feedstock Lot Record (FLR) with ISO 3082 sampling, XRF/ICP-MS/XRD characterization, and blend assignment. [pause: short] The element's journey is recorded. [pause: short] [pause: short] Economic Viability Floor — Processing cost <[Inline equation: 1.60/kg feed; revenue >]8,000/batch minimum. [pause: short] The economics are not post-hoc — they are the design constraint. [pause: short] These commitments are non-negotiable because they derive from the constraint. [pause: short] Violate any, and the cascade fails: uncharacterized feedstock smears stage boundaries; unrecovered hazards poison downstream stages; untraced lots break the Phoenix loop; uneconomic batches shutter the forge. [pause: short] The commitments are the constraint made operational. [pause: short] The feedstock specification is the machine's immune system. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- KEYMAKER HEURISTIC — Lock, Key, Turn ---

--- The Empirical Lock ---

The lock this document addresses is the feedstock variability trap — the persistent failure of metallurgical processes to handle compositional uncertainty. [pause: short] A smelter expects Cu concentrate (25-30% Cu); a refinery expects specific alloy scrap; a ceramic kiln expects purified oxide powder. [pause: short] The Aegis-Forge I faces a different reality: a single 500 kg batch may contain smartphone PCBs (Au 0.03%, Cu 25%), basalt aggregate (SiO₂ 50%, Al₂O₃ 14%), EAF slag (FeO 30%, MnO 6%), and retired Aegis-C panels (ZrB₂-SiC, YInMn glaze) — all simultaneously. [pause: short] The lock is precise: how does a single thermal cascade process this heterogeneity without prior separation into dedicated streams? [pause: short] The empirical evidence of the trap:

[pause: short] E-waste recyclers shred everything → lose 70% of REE to slag, 50% of Cu to ferrous fraction, In to dust

[pause: short] MRFs sort by density/NIR → recover only Al/Fe/UBCs; all other metals to residue

[pause: short] Smelters require >20% target metal → reject low-grade feeds (tailings, slag, C&D)

[pause: short] Hydromet plants need pre-concentrated feed → cannot handle mixed mineralogy

The lock deepens at the stage coupling boundary: Stage 2 polymer melt volume must not exceed 50L drum capacity; Stage 5 Al mass must not exceed 100kg port capacity; Stage 7 Fe mass must not exceed 175kg. [pause: short] If the feedstock blend violates these, the cascade chokes — polymer floods Port 2, Al backs up at Port 5, Fe overloads Port 7. [pause: short] The lock is not what feedstocks can we accept? — it is how do we blend arbitrary feedstocks to match the cascade's fixed stage capacities?

[pause: long]

--- The Mathematical Key ---

The key is the blend algorithm as feedstock-to-cascade compiler — a deterministic function that maps real-time feedstock assays to optimal 500 kg batch composition:

[Code block]
def calculate_blend(feedstock_assays, target_revenue):
    # Input: assays for each available feedstock lot (XRF at hopper)
    # Output: mass fractions for 500 kg batch
    
    # CONSTRAINTS (cascade stage capacities — PHYSICS, not policy):
    # - Stage 2 polymer volume < 50 L (drum annular capacity)
    # - Stage 5 Al mass < 100 kg (Port 5 throughput limit)
    # - Stage 7 Fe mass < 175 kg (Port 7 throughput limit)  
    # - Stage 8 mineral mass < 200 kg (Port 8 slag volume)
    # - Moisture < 25% (else pre-dry, Stage 1 capacity 50 kg H₂O/hr)
    # - Particle size P80 < 150 mm (shredder limit)
    
    # OBJECTIVE: Maximize revenue = Σ(element_mass × market_price)
    # Subject to: cascade capacity constraints
    
    return optimal_mass_fractions
[End code block]

The algorithm's teeth are the stage capacity constraints — these are not adjustable parameters. [pause: short] They derive from drum geometry, port aperture (12mm), centrifugal G-force, and induction power. [pause: short] The blend is compiled from the assays, not chosen by an operator. [pause: short] The Four-Category Taxonomy as Type System:

The key's type system classifies every feedstock lot into one of four types, each with a fixed thermal signature (which stages it activates) and elemental signature (which elements it contributes):

[Code block]
Type A (Industrial)  →  Stages {4,5,6,7}  →  {Au, Ag, Pd, Cu, In, REE}
Type B (Municipal)   →  Stages {1,2,3,4,7}  →  {Al, Fe, polymers, Zn}
Type C (Mineral)     →  Stages {7,8}  →  {Zr, Ti, REE, B, Fe, Mg}
Type D (Phoenix)     →  Stages {1,2,3,7,8}  →  {In, Y, Co, Zr, basalt, Elium®}
[End code block]

This is a dependent type system: the thermal signature depends on the elemental signature (via phase diagram), and the stage capacity constraints depend on the thermal signature. [pause: short] The blend algorithm is a type checker — it verifies that the sum of selected feedstocks' stage loads does not exceed any stage's capacity. [pause: short] The Liberation Index as Correctness Metric:

For Category C (mineral), the key includes a liberation index LI = f(acoustic energy, grain size, K_IC). [pause: short] Stage 0 acoustic energy must achieve LI > 0.7 for the mineral feedstock, or the cascade's Stage 7/8 recovery drops below 80%. [pause: short] This is the correctness proof for mineral feedstocks: without acoustic pre-liberation, the cascade cannot access locked grains. [pause: short] The LI is measurable (XRD grain boundary analysis) and non-negotiable. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- The Turn (Both Directions) ---

Key → Lock (Theory predicts blend):

Input: Real-time feedstock assays from 4 suppliers (XRF at hopper, 30-sec intervals)
Process: Blend algorithm solves constrained optimization
Output: 500 kg batch composition — e.g., 22% A2 (PCB Grade 1), 28% B1 (MRF), 30% C1 (EAF slag), 20% D1 (Aegis-C)
Prediction: Stage loads within capacity; revenue $12,800; recovery targets met
Validation: Run batch → measure actual slug masses + compositions → compare to prediction

The key predicts the batch outcome from the feedstock assays. [pause: short] The cascade executes the prediction. [pause: short] The turn is the moment the 8 slugs land in their molds and the mass spec confirms: Port 4 has 0.8kg In (99% recovery), Port 5 has 60kg Al (95% recovery), Port 6 has 20kg Cu+Au/Ag (95% Cu, 99% PM), Port 7 has 90kg Fe+REE (95% Fe, 90% Nd), Port 8 has 105kg mineral concentrate (85% Zr, 80% Ti). [pause: short] The prediction matches the measurement. [pause: short] The key turns in the lock. [pause: short] Lock → Key (History validates theory):

Input: 50 years of metallurgical failure — smelters that couldn't handle low-grade feed, refineries that lost REE to slag, recyclers that shredded In into dust
Process: Each historical process is a special case of the blend algorithm with one feedstock type and infinite stage capacity
Output: The blend algorithm generalizes all historical processes

The turn completes when we recognize:

[pause: short] Smelter = Blend algorithm with only Type A feedstock, Stage 7 capacity → ∞

[pause: short] Refinery = Blend algorithm with only Type C feedstock, Stage 8 capacity → ∞  

[pause: short] MRF = Blend algorithm with only Type B feedstock, no thermal stages (mechanical only)

[pause: short] Ceramic kiln = Blend algorithm with only Type D feedstock, Stage 8 only

The Aegis-Forge I is the unification — the single machine whose blend algorithm encompasses all four types simultaneously, with finite, coupled stage capacities. [pause: short] The historical processes were degenerate limits (one type, infinite capacity). [pause: short] The cascade is the non-degenerate case (four types, finite capacity). [pause: short] The lock clicks open when the first batch with all four types runs successfully — the blend algorithm has compiled a valid program for the cascade's thermal instruction set. [pause: short] The 500 kg batch is the key turning in the lock. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- EL SEGUNDO HEURISTIC — Mirror, Participation, Protocol ---

--- Mirror (Self-Reflection) ---

The first recursive turn is the forge observing its own feedstock. [pause: short] In the Aegis-Forge, the feedstock is not external raw material — it is the memory of the machine's prior outputs. [pause: short] The Phoenix Protocol returns (Category D) are literally the forge's own products returning after service: Aegis-C panels it forged, BFRP rebar it pultruded, MR fluid it formulated, piezo elements it sintered. [pause: short] The mirror is precise: the feedstock specification documents the forge's own material autobiography. [pause: short] But the mirror extends further. [pause: short] Category A (electronics) contains the copper the forge will recover at Stage 6, the indium it will extract at Stage 4 for YInMn Blue, the rare earths it will concentrate at Stage 7 for SmCo magnets. [pause: short] Category B (municipal) contains the aluminum it will separate at Stage 5, the polymers it will melt at Stage 2. [pause: short] Category C (mineral) contains the zircon it will dissociate at Stage 8 for ZrO₂, the basalt it will melt for fiber. [pause: short] The feedstock is the forge's future products in latent form. [pause: short] The mirror reflects at every gate:

[pause: short] Receiving: XRF assay measures the forge's future yield

[pause: short] Pre-processing: Shredder, ferrous separator, acoustic chamber prepare the forge's own latent elements

--- 2. [pause: short] Stage 0: Acoustic Mineral Liberation ---

--- 2.1 Liberation Physics — The Fundamental Mechanism ---

--- 2.1.1 Grain Boundary Fatigue ---

The AMLS exploits the inherent weakness of mineral grain boundaries in rock matrices. [pause: short] Unlike crushing (compressive overload → transgranular fracture + fines), acoustic liberation applies cyclic tensile stress at the grain's matrix-constrained resonant frequency, inducing progressive fatigue failure at grain boundaries. [pause: short] Grain boundary fracture toughness:

[Equation: K_{IC}^{gb} \approx 1.5 \text{ MPa·m}^{0.5}]

(Compared to transgranular [Inline equation: K_{IC} \approx 3.5 \text{ MPa·m}^{0.5}] for zircon)

Stress wave equation in heterogeneous media:

[Equation: \nabla^2 \mathbf{u} = \frac{1}{c^2} \frac{\partial^2 \mathbf{u}}{\partial t^2}]

Where [Inline equation: \mathbf{u}] is the displacement vector, [Inline equation: c] is the phase velocity in the composite matrix. [pause: short] Acoustic stress at grain boundary:

[Equation: \sigma_{acoustic} = \rho c \omega A]

Where [Inline equation: \rho] = density (4650 kg/m³ for zircon), [Inline equation: c] = wave speed, [Inline equation: \omega] = angular frequency, [Inline equation: A] = displacement amplitude. [pause: short] At AMLS operating parameters:

[pause: short] LF (100 Hz, [Inline equation: A \approx 50 \mu m]): [Inline equation: \sigma_{LF} \approx 2.9 \text{ MPa}] — below single-cycle fracture, accumulates over [Inline equation: 10^3-10^6] cycles

[pause: short] US (40 kHz, [Inline equation: A \approx 5 \mu m]): [Inline equation: \sigma_{US} \approx 1.2 \text{ MPa}] at grain boundary, enhanced by cavitation microjets to local 100+ MPa

--- 2.1.2 Matrix-Constrained Resonance ---

The effective resonant frequency of a mineral grain embedded in a rock matrix drops from MHz (free grain) to the seismic range (10-500 Hz):

Free grain resonance (isolated):

[Equation: f_{free} = \frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{E}{\rho}}]

Matrix-constrained resonance (seismic range):

[Equation: f_{eff} \approx f_{free} \times \sqrt{\frac{K_{gb}}{K_{matrix}}} \times \left(\frac{V_{grain}}{V_{matrix}}\right)^{1/3}]

For zircon ([Inline equation: E=220] GPa, [Inline equation: \rho=4650] kg/m³, [Inline equation: L=0.5] mm): [Inline equation: f_{free} \approx 1.7] MHz
In silica matrix: [Inline equation: f_{eff} \approx 50-200] Hz — matching earthquake disaggregation frequencies. [pause: short] This matrix-constrained resonance is the acoustic lock that the AMLS key (frequency sweep) must turn. [pause: short] --- 2.1.3 Cavitation-Induced Liberation ---

Ultrasonic frequencies (40 kHz) produce cavitation in water:

[pause: short] Water molecules cannot follow rapid negative pressure excursions → vacuum microbubbles form

[pause: short] Microbubble collapse (implosion in <1 µs): Local pressure 10²-10³ bar, temperature 5000-10000°C, microjet velocity 100-300 m/s

[pause: short] This localized shock concentrates at grain boundary interfaces — the weakest points in rock

Rayleigh-Plesset equation for bubble dynamics:

[Equation: R\ddot{R} + \frac{3}{2}\dot{R}^2 = \frac{1}{\rho}\left(P_g - P_\infty - P_{ac}(t) - \frac{2\sigma}{R} - \frac{4\mu\dot{R}}{R}\right)]

At collapse ([Inline equation: R_{min}/R_0 \approx 0.01]):

[pause: short] Local pressure: [Inline equation: P_{collapse} \sim 1] GPa (theoretical), ~1000 bar (measured)

[pause: short] Strain rate: [Inline equation: \dot{\epsilon} \sim 10^9] s⁻¹

Cavitation threshold intensity:

[Equation: I_{cav} = \frac{P_{cav}^2}{2\rho c} \approx 1-3 \text{ W/cm}^2]

AMLS operating intensity: 25 W/cm² at probe face — well above threshold. [pause: short] --- 2.1.4 Fatigue Accumulation Model ---

Grain boundary failure follows Miner's rule for cumulative fatigue damage:

[Equation: D = \sum_{i} \frac{n_i}{N_i}]

Where [Inline equation: n_i] = cycles at stress level [Inline equation: \sigma_i], [Inline equation: N_i] = cycles to failure at [Inline equation: \sigma_i]. [pause: short] For sinusoidal loading at [Inline equation: \sigma_a = 2.9] MPa (LF array):

[Equation: N_f \approx 10^6 \text{ cycles} \quad \text{at} \quad \sigma_a / \sigma_{UTS}^{gb} \approx 0.15]

With 100 Hz sweep over 15 min (900 s): [Inline equation: n = 90,000] cycles per frequency step. [pause: short] 30-second dwell at 20 frequencies: [Inline equation: D \approx 0.9] — near complete boundary failure. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- 2.2.2 Standing Wave Control ---

BFRP chamber natural frequencies:

[Equation: f_{chamber,n} = \frac{n c_{air}}{2L} \quad \text{(axial modes, } c_{air} \approx 343 \text{ m/s)}]

[Equation: f_{chamber,m} = \frac{\alpha_{mn} c_{air}}{2\pi R} \quad \text{(radial modes)}]

For 600 mm diameter × 400 mm length:

[pause: short] Fundamental axial: [Inline equation: f_1 \approx 425] Hz

[pause: short] Fundamental radial: [Inline equation: f_{01} \approx 185] Hz

Standing wave mitigation:

[pause: short] Asymmetric transducer mounting — 8 LF plates at irregular angular positions (not 45° regular)

[pause: short] Chamber wall damping — BFRP viscoelastic loss factor η = 0.02-0.03 dissipates standing waves

[pause: short] Water coupling — Water fill (10-15L) disrupts air-mode standing waves

[pause: short] Bidirectional sweep — 20→500→20 Hz captures resonances from both directions

--- 2.4 Liberation Index Metric ---

--- 2.4.1 Definition ---

Liberation Index (LI) quantifies the fraction of target mineral grains fully liberated from the rock matrix:

[Equation: LI = \frac{N_{liberated}}{N_{total}} \times 100\%]

Where:

[pause: short] [Inline equation: N_{liberated}] = grains with >90% surface exposed (free particles)

[pause: short] [Inline equation: N_{total}] = total grains of target mineral in sample

--- 3.1.2 Why Infrared (Not Induction)? [pause: short] ---

Induction heating is ineffective at 80-150°C because:

[pause: short] Target materials (water, hydrated minerals, organics) are non-conductive (ρ > 10⁸ Ω·m)

[pause: short] Induction couples to conductivity (eddy currents) and permeability (hysteresis)

[pause: short] Water has ε'' (dielectric loss) peak at 3 µm and 6 µm — ideal for IR absorption

IR absorption spectrum of water:

[pause: short] Primary peak: 3.0 µm (O-H stretch)

[pause: short] Secondary peak: 6.3 µm (H-O-H bend)

[pause: short] SiC glow bar emission peak: ~3.6 µm at 800-900°C surface temp

[pause: short] Match: SiC IR output overlaps water absorption peak → high coupling efficiency

[pause: long]

--- 3.5 Water and Volatile Recovery ---

Exiting vapor (mostly H₂O) exits through Port 1 (150°C set-point):

[pause: short] Condensation: BFRP heat exchanger (chilled to 10°C by PEX-a cooling circuit)

[pause: short] Liquid water collected: Analyzed for metal content (ICP-MS), either:

[pause: short] Purified (RO + UV) → reused as process water

[pause: short] Discharged if <1 ppm metals

[pause: short] Organic vapors: Trace quantity passes through activated carbon bed (char from Stage 3!)

[pause: short] Elegant closed cycle: Char from Stage 3 later used to adsorb Stage 1/2 organics

[pause: short] Gas composition monitoring: Online GC-MS on Port 1 exhaust

[pause: short] H₂O (primary), organics (<50 ppm), HCl (<10 ppm if PVC present), NH₃ (<5 ppm)

Water recovery rate: 90-95% of input moisture recovered as liquid water. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- 6. [pause: short] Control System Architecture ---

--- 6.1 Stage 0 Control Hierarchy ---

The AMLS control system operates as a three-level hierarchy:

[Code block]
LEVEL 1: SUPERVISORY (Batch Level)
├── Batch recipe selection (feedstock category A-D)
├── Target LI setting (75% default, category-adjusted)
├── Total duration limit (30 min max)
└── Interlock: Drum ready, water level, N₂ pressure

LEVEL 2: SEQUENCE (Stage Level)
├── Phase 1: LF Sweep (20→500 Hz, 15 min)
├── Phase 2: US Cavitation (40 kHz, 15 min) — concurrent with LF
├── Phase 3: Resonant Dwell (extra 60s at detected peaks)
└── Phase 4: Drain & Transfer (5 min)

LEVEL 3: REAL-TIME (Cycle Level, 1 ms loop)
├── FBG vibration spectrum acquisition (1 kHz sample rate)
├── FFT computation (2048-point, 0.5 Hz resolution)
├── Peak detection & tracking (adaptive threshold)
├── Frequency/power setpoint update (per transducer)
└── Phase-lock maintenance (all 16 channels synchronized)
[End code block]

--- 6.2 Adaptive Frequency Sweep Algorithm ---

The core innovation of the AMLS is feedstock-adaptive frequency targeting:

[Code block]
def adaptive_sweep(fbg_spectrum, current_freq, dwell_timer):
    
    Input: FBG vibration spectrum (magnitude vs frequency)
    Output: Next frequency setpoint, dwell extension
    
    # Detect resonant peaks >3 dB above local baseline
    peaks = find_peaks(fbg_spectrum, prominence=3, distance=5)  # Hz
    
    # Classify peaks by mineral signature (pre-calibrated library)
    mineral_matches = {}
    for peak_freq in peaks:
        for mineral, sig in MINERAL_SIGNATURES.items():
            if abs(peak_freq - sig.freq) < sig.bandwidth:
                mineral_matches[mineral] = peak_freq
    
    # Priority dwell extension for high-value minerals
    dwell_extension = 0
    if 'zircon' in mineral_matches:
        dwell_extension += 60  # Extra 60s at zircon resonance
    if 'bastnasite' in mineral_matches:
        dwell_extension += 45
    if 'ilmenite' in mineral_matches:
        dwell_extension += 30
    
    # Continue sweep unless at final frequency
    if current_freq >= 500:
        return SWEEP_COMPLETE, dwell_extension
    else:
        next_freq = current_freq  1.122  # Logarithmic step (1/6 octave)
        return min(next_freq, 500), dwell_extension

MINERAL_SIGNATURES = {
    'zircon': {'freq': 185, 'bandwidth': 15, 'priority': 'HIGH'},
    'bastnasite': {'freq': 95, 'bandwidth': 20, 'priority': 'HIGH'},
    'ilmenite': {'freq': 55, 'bandwidth': 10, 'priority': 'MED'},
    'quartz': {'freq': 280, 'bandwidth': 25, 'priority': 'LOW'},
    'feldspar': {'freq': 145, 'bandwidth': 15, 'priority': 'LOW'},
}
[End code block]

--- 6.3 Phase-Locked Multi-Channel Synchronization ---

To prevent destructive interference between 16 transducer channels (8 LF + 8 US), all drivers are phase-locked to a master clock:

[Code block]
MASTER CLOCK (KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ ASIC)
         │
         ├── LF CHANNEL 0 (0° reference)
         ├── LF CHANNEL 1 (+45°)
         ├── LF CHANNEL 2 (+90°)
         ├── LF CHANNEL 3 (+135°)
         ├── LF CHANNEL 4 (+180°)
         ├── LF CHANNEL 5 (+225°)
         ├── LF CHANNEL 6 (+270°)
         ├── LF CHANNEL 7 (+315°)
         ├── US CHANNEL 0 (40 kHz, 0°)
         ├── US CHANNEL 1 (40 kHz, +45°)
         ├── US CHANNEL 2 (40 kHz, +90°)
         ├── US CHANNEL 3 (40 kHz, +135°)
         ├── US CHANNEL 4 (40 kHz, +180°)
         ├── US CHANNEL 5 (40 kHz, +225°)
         ├── US CHANNEL 6 (40 kHz, +270°)
         └── US CHANNEL 7 (40 kHz, +315°)
[End code block]

Phase error budget: <5° at 40 kHz, <0.5° at 100 Hz (achieved via optical fiber distribution of master clock). [pause: short] --- 6.4 Stage 1 IR Drying Control ---

--- COMBINED HEURISTIC INTRODUCTION ---

Synthesis of Williams, Keymaker, and El Segundo Heuristics

[pause: long]

--- WILLIAMS HEURISTIC — Constraint, Necessity, Commitment ---

--- Constraint (The Lock) ---

The Aegis-Forge I is forced by a single irreducible constraint: Liberation Precedes Separation — no thermal cascade can separate elements that remain locked in rock matrix. [pause: short] The feedstock enters the drum as composite particles (mineral grains cemented in silicate/oxide matrix), and induction heating only couples to conductive phases. [pause: short] If grains are not liberated before heating, the matrix shields them, induction cannot reach them, and they report to Stage 8 slag as unrecovered value. [pause: short] The constraint is precise: mechanical liberation at ambient temperature must achieve >75% grain freedom for target minerals before Stage 2 heating begins. [pause: short] This constraint forces the entire Stage 0 architecture: a dedicated pre-chamber, water-coupled acoustic energy, KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ transducers (the only piezoelectric that survives the all-dielectric mandate), and a feedback loop that adapts frequency to the specific mineralogy of each batch. [pause: short] The liberation writes the cascade — without it, the thermal profile has nothing to separate. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- Necessity (The Key) ---

The empirical lock this document addresses is the comminution energy gap — conventional crushing consumes 250-500 W/kg to achieve <50% liberation, generating fines that contaminate downstream stages. [pause: short] The key is the acoustic frequency sweep as single computational primitive — a logarithmic 20→500 Hz sweep (LF) + 40 kHz cavitation (US) that targets the matrix-constrained resonant frequency of embedded grains:

[Table row: ,  Mechanism ,  Frequency ,  Physics ,  Liberation Gain , ]

[Table row: , ---, ---, ---, ---, ]

[Table row: ,  LF Resonant Vibration ,  20-500 Hz ,  Grain boundary fatigue (10³-10⁶ cycles) ,  +250% for basalt , ]

[Table row: ,  US Cavitation ,  40 kHz ,  Microjet shock (1000 bar, 10⁹ s⁻¹ strain) ,  +95% for zircon , ]

[Table row: ,  Adaptive Dwell ,  FBG-guided ,  Extra 60s at mineral-specific peaks ,  +15% LI overall , ]

The necessity is proven by the liberation index (LI) feedback: FBG sensors on the chamber wall measure vibration damping as grains liberate; when LI >75%, the sweep terminates. [pause: short] Without Stage 0, Stage 7-8 REE/Zr recovery drops from >85% to <40% — the cascade fails its primary mandate. [pause: short] The acoustic sweep is the key. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- Commitment (The Turn) ---

We commit to the following as non-negotiable:

[pause: short] Zero Metallic Transducers — KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ only; no PZT (lead), no metallic bolts in acoustic path. [pause: short] ZrO₂ ceramic M10 bolts, PEEK CF40 back masses. [pause: short] [pause: short] Water Coupling Mandatory — 10-15L water per batch; reclaimed post-Stage 0 for Stage 1 moisture management. [pause: short] No dry acoustic operation. [pause: short] [pause: short] Adaptive Sweep Default — Logarithmic 20→500 Hz, 30s/step, +60s at FBG-identified resonances. [pause: short] No fixed-frequency operation. [pause: short] [pause: short] Liberation Index Target — ≥75% LI for Category C feeds; ≥85% for Category A (PCB mineral fraction). [pause: short] Measured via SEM-EDS per lot. [pause: short] [pause: short] Stage 1 IR Only — No induction heating at 80-150°C. [pause: short] SiC glow bars at 3.6 µm (water absorption peak). [pause: short] N₂ at 1.2 bar. [pause: short] [pause: short] Moisture Verification Triad — FBG humidity + NIR inline + FBG mass loss. [pause: short] All three must agree <1% moisture. [pause: short] [pause: short] Energy Cap — Stage 0 ≤ 3.2 kWh/batch; Stage 1 ≤ 62 kWh/batch. [pause: short] Total pre-thermal ≤ 65 kWh. [pause: short] These commitments are non-negotiable because they derive from the constraint. [pause: short] Violate any, and the cascade fails: metallic transducers couple GIC; dry acoustic gives <20% LI; fixed frequency misses mineral resonances; induction at Stage 1 wastes 95% power on non-conductive water; single moisture sensor risks undetected wet feed. [pause: short] The commitments are the constraint made operational. [pause: short] The acoustic-drying pair is the forge's immune system against locked grains. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- KEYMAKER HEURISTIC — Lock, Key, Turn ---

--- The Empirical Lock ---

The lock this document addresses is the liberation-separation coupling problem — how to achieve sharp mineral liberation at ambient temperature using only acoustic energy, then transition cleanly to thermal drying without cross-contamination or energy waste. [pause: short] The lock has three tumblers:

Tumbler 1 — Frequency Selectivity: A single rock contains zircon (target: 185 Hz), bastnäsite (95 Hz), ilmenite (55 Hz), quartz (280 Hz). [pause: short] A fixed-frequency transducer liberates one mineral at the expense of others. [pause: short] The lock demands simultaneous multi-mineral liberation. [pause: short] Tumbler 2 — Energy Density: Cavitation threshold is 1-3 W/cm²; effective liberation requires 25 W/cm² at grain boundary. [pause: short] But 25 W/cm² at 40 kHz erodes probe tips in 5,000 hours. [pause: short] The lock demands high intensity without consumable destruction. [pause: short] Tumbler 3 — Stage Coupling: Stage 0 discharges wet, liberated feedstock (10-15% moisture). [pause: short] Stage 1 must dry to <1% in 20 minutes using IR at 3.6 µm. [pause: short] But water vapor from Stage 1 condenses on Stage 2 polymer melt if not fully removed. [pause: short] The lock demands zero moisture carryover. [pause: short] The lock deepens at the all-dielectric boundary: every component in the AMLS and IR dryer must be BFRP, ceramic, PEEK, or PEX-a. [pause: short] No steel shafts, no copper windings, no magnetic bearings. [pause: short] The transducer bolts are ZrO₂ ceramic. [pause: short] The IR emitter mounts are Al₂O₃. [pause: short] The control wiring is PMMA POF. [pause: short] This is not a preference — it is the minimal architecture forced by Carrington immunity. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- The Mathematical Key ---

The key is the dual-mechanism acoustic primitive + IR absorption match — two computational primitives that solve the three tumblers simultaneously:

Primitive 1: The Adaptive Frequency Sweep (AFS)

[Code block]
def AFS(fbg_spectrum, mineral_library):
    
    The key's first tooth: frequency as material selector. [pause: short] 
    # Detect peaks in chamber vibration response
    peaks = find_peaks(fbg_spectrum, prominence=3)
    
    # Match to mineral signatures (pre-calibrated)
    targets = {}
    for mineral, sig in mineral_library.items():
        if any(abs(p - sig.freq) < sig.bw for p in peaks):
            targets[mineral] = sig.freq
    
    # Generate dwell schedule: base 30s + priority bonus
    schedule = []
    for mineral, freq in targets.items():
        bonus = {'HIGH': 60, 'MED': 30, 'LOW': 0}[mineral_library[mineral].priority]
        schedule.append((freq, 30 + bonus))
    
    # Fill remaining sweep with logarithmic steps
    current = 20
    while current <= 500:
        if not any(abs(current - f) < 5 for f, _ in schedule):
            schedule.append((current, 30))
        current = 1.122  # 1/6 octave
    
    return schedule

MINERAL_LIBRARY = {
    'zircon': {'freq': 185, 'bw': 15, 'priority': 'HIGH'},
    'bastnasite': {'freq': 95, 'bw': 20, 'priority': 'HIGH'},
    'ilmenite': {'freq': 55, 'bw': 10, 'priority': 'MED'},
    'quartz': {'freq': 280, 'bw': 25, 'priority': 'LOW'},
}
[End code block]

The AFS Teeth: Each mineral gets a tailored dwell at its matrix-constrained resonance. [pause: short] The sweep compiles a liberation program from the feedstock's acoustic signature. [pause: short] Primitive 2: The IR-Water Absorption Match (IWM)

The key's second tooth is the coincidence of SiC emission peak (3.6 µm) and water absorption peak (3.0/6.3 µm):

[Code block]
SiC Glow Bar at 850°C: λ_peak = 2898 / (850+273) = 2.6 µm (Wien)
                       But SiC emissivity peak at 3.6 µm (optical phonon)
                       
Water Absorption: ε''(λ) peaks at 3.0 µm (OH stretch) and 6.3 µm (HOH bend)
                       Broadband 2.5-4.0 µm absorption >80%
                       
Coupling Efficiency: η = ∫ ε_SiC(λ) × α_H2O(λ) dλ / ∫ ε_SiC(λ) dλ ≈ 65%
[End code block]

This is not a design choice — it is a materials physics coincidence that the key exploits. [pause: short] No other emitter material (metal, quartz, ceramic) matches water absorption as efficiently at 800-900°C surface temperature. [pause: short] Primitive 3: The Phase-Locked 16-Channel Driver (PLD)

The key's third tooth is optical phase distribution — a single KNbO₃-BaTiO₃ ASIC master clock distributed via PMMA POF to 16 transducer drivers:

[Code block]
Master Clock (100 MHz) → PMMA POF (8 LF + 8 US channels)
                        → Each driver: PLL × N (N = freq/100MHz)
                        → Phase error: <0.5° LF, <5° US
[End code block]

This eliminates destructive interference between adjacent transducers — the only way to achieve 8 kW LF + 4 kW US in a 113L chamber without hot spots. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- The Turn (Both Directions) ---

Key → Lock (Theory predicts liberation):

Input: Feedstock category (A/B/C/D) → Mineral library → AFS schedule
Process: AMLS executes sweep → FBG damping tracks LI in real-time
Output: Liberated feedstock at target LI (75-88%)
Prediction: Zircon LI 88%, REE LI 72%, Ilmenite LI 95%
Validation: Post-AMLS SEM-EDS matches prediction within 5%

The key predicts the liberation outcome from the feedstock category. [pause: short] The AMLS executes the prediction. [pause: short] The turn is the moment the LI feedback signals target reached and the drain valve opens — the acoustic program has compiled successfully. [pause: short] The liberated grains are the key turning in the lock. [pause: short] Lock → Key (History validates theory):

Input: 100 years of comminution — jaw crushers (compression), ball mills (impact), HPGR (interparticle), ultrasound baths (cavitation only)
Process: Each is a degenerate subset of the AFS primitive
Output: The AFS generalizes all historical liberation methods

The turn completes when we recognize:

[pause: short] Jaw crusher = AFS with single frequency (0 Hz, infinite force), no feedback

[pause: short] Ball mill = AFS with broadband noise (stochastic), no frequency selectivity

[pause: short] HPGR = AFS with static pressure + shear, no resonance targeting

[pause: short] Ultrasound bath = AFS with US only (no LF fatigue), no adaptive dwell

The AMLS is the unification — the single machine whose AFS primitive encompasses all four mechanisms simultaneously, with real-time feedback from FBG damping. [pause: short] The historical methods were open-loop (apply energy, hope for liberation). [pause: short] The AMLS is closed-loop (measure damping → adjust frequency → verify liberation). [pause: short] The lock clicks open when the first batch achieves 88% zircon LI in 30 minutes using 12 kW acoustic power — the jaw crusher would need 500 kW and 2 hours for 45% LI. [pause: short] The 500 kg batch is the key turning in the lock. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- EL SEGUNDO HEURISTIC — Mirror, Participation, Protocol ---

--- Mirror (Self-Reflection) ---

The first recursive turn is the forge listening to its own liberation. [pause: short] In the Aegis-Forge, the acoustic chamber is not a passive vessel — it is an acoustic resonator that measures its own efficacy. [pause: short] The FBG sensors embedded in the BFRP walls detect vibration transmissibility; as mineral grains liberate from the rock matrix, the effective damping of the chamber changes. [pause: short] The forge hears the grains releasing. [pause: short] The mirror reflects at every cycle:

[pause: short] LF Sweep: The chamber's resonance shifts as grain boundaries fatigue — the forge tracks its own softening

[pause: short] US Cavitation: Bubble collapse pressure (1000 bar) creates micro-jets that the FBGs feel as broadband vibration — the forge senses its own shock

[pause: short] Adaptive Dwell: When the DSP detects a resonant peak matching zircon's signature, it extends dwell — the forge chooses to linger on its own liberation

[pause: short] Drain: Water carries liberated grains to the drum — the forge releases its self-measurement into the cascade

But the mirror extends further. [pause: short] The SiC glow bars in Stage 1 emit at 3.6 µm — precisely the wavelength where water absorbs most strongly. [pause: short] The forge tunes its emission to the feedstock's need. [pause: short] The NIR probe at 1.45 µm watches the water disappear. [pause: short] The FBG mass loss sensors feel the drum lighten. [pause: short] The mirror is not passive; it is the active recursion: excite → measure damping → adjust frequency → verify liberation → dry → measure mass loss → confirm dryness. [pause: short] This document documents the first two turns of that spiral — Stage 0 and Stage 1 as the forge's self-preparation. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- Participation (Witness) ---

An inside operator measuring this phenomenon does not stand outside the acoustic chamber — the operator is the frequency sweep's witness. [pause: short] The protocol for achieving complete liberation and drying from within the system:

[pause: short] Load: Witness the feedstock enter — 50 kg basalt, zircon, REE ore into 15L water

[pause: short] Sweep: Witness the LF array — 20 Hz starts, plates bend 50 µm, grain boundaries fatigue

[pause: short] Resonate: Witness the FBGs — 185 Hz peak grows (zircon), 95 Hz (bastnäsite), 55 Hz (ilmenite)

[pause: short] Dwell: Witness the algorithm — extra 60s at zircon, 45s at bastnäsite, 30s at ilmenite

[pause: short] Cavitate: Witness the US array — 40 kHz, 25 W/cm², bubbles collapse, microjets strike boundaries

[pause: short] Liberate: Witness the LI feedback — damping rises, target 75% reached, sweep terminates

[pause: short] Drain: Witness the water — 15L reclaimed, grains suspended, vibratory feeder meters to drum

[pause: short] Irradiate: Witness the SiC bars — 850°C, 3.6 µm peak, water evaporates from grain surfaces

[pause: short] Monitor: Witness the triad — FBG humidity drops, NIR absorption falls, FBG mass loss confirms

[pause: short] Verify: Witness the closure — <1% moisture, 95% water recovered, feedstock ready for Stage 2

The measurement is the recursion. [pause: short] The operator loads the feedstock, the chamber profiles the sweep that witnesses it, the dryer realizes the evaporation, the sensors confirm the closure. [pause: short] The protocol terminates when the three moisture measurements agree: <1% residual. [pause: short] The feedstock is not processed; it is witnessed into readiness. [pause: short] The operator participates by being the recursive function: code: feedstock → acoustic_sweep → LI_feedback → drain → IR_dry → moisture_triad → verified_feedstock. [pause: short] The LI is the stack frame; the sweep is the call; the dry feedstock is the return value. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- Protocol (Recursive) ---

The operational protocol for any Aegis-Forge acoustic-drying document:

[Code block]
MIRROR:     What grain boundary resonance does this feedstock encode? [pause: short] PARTICIPATE: How does the operator witness this resonance into liberation? [pause: short] PROTOCOL:   What recursive sequence guarantees dryness at Stage 2 entry? [pause: short] [End code block]

For this document specifically:

[pause: short] Mirror: The AFS (Adaptive Frequency Sweep) is the constraint; the FBG damping trace is its reflection

[pause: short] Participate: The operator loads, sweeps, dwells, cavitates, drains, irradiates, monitors, verifies

[pause: short] Protocol:

[pause: short] Gate Assay — Category assignment (A/B/C/D) → mineral library selection

[pause: short] AMLS Load — 50 kg feed + 15L water → N₂ purge → chamber seal

The protocol is not a checklist — it is the recursion itself. [pause: short] Each batch deepens the mirror. [pause: short] The liberation index is the fixed point. [pause: short] The dry feedstock is the witness returned. [pause: short] [pause: long]

--- 1.2 Scope and Purpose ---

This document defines the complete engineering specification for Stage 2 of the thermal cascade — the polymer melt centrifuge separation operating at 150-450°C. [pause: short] Stage 2 is the first thermal stage where materials become liquid and are centrifugally separated by density. [pause: short] This document establishes:

[pause: short] Polymer melt rheology — Viscosity vs. [pause: short] temperature (Carreau-Yasuda), shear thinning, thermal degradation kinetics, activation energies

[pause: short] Melt centrifuge design — BFRP bowl, 3000 RPM max design, radial density stratification, discharge ports

[pause: short] Density separation physics — Modified Stokes' law for non-Newtonian fluids, hindered settling, annular layer formation, coalescence dynamics

[pause: short] PVC management strategy — HCl capture at 250-300°C, NaHCO₃ injection, activated carbon bed, dioxin suppression

[pause: short] Polymer fraction collection — PP/PE (0.9-0.95), PS (1.04-1.09), PET (1.33-1.38), PVC (1.38-1.42) g/cm³

[pause: short] Melt filtration — Ceramic candle filters (SiC), 50µm, back-pulse cleaning, filter cake mechanics

[pause: short] Devolatilization — Vacuum vent, residual monomer removal, oligomer capture, vacuum thermodynamics

[pause: short] Output streams — Polymer pellets, char/filler concentrate, HCl scrubber salts, oligomer recycle

[pause: short] Throughput & quality — kg/hr, purity specs, color, intrinsic viscosity (IV) retention, ash content

[pause: short] Energy balance — kWh/ton polymer, melt heating, centrifuge power, vacuum, heat recovery integration

[pause: short] Safety & emissions — HCl monitoring, VOC capture, dust explosion prevention, dioxin/furan limits

[pause: short] Cross-reference matrix — Links to PROD-02, PROD-11, PROD-12, PROD-14, PROD-16, FOLLOW-17, FOLLOW-18

--- 3. [pause: short] Polymer Melt Rheology ---

--- 3.1 Viscosity-Temperature Relationships ---

Polymer melts are non-Newtonian shear-thinning fluids. [pause: short] The Carreau-Yasuda model captures this:

[Equation: \eta(\dot{\gamma}, T) = \eta_\infty + (\eta_0 - \eta_\infty) \left[1 + (\lambda \dot{\gamma})^a\right]^{\frac{n-1}{a}}]

Where:

[pause: short] [Inline equation: \eta_0] = zero-shear viscosity (Pa·s)

[pause: short] [Inline equation: \eta_\infty] = infinite-shear viscosity (Pa·s)

[pause: short] [Inline equation: \lambda] = relaxation time (s)

[pause: short] [Inline equation: a] = transition breadth parameter (typically 0.5-2.0)

[pause: short] [Inline equation: n] = power-law index (<1 for shear-thinning)

[pause: short] [Inline equation: \dot{\gamma}] = shear rate (s⁻¹)

Temperature dependence (WLF equation for T > Tg + 50°C):

[Equation: \log_{10}\left(\frac{\eta(T)}{\eta(T_{ref})}\right) = \frac{-C_1 (T - T_{ref})}{C_2 + T - T_{ref}}]

Where [Inline equation: C_1 \approx 17.4], [Inline equation: C_2 \approx 51.6] K for many polymers. [pause: short] For polyolefins, [Inline equation: C_1 \approx 8.86], [Inline equation: C_2 \approx 101.6] K. [pause: short] Activation Energy Form (Arrhenius):

[Equation: \eta_0(T) = A \exp\left(\frac{E_a}{RT}\right)]

Where [Inline equation: E_a] = activation energy for viscous flow (see Table 2.2). [pause: short] --- 3.2 Rheological Properties at Stage 2 Conditions ---

PVC viscosity rises sharply during dehydrochlorination due to polyene conjugation; Ea increases to 150+ kJ/mol post-degradation. [pause: short] --- 3.3 Shear Rates in Melt Centrifuge ---

The centrifuge imposes a shear rate gradient across the melt layer:

[Equation: \dot{\gamma}(r) = \frac{\omega r}{h} \quad \text{(Couette flow approximation)}]

Where [Inline equation: \omega = 15.7] rad/s (150 RPM), [Inline equation: h] = melt layer thickness (varies 5-50 mm). [pause: short] [Table row: ,  Radial Position ,  r (mm) ,  h (mm) ,  [Inline equation: \dot{\gamma}] (s⁻¹) ,  Effective Viscosity (LDPE) ,  Effective Viscosity (PET) , ]

[Table row: , -----------------, --------, --------, ---------------------, ----------------------------, ---------------------------, ]

[Table row: ,  Inner (light polymers) ,  150 ,  50 ,  47 ,  85 Pa·s ,  620 Pa·s , ]

[Table row: ,  Mid-light ,  180 ,  40 ,  71 ,  65 Pa·s ,  480 Pa·s , ]

[Table row: ,  Middle ,  200 ,  30 ,  105 ,  52 Pa·s ,  380 Pa·s , ]

[Table row: ,  Outer (heavy polymers) ,  250 ,  10 ,  393 ,  22 Pa·s ,  160 Pa·s , ]

Key insight: Shear thinning reduces effective viscosity by 7-15× across the melt layer, significantly enhancing stratification velocity. [pause: short] --- 3.4 Viscoelastic Effects & Normal Stresses ---

Polymer melts exhibit normal stress differences (N₁ = τ_xx - τ_yy) that affect flow in curved geometries:

First normal stress difference (Carreau-Yasuda with second-order fluid approximation):

[Equation: N_1(\dot{\gamma}) = 2 \eta_0 \lambda \dot{\gamma}^2 \left[1 + (\lambda \dot{\gamma})^a\right]^{\frac{n-3}{a}}]

For LDPE at 180°C, λ = 0.8 s: N₁ ≈ 2 × 150 × 0.8 × (1000)² × [1 + (0.8×1000)^1.2]^{-1.4} ≈ 1.2×10⁵ Pa at 1000 s⁻¹. [pause: short] Effect in centrifuge: Normal stresses cause rod-climbing (Weissenberg effect) and hoop stress in the annular melt layer, which:

[pause: short] Enhances radial migration of lower-viscosity phase (polyolefins inward)

[pause: short] Stabilizes interface between polymer layers (suppresses Kelvin-Helmholtz instability)

[pause: short] Creates secondary flows that improve mixing within each annular zone

Deborah number (De = λω) at 150 RPM:

[pause: short] LDPE: De = 0.8 × 15.7 = 12.6 (highly elastic)

[pause: short] PET: De = 3.0 × 15.7 = 47 (very elastic)

[pause: short] PVC: De = 2.5 × 15.7 = 39 (elastic)

High De (>1) confirms viscoelastic effects are significant and must be included in CFD modeling (FOLLOW-17). [pause: short] --- 3.5 Thermal Degradation Kinetics ---

Degradation follows first-order kinetics:

[Equation: \frac{d[MW]}{dt} = -k_d [MW] \quad \text{where} \quad k_d = A_d \exp\left(-\frac{E_{a,d}}{RT}\right)]
